_comment_family: Syne ships as a family - an Extra, a Bold, a Semi Bold and a Regular
- and every one of those files carries 'Syne' as name ID 1, with the
cut in the subfamily. Asking for 'Syne' alone would let any of them
answer, and this face is used as a HIGHLIGHT: a Regular answering in
its place would put a picked word in the same weight as a hand it is
supposed to be interrupting.
So the full name (name ID 4) is what gets declared, the same way
gilroy-extrabold and the two Telegraf packs declare theirs. This file
spells it with a space and its PostScript name with a hyphen, and
both spellings are listed in `local` below rather than one of them
being tidied into the other.
Weight 700, which is the file's own usWeightClass and what the cut is
called. Asking for 800 here would invite a browser to synthesise a
weight on top of a face that already has its own.

The first is the PostScript name and is also what the installer

_comment_stack: Damage limitation, and the one thing it must not do is fall through
to the same face the block does. This face is a highlight: its whole
job is to be a visibly different hand from Brittany Signature on the
same line, and a stack that ended up at the same substitute would
leave a picked word identical to the words either side of it - a
failure that draws no attention to itself, which is the kind this app
has been bitten by before (see the note in marydale-bold.json).
That is why the two stacks are written as opposites and converge
nowhere: brittany-signature falls through Segoe Script and Brush
Script into `cursive`, and this one falls through Segoe UI and Arial
into `sans-serif`. Whatever a machine is missing, the picked word
stays the grotesque and the block stays the hand.
Impact and Arial Black are absent on purpose. Syne Bold is a display
grotesque, so they are at least the right genus - but they are far
heavier and much narrower than it is, and a highlight substituted by
something louder than the real one is a highlight that has changed
what the caption emphasises rather than merely how.

_comment_family: Garamond Premier Pro is an optical-size family: the same design drawn
four times over for four sizes - Caption, the text cut, Subhead and
Display - and then crossed with the weights and the italics. This file
is one cell of that grid, the Bold Italic of the Subhead optical size,
and which cell it is has to be said out loud twice over.
Its name ID 1 is 'Garamond Premr Pro Subh' - Adobe's own abbreviation,
and the name every weight and both slopes of the Subhead size carry.
Its typographic family, name ID 16, is 'Garamond Premier Pro', which
all four optical sizes carry as well. Either of those, declared here,
would be a name several files can answer to, and on a family drawn per
size the wrong answer is not a variation on the design: a Caption cut
is drawn with sturdier hairlines and wider spacing for small sizes and
a Display cut with fine ones for large, so a caption measured against
this file and set from another would be a different colour of type at
a width nothing measured.
So the full name (name ID 4) is what gets declared, exactly as the two
Telegraf packs and american-typewriter-itc-pro-bold declare theirs,
and it is the longest name in this folder because it is the shortest
one that names this file and no other.
Weight 700, which is the file's own usWeightClass and what the cut is
called. The file's macStyle says bold AND italic, which is the second
half of the story and is dealt with below.
Registered at style normal on purpose, the same way open-sans-italic,
hanken-grotesk-italic and rift are. The slant is drawn into the
letterforms - this is a true italic with its own single-storey a, its
own descenders and its own fitting, not a slanted roman - and the
canvas asks for normal. Declaring the FACE italic here as well would
leave the canvas either missing it or being handed a synthetic oblique
of something else. Normal means 'this file, as drawn'.

_comment_metrics: Two measurements, both of them for the pack that is set in this face
(content/channels/buzzer-beater-de) and neither of them read by
anything at run time. They are here because the next face dropped
into a Snapchat channel will want the same two taken, and korolev-bold
started the habit.
The cap height is the file's own sCapHeight. The widths were taken on
a canvas at the size the pack is set at, which is the measurement that
matters rather than a sum of advance widths: the renderer measures the
same way, so the numbers below have the kerning in them.
Capitals are 660 units of a 1000-unit em, so at the Snapchat preset's
stated 40px they stand 26.4px tall.
It is a WIDE face for its era, which is the surprise. Twenty mixed
capitals (A to T) come out 499px against the 486px a Snapchat line
has - Korolev Bold's come out 434 - so unlike every other pack under
that heading, the width and the preset's twenty-character ceiling land
in the same place here rather than the characters binding first
comfortably. Ordinary prose still fits: nineteen characters of real
sentence measure 433px, because the spaces and the narrow letters that
an alphabet run has none of do most of the work. What it means in
practice is that a line of unusually wide capitals breaks at nineteen
instead of twenty, which the wrapper does on its own and nobody sees
(see the two ceilings in js/caption.js).
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice - a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken, not merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. They are still chosen rather than copied, and here they must be
chosen against the grain of this folder: most of the faces here fall
back through Impact and Arial Black because most of them are heavy
display grotesques, and this is an old-style serif italic. Falling
back to Impact would make the one thing that survives a missing file
the furthest possible thing from it.
So, the nearest garaldes a Windows machine may have: Adobe Garamond
Pro where a design machine carries one, Monotype's Garamond where
Office put one there, and Georgia - which is on every Windows there
is and is at least a serif with bracketed serifs on it - before the
generic. All of them come out upright, because the face is registered
at style normal and there is nothing left to slant it. That is a
caption in the wrong face either way; this only decides what a broken
install looks like.

_comment_family: The family name here is one this app invents. The file is a VARIABLE
font: it calls itself 'Scale VF' and carries a whole family along two
axes, from ExtraCondensed ExtraLight to SuperExtended Black. Asked for
by its own name it hands back its default instance — the Regular at
normal width — which is not the cut anything is designed in.
Registering it under the name of the instance we want, pinned to that
instance by the descriptors below, is what makes 'Scale VF Condensed
Bold' a face the canvas can simply ask for. A second channel wanting a
different cut of the same file declares its own pack the same way;
they are separate faces to the browser and do not collide.
_comment_pinning: wght 700 and wdth 75 — the file's own 'Condensed Bold' instance.
A single-valued descriptor is a clamp, not a filter: whatever weight or
width the canvas asks for is pulled into the range declared here, and
with the range one value wide the face can only be drawn at that
instance. `stretch` is what does the work — canvas takes no
font-stretch, so 75% could not be asked for at the point of drawing
even if we wanted to. `variationSettings` states the same instance
straight to the axes, so the cut survives a browser whose font matching
ever stops clamping. Measured here: 920.5px for the probe string
against 846.2 at wght 400 and 1182.9 at wdth 100, so both axes land.
_comment_css: Not declared in styles.css: this face arrived with a channel and is
registered from this JSON, which is the route content/README.md
describes. It also has to be — the pinning above lives in the FontFace
descriptors, and there is no stylesheet rule for it to inherit.
_comment_local: Deliberately empty. A local() source resolves by NAME, and no font
installed on any machine is called 'Scale VF Condensed Bold' — the
name only exists because of the registration above. Anything Windows
handed back under a name close to it would be some other cut of the
family at best, so the file is the only route, and a missing file is
reported as missing rather than quietly replaced.
scale-condensed-bold.stack: 'Scale VF Condensed Bold', Impact, 'Arial Black', sans-serif

_comment_family: The family name straight out of the file's name table (ID 1), and in
this file it is also the full name (ID 4) and the PostScript name (ID
6) - all three are the single word. It is safe to ask for by family
alone for League Spartan's reason: the app carries one cut of it, so
there is no second weight sharing the name for a request to land on by
accident.
There is a second question here that no other pack in this folder has
to answer, and it is the one worth writing down. 'Helvetica' is a name
the machine ITSELF has an opinion about: Windows carries a substitution
for it, mapping the name onto Arial for anything that asks, and a
handful of machines have a real Helvetica installed by some other
program. Raleway had the same shape of problem and solved it by
declaring a distinct name, because there the collision was a different
typeface wearing the same word.
This one does not need that, and the reason is a measurement rather
than a hope. Arial was drawn to Helvetica's widths, and this file's are
Arial's to the unit - space 569, A and B and E and S 1366, M 1706, W
1933, a and e and o 1139, i 455, all at 2048 to the em. So every rung
of the ladder below lands on the same advances: the bundled file, a
Helvetica the machine already had, and the Arial that Windows hands
back for the name. This is the one face here whose fallbacks cannot
change where a line breaks.
Registration is unaffected by any of it. A face added to document.fonts
wins over an installed font of the same name, so the file below is what
draws whenever it loads - which is every time it is there.
Weight 400, which is the file's own usWeightClass and what its
subfamily (ID 2) calls it. Asking for anything else would invite a
browser to synthesise a weight this file does not contain, and a
synthesised weight is measured as well as drawn - the caption would be
laid out against letters nobody chose.

laid out against the wrong metrics is broken rather than merely

_comment_family: Special Elite ships as a single style - one file, one cut, no
siblings in fonts/ and none at the foundry either - so name ID 1 is
both the family and the only thing that can answer to it. It is
declared as the file's own 'Special Elite' for garet-book's reason:
the honest name is the one the file states, and there is no second
weight here for a bare family name to be confused with.
That is the whole difference between this pack and the two Telegraf
ones, which declare a full name because two files in this folder
carry one family between them. Nothing of the kind is possible with
a family of one. The day a second cut of it appears this pack has to
be revisited - which is the same day telegraf-ultralight's note
describes, arriving from the other direction.
Weight 400, which is the file's own usWeightClass. The face LOOKS
heavier than a 400 because its letters are struck rather than drawn
- ink spreads at the edges of every stem - and that is a property of
the outlines and not of the weight axis. Asking for 700 here would
invite a browser to synthesise a bold on top of a face that is
already carrying its own ink.
One thing to know before measuring anything against this file: its
OS/2 sCapHeight and sxHeight are wrong, by a consistent factor of
about 1.87 - the table says 713 units of cap where the 'H' actually
inks 1412. Nothing here reads them (the renderer measures an 'H'
through the canvas, see capBand in js/text.js), so it costs the app
nothing; it is written down because somebody checking this face's
size against its metrics table will otherwise be checking it against
a number the drawing does not use.

_comment_family: Anton asked for at 700 — a weight this family DOES NOT HAVE as a
file, which is the whole of what makes this pack unusual and the
reason it is this long. Read it before setting anything else in it.
Anton is a single-weight family by design. There is one cut, it is
the Regular in fonts/, and there is no bold of it to ship: a channel
asking to pick its words out in 'Anton Bold' cannot be handed a
second file the way hall-of-femme is handed Telegraf's 200 and 800.
So this face is the same file asked for by a heavier name, and the
browser makes up the difference.
The family is 'Anton' and not an alias, and that is what does the
work. The stylesheet declares 'Anton' at font-weight 400 (see
styles.css) and nothing else on the machine answers to the name, so a
canvas asking for `700 40px "Anton"` matches that one 400 face and
Blink emboldens its outlines itself. Synthetic bold, in other words,
requested deliberately and by the only route there is.
_comment_safety: Why that is not the failure fontguard exists to catch, and why it
would be one under almost any other circumstance.
The thing fontguard is guarding against is a block laid out against
one face's metrics and drawn in another's — a title composed against
numbers that describe a font nobody can see. Nothing of that kind
happens here, because there is only ever one file. The measurement
and the draw go through the same font string (see `styleFor` and
`textProps` in js/text.js), so whatever the browser does to the
outlines it does to both halves at once: the advances a row is
stacked and broken on come back from the same call that paints it.
One caveat, and it is worth a sentence rather than a footnote. An
emboldened glyph is the 400 stroked outward, so it can spill a
fraction of a pixel past the ink bounds measured for it — a box
padded to a picked word therefore sits a hair tighter than the same
box round a word in a real bold cut would. At 40px on a box padded by
about five that is under a pixel, and it is a box, not a line break.
What this face must NOT be asked to carry is a highlight that is
weight and nothing else. Anton is already a heavy condensed display
face; stroking it outward by a fraction of its own weight is a
refinement, not a step somebody reads from across a room. The one
channel set in it picks its words out in near-black on a yellow box
and the weight is the third thing that changes, not the first (see
conspiracy-central). A channel wanting weight to be the highlight
should reach for a family that has two real cuts, the way
hall-of-femme does.
fontguard keys its check by family, so this face and anton.json
share one answer rather than being verified separately. That is
correct here for the same reason all of the above is: they are one
file, and verifying 'Anton' verifies both of them.
_comment_css: Declared in styles.css, like anton.json beside it — and here that is
load-bearing rather than bookkeeping. Registering a second FontFace
under the family name 'Anton' at weight 700 is the one thing that
must not happen: the browser would then have an exact match at 700,
would stop emboldening, and would hand back the Regular's own
outlines. The 'bold' would come out pixel-identical to the block it
is meant to be picked out of, silently, with every measurement
agreeing.
`registerFace` in js/channels.js also skips a family that is already
present, so this is stated rather than relied upon — two answers to
one question, because the failure has no symptom to notice.
_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by. Unused while `css` is
true — the stylesheet's own declaration carries the same two local()
sources after the url() — and kept in step with anton.json so that
the two packs describing one file do not describe it differently.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice: a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken rather than merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. Impact and Arial Black behind it because Anton is a heavy
condensed display cut and those are the nearest things a Windows
machine is certain to have. The same stack as anton.json, for the
reason `local` above is the same list.

_comment_family: The one face in this folder whose file gets its own family name wrong,
and the reason this pack has to be read before the name is touched.
The four names in the file disagree: the family (name ID 1) says
'Mongoose Regular', the subfamily (ID 2) says 'Bold', the full name
(ID 4) says 'Mongoose Bold' and the PostScript name (ID 6) says
'Mongoose-Bold'. Only ID 1 is wrong, and it is wrong in the worst
direction: it names a cut this file is not, so a machine that went
looking by family would be told this is the Regular.
None of that reaches the app, because a pack-declared face is
registered with the browser under the name stated HERE, against the
url below (see registerFace in js/channels.js). The family in this
file is a label the app chooses for a file it already has, not a
question it asks the machine. 'Mongoose Bold' is therefore both true
and safe to declare, and it is what the rest of the pack is written
against.
Where the file's names DO matter is `local` below, which is the one
route that asks the machine for a face by name - and that list is
written out of ID 4 and ID 6 for exactly this reason. 'Mongoose' alone
is deliberately absent, the way 'Telegraf' is absent from the two
Telegraf packs: it is a family name with cuts under it, and a machine
with the Regular installed would answer with a face at half this
weight. 'Mongoose Regular' is absent for the stronger version of the
same reason - it is the name this file gives its family, and it names
the wrong cut.
Weight 700, which is the file's own usWeightClass, what the subfamily
calls it, and what the bold bit in fsSelection says.

_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by, tried after the file:
the Windows full name (ID 4) first, the PostScript name (ID 6) behind
it. Both name this one cut rather than the family it sits in - see the
note above, which is the whole of why this list is two names and not
three.
The first is also the name the installer registers the face under. It
copies each pack's font into the user's font folder and keys it by
local[0] (see engine.install_fonts), and Windows keys installed fonts
by their full name, so the installed copy lands under the same name
the local() source asks for.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice, and on
this face they are barely even that. Mongoose Bold is an ultra
condensed: its capitals average 0.300em - an O at 0.296, an M at 0.478
- which is under half the 0.620em of the New Order Medium it picks
words out of. Twenty capitals at the Snapchat preset's 40px come out
at 240px of a 486px line.
Nothing a Windows machine can be relied on to have is within reach of
that. The same twenty capitals measure: Impact 407px, Segoe UI Bold
526px, Arial Bold 550px, Arial Black 615px. The nearest of them is 70%
wider than the face, which is not a substitution anybody would ship -
it is the difference between a picked word that is half the width of
its neighbours and one that is wider than them.
So the order below is nearest-first among faces that exist, and it is
written knowing it cannot save the layout. What actually protects this
channel is fontguard, which verifies BOTH of a two-face channel's
faces before anything is measured and names the missing one in the
banner rather than drawing with a stand-in (see js/fontguard.js and
`highlight.face` in js/channels.js). This stack is what a browser
reaches for in the seconds before that check answers, and Impact is
the least wrong thing to reach for: a heavy condensed grotesque is at
least the same KIND of face, where the Segoe UI and Arial behind it
are only a promise that something will be drawn.
Arial Black is absent, as it is everywhere else in this folder. At
157% over it is not a fallback, it is a guarantee of overflow.

_comment_family: The Regular, and fitness-story-de's block face. Its picked words are
set in acumin-pro-bold — the same family's 700 — so the two are told
apart by weight alone.
Acumin is Adobe's neo-grotesque: an Akzidenz descendant drawn on the
same bones as Helvetica, with a large x-height and flat, closed
terminals. That lineage is the whole of why the fallbacks below are
what they are, and it is the reason a missing file here does less
visible damage than it does to the display faces in this folder —
which is not the same as doing none.
Declared as the bare family name, and this is the one pack in the
folder where that is the honest answer rather than a shortcut. The
two Acumin files share name ID 1 ('Acumin Pro') the way the two
Telegraf files share theirs, so by the rule telegraf-ultralight sets
out each should be declared under its full name instead — except
that this file's full name (ID 4) IS 'Acumin Pro'. A RIBBI family's
Regular has no name of its own to be declared under; the family name
is its full name, and inventing one would be declaring a face under
a name nothing on any machine answers to.
What keeps that from colliding with the Bold is the weight. This
face is registered at 400 and the Bold declares a different CSS
family entirely ('Acumin Pro Bold', its own ID 4), so the canvas
asking for `400 40px "Acumin Pro"` can only reach this file and
nothing asks for 'Acumin Pro' at 700 at all. The one place the
sharing still costs something is `local` below, which is where it is
dealt with.
Weight 400, which is what the file's OS/2 table says.

lives in GPOS: the two figures come out within half a pixel of each

decides anything - the face is simply wide.

hanken-grotesk-extrabolditalic names Segoe UI Black, which it does
only because 800 is past where Segoe UI's own family stops.
acumin-pro-bold.stack: 'Acumin Pro Bold', Arial, 'Segoe UI', Helvetica, sans-serif

_comment: The halo behind Karens Unleashed's type: the letters over again,
without their outline, blurred until they read as light rather than
as letters.
This replaces a Photoshop drop shadow that could not be reproduced —
canvas has no equivalent of its Spread or Contour, so the faithful
translation came out flatter and weaker than the original. Drawing the
glyphs a second time and blurring them is not an approximation of that
effect; it is the effect, built the way the reference thumbnails' own
ethereal glow is built.
`blur` is the gaussian radius. `layers` is how many times the blurred
copy is stacked — one pass at this alpha is barely there, and stacking
is how the halo gains body without turning into a hard edge.
`color` is the light itself, and it is white for every line INCLUDING
the highlighted one: the halo is what the type is lit by, not
something the type emits, so it does not change when a line changes
colour. (null instead makes each line glow in its own colour.)
The frame fetch every channel under the Snapchat heading runs.
Named rather than repeated per channel, and that is not tidiness. A
pack under this heading is made by copying the folder next to it and
changing the brand, and every key restated in each of them is a key a
new channel can silently be missing — which is exactly what happened:
channels arrived captioning their frames with the transcript as
spoken, because the copy they were made from predated `rewrite`. One
definition means a new channel inherits the whole of this by writing
one line, and means a change to it reaches every channel at once.
_comment_frames: Forty is where the slider OPENS, and one is as low as it goes.
The opening figure is the ask these channels exist for - a set to work
through - and it stays forty because that is what somebody who does
not touch the slider should get. The floor used to be forty as well,
on the argument that a set of five is not a set; that argument is
about the usual job and not about every job, and it cost the user the
one case the slider is quickest for, which is pulling a single frame
Two hundred is the upper end, which is a long video's worth at this
spacing and well inside what the up-front edit pass can get through.
The count is not only a number of pictures. The rewrite is told how
many stills it is writing for and produces that many captions, so
forty is an account in forty lines and two hundred is the same account
_comment_output: 540x960 is the vertical full-screen frame these are cut for. It is the
one number both halves of the app have to agree on, and they do not
each hold a copy of it: this is where it is stated, the backend is
told it in the framing the pack sends (see channels.framingFor), and
the frontend canvas is set from it (see config.setCanvasSize).
_comment_captions: What puts words back on a frame that was originally handed over bare.
The run transcribes the video's voice track and each still comes back
with the sentence that was being said at the moment it was cut from -
the frames already knew when they happened, so all it took was the
words knowing the same thing. See backend/transcriber.py.
A per-RUN decision and not a per-frame one: it decides whether the
_comment_rewrite: The transcript is not set as spoken. It is REWRITTEN before it is set:
the same words, on the same timeline, turned from speech into reported
information. See backend/narrator.py for what that means and for what
it refuses to do.
It exists because these videos are half narration and half interview,
and only the narration half already reads as information. An interview
is somebody talking about themselves to a reporter who is not on
screen, and a still captioned "I am Brian, Dolly's son" is a caption
of nobody - the viewer has no previous card to learn it from, because
every frame is read alone. Reported instead, the same two facts become
one line that stands up by itself.
It does not translate. The caption is the video's own words over the
video's own pictures, so a Portuguese interview reported in English
captions something nobody said - and that is the one failure here that
does not LOOK like one, since it reads perfectly. Asking for "the same
language as the transcript" was measured and failed on every line of a
Portuguese transcript and every line of a French one. The language is
NAMED instead, from what Whisper detected on its way to the words, and
a second check drops any line that still reads as English on a video
that was not.
One caption per thought, not per transcript sentence. A speaker
introducing themselves and then saying what they came to say is three
sentences and one piece of news, so the three are gathered into one
item before the model sees them. It is never asked WHERE a caption
should begin - offered a syntax for joining lines itself, it used it
zero times in sixty-three sentences, and zero times again when told
joining was the expected move.
The timeline is not the model's to move. It is handed numbered
sentences and asked for numbered text, and the seconds each one covers
are the ones the transcript already carried - so a rewrite can come
back worse, but it cannot come back describing a different moment of
the video.
Read once as the run starts, in the same breath as `captions`, the
frame count and the output size. It cannot be a per-frame answer for
the reason none of those can: it decides what the RUN produces, and by
the time there is a grid to look at, the words on it have already been
chosen.
It needs `captions` to mean anything, a rewrite of a transcription
nobody asked for being nothing at all. Set without it, the backend
ignores it - there is no transcript to rewrite.
Nothing about it is fatal, which is the rule every model in this app
is held to. A machine that has never fetched the weights, a generation
that comes back malformed, a line that comes back too long to set -
each of those leaves the frame the sentence as spoken. Plainer, not
wrong.
There is no channel under this heading that turns it off, and the two
that existed to be compared with and without it are gone. If one ever
wants the transcript as spoken it says so here, in its own pack, by
overriding this key - which is the shape every exception to a shared
guideline takes.

_comment: How a caption is SET under the Snapchat heading - everything about the
type that is the same on every channel there, which is everything
except the brand's own face and its colours.
It is one design and not five that happen to match. Each of these
numbers was arrived at by looking at the same thing (a sentence
somebody said, over a vertical still, read on a phone at arm's
length), so a change to one of them is meant to reach every channel
under the heading - and five copies drift the first time only one is
edited.
A pack states this and then states what makes it that show: the face,
the colour of the type, the colour of the card, and the palette the
user may swap between. Anything else it states is an EXCEPTION and
should say why - see `uppercase`, which one pack overrides.
_comment_uppercase: Capitals. At 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is
three short beats rather than a paragraph, and that is the length
capitals are for; it is also how burned-in speech is set everywhere it
is actually watched.
The old argument against it - that a whole spoken sentence in capitals
stops being read and starts being decoded - was about a caption set
small enough to need three or four long lines of it, which this is not
any more.
Applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so the text box still
holds what the user typed and the highlight buttons still offer the
words as the canvas will set them (see `cased` in js/text.js and
editor.renderWordButtons).
This is the guideline a pack is most likely to have a real reason to
break - a face whose lower case IS the brand. Killer Bites does, and
says so where it overrides it.
_comment_shadow: None. A drop shadow is what keeps type legible over a photograph
nobody chose the contrast of, and there is no photograph under these
letters - there is a solid card, in a colour the user picked, doing
that job completely. A shadow as well would only smear the inside of
the card.
The card casts one of its own - see `panel.shadow` below, which is
where the lift off the photograph actually comes from.
_comment_highlight: Word scope. A caption's line breaks are wherever the sentence happened
to run out of width, so picking a LINE out picks out a fragment rather
than a thought. The words are what carry meaning, and the one worth
picking out - a name, a number, the verb the clip turns on - sits in
the middle of a line as often as it fills one.
Colour mode rather than box, because there is nothing to box against:
the words are already on a solid ground of their own. What a pack
actually changes at a picked word is therefore the FACE, and the face
is the pack's to name (`highlight.face`) along with the colour it
keeps.
A row whose picked words are in another face is built out of runs,
each measured and drawn in its own face at the pen the runs before it
reached (see `runRows` in js/text.js). What that costs is the kerning
across a join, and every join is a space.
No shadow, and it has to be said HERE rather than left to the `shadow`
above. They are two different keys with two different defaults: the
block's is null because of the card, and a picked word's is the
skeleton's own soft halo (see `highlight.shadow` in BASE_TITLE_STYLE,
js/channels.js). So a pack that stated neither - which is most of them
- got a caption whose ordinary words cast nothing and whose picked
words cast a wide blurred shadow, which is the one difference between
them nobody asked for.
It is wrong here for the reason the block's shadow is: there is no
photograph under these letters, there is a solid card in a colour the
user picked. A shadow on the picked words alone puts them at a
different depth from the words either side of them on the same line,
on a ground whose whole job is to be flat.
And it makes the highlight legible by its own outline rather than by
the design. Set the type and the card to the same colour - which these
palettes allow on purpose, see `colors` on any pack under this heading
- and every ordinary word disappears into the card while the picked
ones stay readable, outlined in black. That is how this was found, and
it is the clearest statement of what the inherited shadow was doing:
drawing a word the design says is invisible.
Stated in this preset rather than changed in the skeleton, because the
skeleton's answer is right for what it is for - a filled box over a
photograph, which is what that shadow is drawn under everywhere else
in the app. What is wrong is inheriting it under THIS design, and this
design is exactly what the preset is.
A pack under this heading that drops the card overrides it, exactly as
it overrides `shadow` above and for the same reason: over a photograph
a picked word needs the same lift its neighbours have. Conspiracy
Central and Expulsion Science both do, and both state the block's own
numbers rather than a second set, so a picked word is lit like the
words around it.
_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on: one box per LINE, welded into one
continuous background.
`scope` line rather than block. A card drawn round the whole block
takes the width of its longest line, so every shorter line sits in a
rectangle with air on both sides of it; a box the width of its own
line is the shape the sentence actually has.
`joined` true. Left separate those boxes are a stack of tags with a
stripe of photograph between each pair, and that stripe is what the
eye reads first - three graphics rather than one caption in three
lines. Joined, they overlap into a single solid shape with one outline
and one shadow round the whole of it, still stepping in and out with
the sentence. See `panel.scope` and `panel.joined` in js/channels.js
for the three things scope changes besides the drawing.
Joining is also what brings the lines together without `lineGap`
having to say so: separate, that number is the gap between the BOXES,
so two lines sat a whole box-height apart. Joined it is the gap
between the lines, and the shipped 10px is a band of colour rather
than a hole in one.
Padding 12, not the 22 a card wants. 22 is the margin of a CARD, one
rectangle round a whole block of type, where the air at the edges is
what makes it read as a card and not as a highlighter. A box cut to
one line IS a highlighter, and a highlighter sits close to the
letters: at 22 the shape had more colour in it than words.
13px of corner radius. A square-cornered slab reads as a crop or a
letterbox, something the player did; a rounded one reads as a graphic
somebody made. Stated in pixels rather than as a fraction of the type,
so a four-word caption and a fourteen-word one are rounded
identically - see `radius` in js/channels.js.
No border, and the width is stated at zero rather than left out
because the renderer measures with it either way. Its colour is stated
for the same reason and is never drawn: at width 0 the outer rectangle
takes the card's own fill instead, which is what stops the two
rectangles blending into a pale rim along every rounded edge.
The shadow falls straight down and is soft. It is what lifts the card
off the photograph, and it has to survive being thrown by a white slab
onto a white wall, which is why it is half opaque and offset far
enough to be seen as a shadow rather than as a dirty edge.
`fill` is deliberately absent. It is the one thing about the card that
IS the brand, so every pack states its own.
_comment_movable: The card starts at the foot of the frame and the user moves it from
there. The bottom of a captured still is only where a caption usually
belongs: it lands over somebody's face often enough that being able to
drag it clear is part of the job, and a solid card covers more of the
picture than four lines of type do, so it needs the drag more than
they would, not less.

_comment: The block spans nearly the whole width and stands on a margin off
the bottom edge, which is what burned-in speech looks like on a
vertical video.
`fontSize` is the whole of how big a caption comes out, and it is
stated rather than solved for. These channels used to fit each
line to the width at its own size, which made the type as large as
the frame would allow and made it a different size on every still:
a six-word sentence came back set huge and an eighteen-word one
small, so a grid of forty frames cut from one video was forty
different type sizes. Burned-in speech is one size, always. 40px
on a 540-wide frame is that size - read at arm's length on a phone,
which is the only place these are ever seen - and a longer sentence
takes more lines instead of smaller letters. See `fontSize` in
js/channels.js for what else follows from stating it.
`uniformSize` is absent with it. It decided whether the lines
shared one fitted size or each took its own, and there is no fit
left to decide anything about.
`maxChars` is the second ceiling on where the lines break, and it
is a different question from the width: the width asks what the
frame holds, this asks what a viewer reads at a glance. Twenty
characters is a caption line. Four of them is eighty, which is
exactly the length one rewritten caption is written to (see
transcriber.CAPTION_CHARS) - the two numbers agree on purpose, so
one screen of the account fills one card.
`lineGap` is absent, so the lines are spaced by the renderer's own
10px. It was 6 for years and 3 for an afternoon, and neither
number was ever measured against anything; a pack with no reason of
its own should not carry a copy of a number it agrees with.
`freeform` on, and four lines, because a caption is a sentence
rather than three typed beats - nobody writing one can say where it
should break, so it arrives already broken (see js/caption.js) into
one text box the user rewraps by hand. Four is a count of SLOTS and
a freeform channel has none, so it does nothing here.
bottomRatio is 120px off the foot of a 960-tall frame, written as
the fraction every layout number here is written as. It is the
margin the BACKGROUND stands on and not a position: a caption that
gains a line grows upward off it, so the distance from the bottom
edge is the same on every still whatever was said over it. 120 and
not 30, because 30 was measured against the frame and not against a
phone - a vertical video is watched inside a player with its own
furniture along the bottom edge.
maxBlockHeightRatio no longer decides the caption's size, and no
longer pulls a block in either: a size the renderer may shrink is
not a stated size. It is left at 0.30 as the figure this look was
built around - roughly what a caption at this size and four lines
long occupies once the card's padding is taken out of it (see
BLOCK_BUDGET in js/text.js), and about as much of the picture as
words may cover before the still stops being the thing on screen.
How a Snapchat run CHOOSES and crops its frames, shared by every
channel under the heading because none of them has a reason to differ.
The frames are not composed around anybody. Most of them have no face
in them at all, and the ones that do are not being cropped to put a
person beside a title - the picture is the product, so it is fitted to
the canvas centred and left alone.
min_text_space is zero because it asks how much room is clear BESIDE
the subject for a title to go in, and these titles do not go beside
anybody: the caption lies across the foot of the picture on a card of
its own. No frame should be rejected for failing to leave a column
nothing is ever set in.
Named rather than repeated for the reason snapchat-capture is: a pack
under this heading is made by copying its neighbour, and every key
restated in each of them is a key a new channel can be missing.
The black slab a title is set on, shared by the channels that use one.
Named rather than repeated per channel because it is one design, not
two that happen to match — a change to the border or the shadow is
meant to reach both, and two copies would drift the first time only
one was edited.
The shadow falls straight down, with no sideways offset, because the
panel sits hard against one side of the frame: with the block on the
right, a shadow offset to the right ran off the canvas and was clipped
along its whole edge — the slab stopped reading as lifted on exactly
the side you look at first. Straight down is the one direction that
survives the block being on either side.

channels.name: Beauty Hacks
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Proxima Nova Bold with picked words in Proxima Nova Black, on a
magenta card, in four colours offered for the type and the same four
for the card.
It is not a second skin for Beauty-Tipps, which sorts next to it and
shares half a word with it. That show has no card at all: Syne
Regular with picked words in Bebas Neue, one deep violet, a white
halo, set straight onto the photograph. This one was cut from Hall of
Femme on the instruction that it follow that pack, so it keeps the
card, keeps the palette and keeps the two-face highlight. Two shows
about the same subject are not two colourways of one pack, and a
change to either is not a change to the other.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the pack it was cut from, which is
in the type and in the colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme sets
its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline for the block, the
800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card, in sixteen pairings the
user chooses between. This one is set in Proxima Nova, Bold for the
block and Black for a picked word, on a magenta card, in sixteen
pairings of a white, a black and two magentas.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, the shape of the card, its padding and corners and
shadow, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show, which is the whole of what a pack under this
heading should be.
The type here is heavy where Hall of Femme's is thin, and that quietly
removes the risk its note spends a paragraph on. A 200-weight face
needs the card or it disappears on a blown-out sky; a 700 would
survive without one. The card is kept anyway, and for a better reason
than inheritance: it is the magenta, and the magenta is the brand. On
this show the card is the shape that is a fifth of the frame and reads
before anything on it, so it is what carries the colour, and the type
is what has to stay legible against it.

_comment_face: Proxima Nova Bold. Which cut that is, why the full name rather
than 'Proxima Nova' is declared, and what the machine may already
know it by are written out in
content/faces/proxima-nova-bold.json rather than repeated here.
The Bold and not the Black - the lighter of the two cuts this
pack carries - and the choice is made HERE rather than in the
highlight below: whichever cut the block takes, a picked word has
the other one, and an emphasis goes heavier than what surrounds
it - the way every other pack under this heading goes heavier.
Setting the block in the heaviest cut there is leaves the emphasis
nowhere to go but down, which is what this pack used to do and
what `_comment_highlight` below records.
Capitals come from the preset and cost this face nothing: it is a
geometric grotesque whose capitals are what it is usually seen in,
and the two cuts share a cap height, so at the preset's 40px they
stand 26.7px tall - within a tenth of a pixel of the Telegraf the
design was measured on, so a caption here occupies the same band
of frame as one on the pack next door.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the four in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is
found by matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the magenta card is the pairing this show opens
on, and it is the pairing to open on rather than merely the first
one written down. White on #FF00F0 is 3.2 to 1, which is thin for
type in general and sound for this type in particular - a
700-weight grotesque set at 40px, which is the case the 3:1
large-text threshold exists to describe. Black on the same card is
6.5 to 1 and is a button away for anyone who wants it.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does and for their reason: the point
is the PAIRING. Sixteen combinations of a white, a black, a
magenta and a violet-magenta, and the ones worth having are the
ones that read. A palette that could only ever be used one way
round would be a palette of four cards, and this show's look is
the pairing rather than any one of them.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the two
neutrals, then the two brand colours - and the two defaults are
picked out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens
on the first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom
Hall of Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one
order.
Nothing stops the user setting #FF00F0 on #BB15D9, and that is the
one pairing in this palette worth knowing about before somebody
reports it: at 1.5 to 1 the two magentas are near enough the same
value that a caption in one on a card of the other is a caption
nobody can read. It is left available all the same, for the reason
the packs either side give about white on white - the two lists
are independent because the pairing is the feature, and a rule
barring the combinations that fail would cost the panel more
explaining than an invisible caption costs a user who can see it
is invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Proxima Nova Black, in the same colour as
the rest of the block. The highlight here is WEIGHT, which is Hall
of Femme's highlight exactly - one family's cuts on one card, so
the card stays one clean shape instead of a shape with a second
shape inside it - with one difference from it that is worth
stating plainly.
The pair used to be the other way round: the block in the Black
and a picked word stepping DOWN to the Bold, on the argument that
what the eye catches is the change of weight and not its
direction. That was asked for and then asked back, and the reason
is the one the argument left out - a step down makes the picked
word the thinnest thing on the card rather than the thickest,
which is an odd place for the word that was worth picking out, and
it is backwards from every other pack under this heading. It
climbs now, 700 to 900, the way Hall of Femme climbs 200 to 800.
The step is a short one whichever way it runs. 700 against 900 of
one family is two adjacent weights, where 200 against 800 is the
family's two ends: THE VERDICT WAS GUILTY measures 495px in the
Bold and 511px in the Black at 40px, 3.2% apart, against the 11.4%
Telegraf's two cuts put between the same string. So a picked word
here changes the colour of the stroke and almost nothing about the
shape of the line. It is a quieter highlight than the pack this was
cut from, and on a short caption read at arm's length it is close
to the quietest a highlight can be and still be one. Two faces were
named and these are the two; if it ever wants to be louder, the
honest fix is a third cut of the family rather than a box - see the
preset, where the argument for a recolour over a box lives.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
Both cuts have the same cap height, the same ascender and the same
descender, so the shared vertical band every box in the block takes
is the band the Bold alone would have asked for. A caption with
picked words in it is exactly as tall as one without.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are on
a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts the
one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Magenta, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are the
Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching this
value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be written in
the order the show states its colours in while the channel still
opens on white type and a magenta card.
#FF00F0 and not Hall of Femme's #FF008A. They are the same idea one
step apart on the wheel - that pink is a red-magenta and this is a
true one - and the step is what makes this a different show at a
glance rather than the same show in a slightly different pink.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.

channels.name: Beauty Studio
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Proxima Nova Bold with picked words in Proxima Nova Black, on a
violet-magenta card, in three colours offered for the type and the
same three for the card.
beauty-hacks is the second pack to read, because it is the one that
already made this move - Hall of Femme's design in Proxima Nova - and
everything about the two cuts of that family is argued out there with
the measurements. This pack differs from it in the card and in the

_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's
and comes from the same two presets rather than being restated here:
the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription, the
rewrite that turns speech into report, the stated 40px, the twenty
characters to a line, the freeform text box, the drag.

they are the three that were asked for: it is set in Syne Regular
with picked words in Bebas Neue, it is one colour throughout, and it
has no card. The last two reach further than they look - a caption on
the photograph instead of on a slab changes what has to hold it
legible, and a show with one colour has no palette to hand over - so
each is argued where it is stated.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand, hyphen and all.

the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has

_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the pack it was cut from. Hall of
Femme sets its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline for the
block, the 800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card, in sixteen
pairings the user chooses between. This one is set in Syne Regular,
with picked words in Bebas Neue, in one deep violet, on nothing at
all.
Dropping the card is the decision the other two follow from. It takes
the caption off a ground somebody chose and puts it on forty
photographs nobody chose the contrast of, which is why `shadow` comes
back below; and it takes away the second thing a palette would have
had to colour, which is half of why there is no palette here.
Capitals are inherited from the preset, and this pack could not
sensibly turn them off even if it wanted to. Bebas Neue has no lower
case - its lower-case codepoints are drawn as capitals - so a block
set in Syne's lower case would still have its picked words standing
in capitals, and the highlight would be carrying a difference nobody
chose. Set throughout, the capitals are the preset's own argument: at
40px with twenty characters to a line a caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and beats are what capitals are for. It
costs nothing here either - both faces are display cuts, and their
capitals are what they were drawn for.

_comment_face: Syne Regular, the text weight of a display grotesque, and the
whole of what its family name costs is written out in
content/faces/syne-regular.json rather than repeated here. The
short version is that this app already carries Syne Bold, so the
cut has to be asked for by its full name or the block and a
neighbouring channel's highlight become the same request.
It is a lighter face than any card-bearing pack under this
heading has to worry about, and a far sturdier one than re-belle's
signature hand, which is the other pack here with no card. That
difference decides how hard the shadow below has to work. It does
not decide whether there is one.
_comment_color: The show's violet, and it is what every frame is set in for good
rather than what one opens on: this channel offers no palette
(see `_comment_colors` below), so there is no swatch that could
change it.

makes it the colour of the whole caption. What separates a picked
word here is the face and nothing else, which is Hall of Femme's
highlight exactly; the difference is that its two faces are two
cuts of one family and these two are two unrelated designs.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because the pack this
one was cut from is the pack that INTRODUCED the feature, and the
next person to copy this folder will wonder where it went.
Hall of Femme offers four colours for the letters and four for
the card, and the point there is the pairing: what that show is
set in is which of sixteen combinations the user picked, so the
choice is genuinely part of the look. This show has one colour
and no card. `colors.panel` could not be offered even if somebody
wanted it - a palette for a slab needs a slab (see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js) - and `colors.text` with a single
entry in it would be a row containing one button that repaints
the caption the colour it already is.
So the violet is stated as the channel's own answer above and
nothing is handed over. If the show ever gains a second colour
this is two lines and the row appears with it; a palette is for a
channel where the choice is part of the look, and not a way for a
pack to avoid deciding. re-belle made the same call for the same
reason and is the pack to read beside this one.
_comment_shadow: Back, and this is the one place this pack contradicts a sentence
the preset writes. Every channel under this heading that keeps
its card sets `shadow` to null, on the argument that a drop
shadow is what keeps type legible over a photograph nobody chose
the contrast of and there is no photograph under those letters -
there is a solid card doing the job completely.
The argument is right, and it is exactly why dropping the card
means picking the shadow back up. There IS a photograph under
these letters, on all forty stills, and #330969 is a deep violet:
on a night scene, on dark hair, on a shadow in the corner of a
room it is a caption nobody can read at all. The face being a
text weight rather than a hairline changes how MUCH work the
shadow does, not whether it is needed - a sturdier stroke that is
the same value as what it lies on is still invisible, it is
merely invisible in a wider stroke.
The numbers are NOT the skeleton's, and they are re-belle's
rather than a fresh set invented here: that is the only other
pack on this heading setting dark type straight onto the picture,
which is the same problem to the pixel. Every other channel in
this app shadows LIGHT type, so it throws black down and to the
right and the dark rim is what the letters are found against.
Black behind deep violet adds dark to dark, and on the frames
where the caption is in trouble it would be invisible in a
slightly larger way. What separates dark ink from a dark picture
is light, so the shadow is white.
Centred rather than offset, which is the other consequence of the
colour being inverted. An offset shadow reads as a shadow - a
direction, a light source, something the letters are casting -
and white light falling three pixels down and to the right reads
as a printing misregistration instead. With no offset it is a
halo: the letters lifted off the picture on every side equally,
which is what they need when the picture could be anything.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Bebas Neue, in the same violet as the
rest of the block. The colour is stated and it is the block's, so
the recolour draws exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and
the FACE is the whole of the difference - which is Hall of
Femme's highlight, with the one change that these two faces are
not two cuts of a family but two unrelated designs.
Which is why it can stay a recolour with no card under it, where
Conspiracy Central had to become a box the moment it dropped its
own. That pack sets near-white Anton and picks words out in
near-black on yellow, because a recolour of two words in a block
of near-white would be two words in a slightly different white as
far as anyone scrolling is concerned. Nothing here is slightly
different: Bebas Neue is a tall condensed face whose capitals
fill the em, so at the block's own 40px a picked word comes out
visibly taller and much narrower than the words either side of
it. It changes the shape of the line and not only its texture,
and it does it at a glance on a phone.
That two faces set at one size come out at two apparent sizes
costs nothing here, and it is worth saying why, because under a
boxed highlight or a fitted size it would cost something: there
is no rectangle to be sized to the taller letters, and no
per-line fit for the wider face to win, because the preset states
`fontSize` and that takes `uniformSize` out of the question (see
the note on two faces in content/README.md). The difference lands
on the letterforms and nowhere else.
Colour mode and word scope are the preset's, and the argument for
picking out words rather than lines lives there: a caption's line
breaks are wherever the sentence ran out of width, so picking a
LINE out picks out a fragment rather than a thought.
The shadow is stated to the same numbers as the block's letters,
and it has to be. A picked word takes `highlight.shadow` and not
the block's (see runRows in js/text.js), and the skeleton's
answer there is a soft black halo - which on this channel would
put the one dark rim in the block behind the one word that is
supposed to be the easiest to read, and light every other word
from a different source. The card-bearing packs never notice
because their letters are on a slab; on the photograph it is two
light sources in one sentence.
_comment_panel: No card. The argument is in `_comment_title` above and the two
consequences are the `shadow` and the `colors` beside it.
Stated as null rather than left out, because it cannot be left
out: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the card's shape, padding, corners and shadow
arrive from snapchat-caption.json whatever this pack says about
them. Null is how a pack cut from that preset declines the one
part of it that is a whole shape rather than a number.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading. The two usual
reasons are already written out by the packs either side of this one:
its card-bearing siblings say the gradient has nothing to do because
their titles are not on the photograph, and Conspiracy Central - the
first pack here with no card - says that even when the title IS on
the photograph the gradient is still the wrong tool, because it is a
SIDE gradient drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline beside
the subject (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient). A caption lies
across the width of a vertical still, so darkening one half of forty
pictures would shade half of every line and leave the other half
exactly as it was.
There is a third reason here, it is re-belle's, and it is the
decisive one: this type is dark. A gradient that darkened the picture
behind it would be working against the halo rather than with it - see
`shadow` above, where what these letters need from the picture is
light.

channels.name: Binge US
_comment_group: A show under the Snapchat heading, built to Noisy Dish's brief and
departing from it in one place: what the card is MADE of.
Everything that makes this a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's and is
stated in the same two references - the frame fetch, the vertical
output, the transcription, the rewrite, and how the caption is set.
Noisy Dish was the first pack here to say the still is a card lying on
something rather than the surface itself. This one keeps the card and
takes the photograph out of it. What is left is a sheet of paper, and
the picture reaches the frame twice around it: blurred and enlarged
UNDER the card, where it is the colour of the margin rather than
anything anyone reads, and cut to the person ON the card, where it is
the only sharp thing in the frame.
That is the whole design, and it is one idea rather than three effects:
a still cannot be both the background and the subject at full strength,
so it is spent entirely on the subject and the background is made out
of what is left over. It is also why the type can be absolute black
with nothing behind it - there is no photograph under the letters to
hold them off, only paper.
First pack under this heading to compose from a cutout. Nothing about
the frame fetch changes for it: a capture slot is an ordinary frame
record and /cutout-frame takes it like any other (see
api._capture_frames_sync). The face-fill penalty Laugh Society has to
turn off is not in this path at all - a capture run picks its frames on
whole-picture quality through frame_grab and never reaches the
face-based scorer - so there is nothing here to turn off.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of a sibling, for
the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that gets
dropped in. The prose below points at noisy-dish and laugh-society-1
wherever the reasoning is theirs and states its own where this pack
decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into report.
