nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a pack
that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
it.
_comment_framing: The shared answer, unchanged. A cutout channel elsewhere in this app
states a framing profile of its own because the crop it never shows
would otherwise decide which frames it gets; here the crop is chosen by
the capture run rather than by the face scorer, so there is no such
decision to correct. See the group note above.
_comment_photo: The card, and what is under it. Noisy Dish's geometry to the pixel -
the same 85% and the same 13px of rounding, for the reasons its own
`photo` note gives - and neither of its two gradients.
`fill` is the departure and it is the channel. The card is a sheet of
warm off-white paper and the still is not drawn on it, which is what
makes everything else here possible: the subject stands on a known
colour instead of on an unknown photograph, and so does the type. A
printed cream rather than pure white, because white is what the type is
NOT - a card at #FFFFFF under black capitals is a screenshot of a
document, and #F5F2E3 is paper, which is what a news card is pretending
to be.
The backdrop is the frame's own still, cropped to its middle half and
blurred by 30px - see `photo.backdrop` in js/channels.js for what the
two numbers do and why the crop happens before the blur. It is not
decoration and it is not a colour picked to go with the card: it is the
one ground that is different on every thumbnail and right on every
thumbnail, because it is made of the picture the thumbnail is of. A
flat colour in the margin would have to be chosen once for a channel
whose stills are a nightclub, a courtroom and a beach.
0.5 rather than the whole frame, and the reason is what a blur does
rather than what a crop does. A 30px blur spreads every piece of detail
across 30px of the result, so what survives it is whatever was already
larger than that; on a 540-wide still at full size very little is, and
the margin comes back an even grey carrying the picture's average
colour. At half the frame every shape is twice the size going in, and
what comes out still has the picture's lighting and its large masses in
it - which is the difference between a soft version of the photograph
and a smear of its mean.
30 rather than less, though, and that is the other end of the same
trade. The margin is 41px wide down the sides: anything still legible
in a band that narrow competes with the card, and the one thing this
ground must never do is look like a second picture.
No tint, and it is not an omission. A tint is what ties a photograph to
the ground it is lying on, and the thing lying on this ground is not a
photograph - it is a flat colour that was never going to be mistaken
for one. Laid on anyway it would only be a wash of colour over the
paper, and the paper is the brand.
_comment_cutout: The person, cut out of the frame whole by the backend (see
/cutout-frame and backend/background_remover.py) and stood on the card.
The fit and the zoom range are Laugh Society's, number for number, and
deliberately so - the two channels ask the same thing of a subject,
which is that they arrive somewhere sensible and are then composed by
hand. Its own `cutout` note carries the reasoning for every one of
those and is worth reading before any of them is changed; what follows
is only what this channel had to decide for itself.
Two of them are this channel's own and are where it parts company with
the pack it copied.
anchorX 0.5 puts the subject in the MIDDLE. Laugh Society stands them
in the left half because the title is in the right half, and that is a
composition this channel does not have: the caption is above them, at
the top of the card, across its full width. With the type out of the
way sideways there is nothing for a subject standing to one side to be
beside, and an off-centre figure on a symmetrical card reads as a
layout that slipped rather than one that was chosen.
It moves the room without resizing it, which is the reason it is a key
of its own rather than fitWidthRatio 1. The subject still arrives
fitted to half the frame's width - 270px of a 540-wide canvas - and
that half still leaves air around them. Fitted to the WHOLE width they
would arrive height-limited instead on any full-length shot, standing
nearly 900px tall on a 960px canvas, which is a figure reaching up
through the caption and out of the top of the card.
And there is exactly one of them, on every slot. Laugh Society offers
the subject twice and three times on half its grid, because a comic
shown three times in three poses is a look that show is FOR. A news
card is not: it is one person, one moment, one headline, and a second
copy of the same face on it reads as a mistake in the cut rather than
as a device. Said by leaving copiesBySlot out rather than by writing a
list of ones - absent means one (see editor.copiesForSlot), and
copyScale and copyOffsetGap go with it because they exist only to
place a figure that is not there.
That also takes a real cost off every thumbnail. Each extra figure is
a separate restoration of a separate moment on the one GPU (see
editor.cutOut, which runs them in sequence), so a grid that used to
cost twenty cut-outs plus twenty more for the doubled and tripled
slots now costs twenty.
bottomRatio 0.925 stands them on the CARD's bottom edge rather than
the canvas's, and it is the one number here that is neither Laugh
Society's nor arrived at from scratch. It is read off `photo` above:
the card is fillRatio of the canvas and centred, so its foot sits at
(1 + 0.85) / 2 of the height - 888px of 960 - and the two numbers have
to be changed together. A card resized without this is a figure
standing in mid-air or buried, and nothing in the app will say so.
It was Laugh Society's 1 until it was asked to line up, which stood
them on the canvas's own edge and let the figure cross the card's foot
and finish on the blurred ground. The argument for that was that a
subject breaking out of the card reads as a person in front of a
graphic, where feet tucked inside a rounded rectangle read as a smaller
photograph pasted into a larger one. What it did NOT survive is that
the card here is a solid colour and not a picture: a figure whose feet
stop 72px below the one hard edge in the composition reads as a layer
that missed its mark rather than as depth. Standing them ON that edge
is the alignment the card is asking for, and the overhang is still
available to anyone who wants it - the figure is draggable and
resizable from wherever it lands, as it is everywhere else.
The shadow is where the two Laugh Society packs disagree, so it is the
one thing here that had to be chosen rather than copied. They share the
blur (24) and the alpha (0.8) and differ on the throw: 24px on the
stage channel, 6 on the other.
6, and for the ground rather than for the figure. A 24px throw says
the person is standing well in front of what is behind them, which is
true of a lit stage and false of a sheet of paper. At 6 the shadow
stays under the figure and does what it is actually here for:
separating a cut edge from a flat colour.
It was also chosen against the overhang this pack used to have, where
the figure crossed the card's foot and the shadow had to fall on two
surfaces at once - at 24 the part below that edge threw a hard
diagonal across the blurred ground. That case is gone now that the
feet land on the card's edge (see bottomRatio above), but the number
is kept, because the first reason was always the load-bearing one and
a user who drags a figure down still gets the overhang back.
overTitle is this channel's own, and it is the whole of why the caption
can sit where it does - see the layout note below.
_comment_title: Anton, absolute black, at the top of the card, under the figure.
Everything else about how a caption is set under this heading - the
size, where the lines break, the capitals, the character count, that
the user can drag the block off a face - is the Snapchat caption design
and is stated once in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.

_comment_face: Anton. A grotesque with almost no counter and almost no
sidebearing, which is the face a headline is set in when the
headline is the point - it holds a whole sentence across 90% of a
540-wide frame at 40px without the preset having to shrink
anything.
It has a lower case, unlike the Bebas its neighbour is set in, so
the preset's capitals are a transformation laid over the face here
rather than the face's own answer. That is the right way round for
this channel: the capitals are the caption's decision and not the
type's, and a pack that later wants sentence case has one key to
change instead of a different font to find.
_comment_color: Absolute black, on every frame, with no palette offered beside it.
Black is not the default that white would have been - it is what
the card being paper makes possible. Every other channel under this
heading sets light letters because there is a photograph somewhere
under them; this one has a known colour under every letter of every
caption, and on #F5F2E3 the strongest thing a word can be is
#000000 with nothing behind it.
Absolute rather than a soft near-black. A near-black is what you
reach for to stop type vibrating against pure white, and this is
not pure white - the card is already warm and already a step down
from it, so the pair is a printed one and #000000 is simply the
ink.
No second colour, for the reason Noisy Dish gives: the colour in
this channel is the ground, and a palette in the type would be a
third thing competing with the paper and the blurred margin. Hall
of Femme hands two of its colours to the user because the PAIRING
of card and letters is what that show is; here the card is one
colour on every frame, so there is no pairing to offer.
_comment_panel: None. The preset's card is exactly what this channel already has
and cannot have twice: the still has been taken out of the photo
card and replaced by a flat colour, so the caption is ALREADY on a
solid ground somebody picked. A second slab laid on it would be a
background on a background, in a colour that has to either match
the paper - and be invisible - or not, and be a patch.
Dropping it drops the preset's shadow with it, which is correct and
not a loss: that shadow lifts a card off a photograph, and there is
no photograph here for anything to be lifted off. The preset's own
`shadow: null` for the letters stands unchanged too - black on
cream needs nothing under it, and the sibling that puts an opaque
shadow back does so because its letters stand on the amber foot of
a gradient.
Stated as null rather than left out, because the preset states one
and a pack that says nothing inherits it whole.
_comment_highlight: None, and here it is a brand decision rather than a consequence.
A highlight under this heading is one of three things: another
colour, another cut of the face, or a box. All three are available
- Anton is one weight, but a colour or a box on cream would work
perfectly well - and none is wanted. This caption is a news
headline, and a headline with one word picked out in a second
colour is an advertisement; the whole line is the emphasis.
The word buttons in the panel stay where they are and go dead, with
a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderWordButtons) - a live button that produced no visible
change would read as the app ignoring the click.

_comment: The preset's block, moved to the other end of the frame.
vAlign top with topRatio 0.125 is the mirror of the preset's own
bottom margin, and it lands in the same place measured from the
other edge: 120px down a 960-tall frame, which is 48px inside
the card's top edge at fillRatio 0.85. Noisy Dish's caption sits
48px up from the card's foot for the same reason, so the two
channels put their type the same distance into the card and
differ only in which way up.
Measured off the FRAME rather than off the card, like every
other layout number here. That is a relation worth knowing
before either number is touched: shrinking the card moves its
top edge DOWN while the type stays where it is, so a smaller
fillRatio eventually puts the first line on the blurred ground
above the card. Nothing breaks when it does - the type just
stops being on paper, which is the whole design.
A caption that runs long grows DOWNWARD from here, which is the
other half of why this end of the frame is the right one. The
subject stands on the bottom edge, so the two things grow
towards each other from opposite ends and a long caption meets
the figure rather than being pushed off the card by it - and
where they meet, the figure is in front (see `overTitle`
above). The type passing behind a shoulder is the picture this
channel is for; the type sliding off the paper would not be.
Everything else is the preset's and is not restated: the size,
the width, the character count, the four lines, the freeform
box. Only the end of the frame has changed.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and there is no photograph under this title at all - it is
on the channel's own paper. Left on, the backend would darken the foot
of a still that is only ever seen blurred to a margin and cut to a
person, which is work spent on two places it cannot reach and one it
would only muddy.

channels.name: Burst Out Loud
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Proxima Nova Bold with picked words in Proxima Nova Black, on a
black card, in two colours offered for the type and the same two for
the card.
beauty-hacks is the second pack to read, because it is the one that
already made this move - Hall of Femme's design in Proxima Nova - and
everything about the two cuts of that family is argued out there with
the measurements. This pack differs from it in the palette alone, and
the difference is that there is no brand colour in it.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs it was cut from, which
is in the colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme sets its captions
in Telegraf on a hot pink card; beauty-hacks sets them in Proxima
Nova on a magenta one. This one takes beauty-hacks' type exactly and
reduces the palette to its poles: white and black, offered for the
letters and for the card, opening on white on black.
That makes it the plainest of the packs cut to this design, and
plain is the design rather than the absence of one. Every other one
of them carries a brand colour on the card, which is the shape that
reads first; this one has none to carry, so what reads first is the
contrast itself and the words in it. The card still earns its place -
it is what holds a caption legible over forty unknown photographs,
which is the whole argument for a card, and it is doing that job
alone here rather than doing it while also being the brand.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, the shape of the card, its padding and corners and
shadow, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show, which is the whole of what a pack under this
heading should be.

_comment_face: Proxima Nova Bold. Which cut that is, why the full name rather
than 'Proxima Nova' is declared, and what the machine may already
know it by are written out in
content/faces/proxima-nova-bold.json rather than repeated here;
what capitals at the preset's 40px cost this face, which is
nothing, is written out in beauty-hacks.
The Bold and not the Black, so that a picked word has the heavier
cut to climb into - the argument, and what this pack did before
it, are in beauty-hacks with the measurements.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the two in `colors` below,
so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is found by
matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the black card, which is the strongest pairing
there is: 21 to 1, the full range, with no brand colour in the way
of it. Nothing about this pairing is a compromise between a colour
and its legibility, which is what the note on this key in every
other pack cut to this design is about - here the two questions
have the same answer. Three older packs under this heading already
open on that same 21 to 1 - fight-source and killer-bites on black
like this one, fitness-story-de on white - so the pairing is not
this show's alone, and nothing about it needs to be.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - two buttons each in the title panel (see
editor.renderColorButtons).
The same two in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does, and here it is the whole of the
feature rather than one part of it: the show has no colour to
choose, so what the user is being handed is the DIRECTION. Four
combinations, of which two are a colour on itself and two are the
same 21:1 contrast the opposite way up - white on black for a
caption that sits into a dark still, black on white for one that
cuts out of a bright one. That is a real choice on a grid of forty
frames from one video, and it is the only one this palette makes.
Two rather than the three or four the packs this was cut from
offer. Nothing counts the list - the panel draws a swatch per entry
and the row wraps - so a two-colour row is a two-button row and
costs nothing anywhere. Several packs under this heading offer
exactly two, and fight-source offers these two: the same white and
black, on the same black card, opening the same way round. That is
worth knowing and is not a problem - it is a different show in a
different face, and a palette of the two poles is not a brand
anybody owns.
The two failing combinations are white on white and black on black,
and they are left available for the reason Hall of Femme gives
about precisely them - the two lists are independent because the
pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the matching ones would
cost the panel more explaining than an invisible caption costs a
user who can see it is invisible and presses the other swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a different
CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what colour the type
is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Proxima Nova Black, in the same colour as
the rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and beauty-hacks' both. That the step climbs -
700 to 900, the way Hall of Femme climbs 200 to 800 - and that a
step this short makes a quiet highlight are measured out in
beauty-hacks, which is where that argument belongs and is not
repeated. This pack ran it the other way round until the seven
shows cut to that design were turned together.
It is worth knowing that this is the pack where that quietness
costs the most. On a magenta card a picked word has the colour of
the card working with it; here there is nothing in the frame but
two weights of one family in one colour, so the 3.2% of set width
between the Bold and the Black is the entire highlight. If this
show ever needs its picked words to carry further, the honest fix
is the one beauty-hacks names - a third cut of the family - rather
than a box, and not a second colour, which would make the
highlight its own question and the palette a different feature.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Black, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are the
Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the second entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom every pack under this heading
uses - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching this
value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be written in
one order while the channel still opens on white type and a black
card.
The only card among the packs cut to this design that is not a
colour - fight-source and killer-bites are carded in black too,
from a different lineage. It is also the case where the preset's
drop shadow - black at half alpha, 24px of blur, 10px down - is
doing something other than lifting a bright shape off a
photograph: a black card on a dark still would otherwise have no
edge at all, and the blur is the whole of what keeps the rectangle
a rectangle. That is worth knowing before anybody considers
turning the shadow off on this pack in particular.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved - and on this
pack it would be the same colour as the card as well, which is how a
black card ends up with no edge.

channels.name: Buzzer Beater DE
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite that turns speech into report, the stated
40px, the twenty characters to a line, the freeform text box, the
block at the foot of the frame and the drag are all the same and are
named here rather than restated. Where it parts company with Hall of
Femme is the card - there is none - and for that half of it the packs
to read are conspiracy-central and fight-source-de, which are the two
other channels here that set their captions straight onto the
photograph.
The DE in the name is the account's, the way the DE in Hall of Femme
DE, Fitness Story DE and Fight Source DE is: it says which of the
brand's feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What lands
on the frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put
through the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel
here; nothing in this pack changes that, and everything the app itself
says is English like the rest of it (see CLAUDE.md).
The glyph check the DE feeds before this one made a habit of, and this
face passes it with the same footnote Fight Source DE's does. Garamond
Premier Pro Bold Italic Subhead carries 1268 codepoints - the umlauts,
the eszett and the low quotes German sets speech in among them - so a
caption is drawn from the file rather than from whatever the browser
substitutes for a missing glyph, which would be a different face at a
width nothing measured. The footnote is the capital eszett: U+1E9E is
not in the file, and is never asked for, because the preset's
`uppercase` goes through toUpperCase (see `cased` in js/text.js) and
JavaScript maps a lower-case eszett to SS rather than to its capital.
A face chosen for how it looks in English is not automatically a face
that can SET another language, and the check is two minutes against a
cmap.
_comment_order: Last under the heading, which is where a new show goes: the numbers
are a running order rather than a ranking, and the foreign feeds have
been landing at the end of it since Hall of Femme DE took 920.
927 and not 926, which is the second time this has happened and is
worth recording as such. Fight Source DE's note says 924 was taken by
Re-belle between that pack being written and being saved; 926 was
taken by Beauty-Tipps between this one being written and being saved.
A shared number is not an error - the server breaks the tie
alphabetically by name (see serve.py) - it is simply an order nobody
chose, and Buzzer Beater DE would have sorted above Beauty-Tipps for
no reason. Two collisions in two new packs says the real answer is to
read the heading's last number at the moment of saving rather than at
the moment of writing.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Garamond Premier Pro Bold Italic Subhead, in one pale pink,
straight onto the photograph, with no card behind it and nothing
picked out of it.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show and then declines two whole shapes that preset draws, which
is what fight-source-de does and for the same reason.
Why no card. On Hall of Femme the slab and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears, and
the card is what turns that weight from a risk into a choice. This
show answers the same question the other way. A bold old-style italic
is a face with weight in its stems and real modelling in its curves,
and it is the SHAPE of it that has to be read - the slant, the
single-storey letterforms, the serifs - which a card of flat colour
does not help with and a fifth of the frame of pink would fight. What
is left is a sentence lying on the picture: no graphic, no second
shape, nothing between the words and the footage.
It is also the one pack under this heading where the width matters,
and it was measured before the face was settled on - on the canvas
the renderer uses, so the numbers include the kerning. Twenty mixed
capitals in this face come out 499px against the 486px a line has,
where Korolev Bold's come out 434 - so here the frame's width and the
preset's twenty characters land in the same place rather than the
characters binding first. Ordinary prose still fits, because the
spaces and the narrow letters an alphabet run has none of do most of
the work: nineteen characters of real sentence measure 433px. What it
means in practice is that an unusually wide line breaks at nineteen
instead of twenty, which the wrapper does on its own and nobody sees
(see the two ceilings in js/caption.js). The measurements themselves
are in content/faces/garamond-premier-pro-bold-italic-subhead.json.
Uppercased, for the reason every one of its neighbours is: at 40px
with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in. It
costs this face more than it costs the others, and that is worth being
honest about - an italic of this kind is drawn around its lower case,
and its capitals are the calmer half of it. They are still italic
capitals, which almost nothing else on Snapchat is, and the preset's
`uppercase` is the guideline a pack may break with a reason (Killer
Bites does). This show has no such reason yet; the day it decides its
lower case IS the brand, `uppercase: false` is one line in this file.

_comment_color: The pale pink, and it is what every frame is set in for good: this
channel offers no palette (see `_comment_colors` below), so this is
the colour rather than the colour a frame opens on.
There is no card for it to be read against, so what it is read
against is the footage, and this colour cuts the opposite way to
Fight Source DE's dark plum. A pale pink is near the top of the
lightness range: on night footage, on a dark crowd, on a shadowed
court it is the brightest thing in the frame, and on a blown-out
sky or a white jersey it is nearly gone. That is what the shadow
below is for, and it is the half of the problem a shadow can
actually solve - which is why this pack picks one up where Fight
Source DE could not.
If the show ever wants the other half solved, the two honest
remedies are the ones that change the brief rather than patch it:
a card, which is the decision `panel` declines, or a second colour
in a `colors` list for the user to switch to on a bright still.
Both are one edit to this file.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because most of its
siblings under this heading have one and the next person to copy
this folder will wonder where it went.
Two of the three could not be offered even if somebody wanted them:
`colors.panel` needs a panel and there is none, and
`colors.highlight` needs a highlight and there is none either - the
rows are hidden rather than drawn dead (see editor.paletteOf).
The third is the decision fight-source-de argues and this pack
inherits whole. One colour is one swatch, and a row of one swatch
is a button that is already pressed - the one kind of control this
panel does not have anywhere, because a button that visibly does
nothing reads as the app ignoring the click. A palette is for a
channel where the CHOICE is part of the look, which is what Hall of
Femme's sixteen pairings are; it is not a way of showing that a
pack has a colour. The day this show has a second colour the list
is two strings in this file, and it becomes a palette by being one.

the preset writes. Every channel with a card sets `shadow` to null

The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow in
js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here: they are
what every channel that sets light type on a photograph in this app
uses, and a pack with no measurement of its own should not carry a
number it merely guessed at. If anything here is ever revisited it
is this - a hard 3px offset was chosen under a heavy condensed
grotesque, and these letterforms are finer at the terminals - but

_comment_highlight: None. Not a highlight that happens to look like the rest of the

channels.name: Cas Mortels
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the
rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame and every number in it are
the same and are named here rather than restated. What makes this show
itself is one sentence long - it is set in Special Elite, on a sand
card, in two colours the user pairs per frame, with a picked word in
Courier Prime - and everything below is that sentence.
The name is French and stays French: a channel's `name` is a brand and
is whatever that channel is actually called (see CLAUDE.md). What
lands on the frames is whatever the video's own voice track was
saying, put through the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on
every channel here; nothing in this pack changes that, and everything
the app itself says is English like the rest of it.
One thing this pack checked that most of its siblings had no reason
to, and that hall-of-femme-de and fitness-story-de checked before it.
A face chosen for how it looks in English is not automatically a face
that can SET another language, and the check is two minutes against a
cmap: both files here carry the accented vowels French needs in both
cases, the cedilla, the oe ligature and the guillemets it sets speech
in - 368 codepoints in Special Elite and 383 in Courier Prime, with
nothing missing from that list. So a caption is drawn from the file
rather than from whatever the browser substitutes for a missing glyph,
which would be a different face at a width nothing measured.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Special Elite, on a sand card, in colours the user picks per frame,
with a picked word in Courier Prime.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame, what a picked word
does - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show, which is the whole of what a pack under this
heading should be.
Special Elite is a struck face rather than a drawn one: its letters
are a typewriter's, with ink spreading unevenly at the stems and a
baseline that does not quite hold. That is a caption's worst instinct
on a photograph - uneven edges are exactly what grain and detail eat -
and it is a thing this channel can have only because of the card. On a
solid ground somebody chose, the unevenness is a texture the eye reads
as a document; over a still it would read as a rendering fault. It is
the same argument Hall of Femme makes for its hairline and
hall-of-femme-de for its text face, from a third place on the same
axis.
The card also pays for the capitals the preset sets. A typewriter face
in capitals is a one-line dossier heading, which is what this show's
captions are; the same capitals over a photograph would be a band of
broken ink with nothing behind it to make the breaks look deliberate.
The preset is therefore left alone here - the only pack under this
heading that overrides it is Killer Bites, and it says why where it
does.

_comment_color: The near-black, and it is the channel's own answer - therefore what
every frame is set in until somebody presses a swatch, since a
frame stores no colour of its own until it is given one (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below, so the
near-black swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame; the swatch is found by matching this value rather than by
being listed first, which is why it sits second in a row that opens
with the sand.
Near-black letters on the sand card is the pairing this show opens
on, and with a palette of two the choice that matters is which of
them is the CARD. The card is a fifth of the frame and reads before
anything on it, so it takes the colour that is the brand at that
size and at that distance - the sand - and the type is then what
has to stay legible against it. At these two values it comfortably
is: 8.2 to 1, which holds at caption size on a phone over any still
underneath.
#1C1C1C rather than #000000, and the difference is the face. Special
Elite's letters are struck, so their edges are already broken and
their interiors already uneven; pure black on a warm mid-tone
sharpens that into something that reads as a print fault rather
than as ink on paper. A near-black is the colour a typewriter
ribbon actually leaves.
The other three pairings are a button away, the inverse among them.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and for
the card behind them - two buttons each in the title panel (see
editor.renderColorButtons).
The same two in both lists and in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is the
PAIRING. Four combinations of a sand and a near-black, and the two
worth having are the two that read. A palette that could only ever
be used one way round would be a palette of one card, and this
show's look is the pairing rather than either colour on its own.
Two colours rather than the three or four its neighbours offer, and
that is the brand and not an unfinished list. Nothing counts these
entries - the panel draws a swatch per colour and the row wraps - so
a third is one string in this file the day the show has one.
Nothing stops the user setting sand on sand. That is not an
oversight either: the two lists are independent because the pairing
is the feature, and with a palette this short a rule barring the two
matching combinations would be a rule removing half the buttons. The
user can see the caption has gone and presses the other swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a different
FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type is has one
answer and not two. That matters more on a palette of two than on
one of four: with the block near-black, a highlight left to pick its
own colour from the same list could only ever be sand, and sand on
sand is a picked word that vanishes into its card.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Courier Prime, in the same colour as the
rest of the block. The highlight here is the CONDITION OF THE
MACHINE: two typewriters, one worn and one serviced, on one line.
It is a third answer to the question its siblings answer two ways.
Hall of Femme picks words out by weight, 200 against 800 of one
family. Laugh Society picks them out by colour and by voice at
once, a geometric against a humanist. This channel changes neither
the weight nor the colour: Special Elite and Courier Prime are the
same idea drawn twice, so the picked word does not arrive as
another typeface but as the same sentence typed cleanly - which is
the emphasis a case file wants, a line somebody went back and set
down properly.
Three measurements say what the pairing actually does, taken the
way hall-of-femme-de takes its own - through the renderer's own
measuring path (measureVisualBounds in js/text.js) rather than off
the files, which is the only version of these numbers that
describes what gets drawn. The first is the one to know before
changing anything here. At the preset's 40px the cap band is 29px
in Special Elite against 24px in Courier Prime, so a picked word
stands about 17% shorter than the words either side of it on the
same baseline. That is real and it is visible.
It is also the right way round: the clean face is the quieter one,
and a picked word that is shorter AND sharper reads as inset
rather than as shouted. Turned around - the worn face picking words
out of the clean one - the highlight would be both bigger and
rougher, which is a smudge rather than an emphasis.
Second, it costs nothing structural. Nothing in the card is
measured from the picked run: the band every box takes is the union
of each ROW's ink and cap band, in the row's own face (see the
band note in js/text.js), so a shorter run leaves every box the
same height it would have had and leaves the stack of them
unchanged.
Third, the widths. Nineteen capitals come out 420px in Special
Elite against 454px in Courier Prime - 8%, which is close to the
11% Hall of Femme already carries between its two cuts, so which
words are picked out moves a line's width about as much as it does
on the pack this one is cut from. The worst case is worth writing
down because this face is a true monospace, every glyph advancing
23.98px at 40px: a full 20-character line (`maxChars` in the
preset) entirely picked out is 481px of ink and a 503px card with
the preset's 12px padding, which centred in the frame runs from
x=19 to x=522 - 18px clear of the right edge. It fits, and it is
the widest thing this pack can produce, so a pack raising
`maxChars` or `fontSize` is a pack that has to measure this again.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as face
would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Sand, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are the
Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the first entry in `colors.panel` above as well, so the swatch
that shows as chosen on an untouched frame is the one at the start
of the row. Nothing requires that - the swatch is found by matching
this value rather than by being listed first - and the type's own
colour is deliberately NOT first in its row, which is the same
freedom used the other way round.
The card is doing more work on this channel than on most of its
siblings. Everywhere else it is the brand's colour holding a
legible ground under the type; here it is also the PAPER the face
needs - a struck typewriter letter is a mark on a sheet, and a warm
mid-tone is what makes the unevenness read as ink rather than as a
bad render. The preset's shadow matters for hall-of-femme-de's
reason too: a sand card thrown onto a sunlit still has less to
separate it from the picture than a hot pink or a near-black does,
and the shadow is what keeps it a graphic lying on the frame.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it is
on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.

channels.name: Conspiracy Central
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, and one more cut to Hall of
Femme's design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of
Femme's and is taken from the same two presets rather than restated:
the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription, the
rewrite that turns speech into report, the stated 40px, the twenty
characters to a line, the freeform text box, the drag.
What makes it a different show is three decisions, and two of them go
further than any pack under this heading has gone before. The face is
Anton. The card is GONE — the words are set straight onto the
photograph and only the picked ones get a background, in yellow. And
the block is hung from the top of the frame rather than stood on the
foot of it. Each is argued where it is stated.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and its siblings, and
unlike most of them it is not only a swap of face and colour.
Set in Anton, near-white, with picked words in near-black on a yellow
box, across the HEAD of the frame. Everything else — the size, where
the lines break, the capitals, the freeform box, the drag — is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
Three things this pack overrides in that preset, and all three follow
from one decision. The card is dropped, so the type is over the
photograph; therefore the drop shadow comes back, because that is what
holds type legible over a photograph nobody chose the contrast of; and
therefore the highlight becomes a BOX rather than a recolour, because
with no card behind the block there is finally something to box
against.
Why drop the card. On Hall of Femme the slab and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears, and
the card is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk. Anton
is the opposite face — a heavy condensed display cut that was drawn to
be read large over a picture — so it needs no rescuing, and a card
under it would be a fifth of the frame of flat colour spent on a
problem this face does not have. What is left when the card goes is
the yellow box, which now reads as the one graphic in the frame rather
than as a shape inside another shape.
Uppercased, for the reason every one of its neighbours is: at 40px
with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in. It
costs nothing here — Anton has no lower case anybody would call the
brand, and its capitals are the whole point of the face.

_comment_color: Near-white, and it is what every frame is set in for good: this
channel offers no palette (see `_comment_colors` below), so this
is the colour rather than the colour a frame opens on.
#FEFEFD and not #FFFFFF, which is a real decision and not a typo
to be tidied away. It is a white with the faintest warmth left in
it, and against the yellow of the highlight box that is what keeps
the two from reading as one temperature — a pure white beside
#FAE414 looks blue by comparison. It is also the value the brand
states, and a brand that states a colour to five parts in a
thousand is stating that it is not white.
_comment_shadow: Back, and this is the one place this pack contradicts a sentence
the preset writes. Every other channel under this heading sets
`shadow` to null, on the argument that a drop shadow is what keeps
type legible over a photograph nobody chose the contrast of and
there is no photograph under those letters — there is a solid
card doing the job completely.
The argument is right, and it is exactly why dropping the card
means picking the shadow back up. There IS a photograph under
these letters, on all forty stills, and near-white type over an
unknown frame is the one thing a caption must never be: on a blown
sky it disappears.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow in
js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They are
what every channel that sets white type on a photograph in this
app uses, which is the same job this is; a pack with no reason of
its own should not carry a number it merely agrees with, and where
it has to state one anyway it should state the one already in use.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because every sibling
under this heading has one and the next person to copy this folder
will wonder where it went.
Two of the three colours here could not be handed over even if
somebody wanted to. `colors.panel` needs a panel and there is none
(see the note on `colors` in js/channels.js), and `colors.text`
recolours the highlight along with the block unless `highlight` is
stated too — which on this channel would take the near-black off
the yellow, where the contrast between the two is the highlight.
The deeper reason is the one that would hold even without those:
this show's three colours are the brand and were given as the
brand. A palette is for a channel where the CHOICE is part of the
look, which is what Hall of Femme's sixteen pairings are; it is
not a way for a pack to avoid deciding.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Anton at 700, near-black, on a yellow box.
Three things change at once and that is the point — this is the
loudest highlight under the heading because it is the only one
with the photograph to shout over rather than a card to sit on.
Box mode, which is this pack's override of the preset's `color`.
The preset chose colour because there was nothing to box against:
its words are already on a solid ground of their own, and a box
inside a card is a shape inside a shape. With the card gone the
block is on the picture, and a box is the only version of a
highlight that survives being on the picture — a recolour of two
words in a block of near-white would be two words in a slightly
different white as far as anyone scrolling is concerned.
Word scope, inherited, for the preset's reason: a caption's line
breaks are wherever the sentence ran out of width, so picking a
LINE out picks out a fragment rather than a thought.
The face is Anton at 700, which Anton does not ship. The bold is
the browser emboldening the one cut there is, and the whole of
what that means — why it is safe, what it costs to the pixel, and
what it must never be asked to carry on its own — is written out
in content/faces/anton-bold.json rather than repeated here. The
short version is that it is the third thing that changes at a
picked word and not the first: what makes these words read is
near-black on yellow, and the weight is a reinforcement of it.
#020200 rather than #000000, for the reason `color` above is not
#FFFFFF: it is the value the brand states, it is a black with a
trace of warmth in it, and on #FAE414 that trace is what stops the
pairing looking like a print registration error. There is nothing
here for a true black to be too harsh against either way — the box
is a flat shape, not a photograph seen through it.
The box's own shadow is stated to the same numbers as the block's
letters, which is the one thing that has to be true of it: the box
and the words beside it are lying on the same photograph, and two
different shadows in one block is two light sources. Stated rather
than left to the skeleton, whose answer here is a softer, centred
halo (blur 20, no offset) — right for a box on a card, wrong
beside letters that are casting 3px down and to the right.
`padRatio` is left at the skeleton's 0.12, which is about five
pixels at this size. That is a highlighter's margin and not a
card's, which is what a box cut to one word wants — the preset
makes the same argument at greater length for the 12px it gives
the card it draws.
13px of corner radius, which is the number every rectangle under
this heading is rounded by: a square-cornered one reads as a crop
or a letterbox, something the player did, and a rounded one reads
as a graphic somebody made. Restated here rather than inherited
because the preset states it on the `panel` this pack does not
have, and the argument for it is an argument about rectangles
rather than about cards.

_comment: The preset's block, with the one thing this show measures
differently: it is hung from the top of the frame instead of
stood on the foot of it.
Everything else is inherited and argued there — nearly the
full width, a stated 40px so that forty stills cut from one
video are one set rather than forty type sizes, twenty
characters as the second ceiling on where the lines break,
`freeform` because a caption is a sentence and not three typed
beats, and the renderer's own 10px between the lines.
vAlign `top`. The foot of a vertical still is where a player
puts its own captions and where burned-in speech usually goes,
which is why every pack under this heading is there — and it
is also, on a phone, where the player's furniture is and where
a viewer's thumb rests. A caption at the head of the frame is
read before the picture rather than after it, which is the
register this show wants: the claim first, the footage as the
evidence for it. It is the same reasoning that puts these
captions at an end of the frame at all rather than across the
middle, applied to the other end.
topRatio is 50px off the head of a 960-tall frame, written as
the fraction every layout number here is written as
(50 / 960 = 0.052083). Small on purpose, and it can afford to
be where the bottom margin cannot: 0.125 at the foot is 120px
because a vertical video is watched inside a player with its
own furniture along the bottom edge, and there is nothing
along the top edge but the picture.
Like its opposite number it is a margin and not a position,
but it buys the constancy for nothing: a block hung from the
top grows DOWNWARD, so a caption that gains a fourth line
grows into the picture and its first line stays exactly 50px
down whatever was said over it. It is measured to the first
thing drawn, so a first line with a picked word in it puts the
yellow box on the margin and the capitals a padding below it
— five pixels, and the same distinction bottomRatio makes at
the other edge.
The preset's `bottomRatio` survives the merge and is simply
not read under vAlign `top` (see blockTop0 in js/text.js).
Left rather than nulled: it is the number this pack would go
back to if it ever came down to the foot of the frame, and a
null there would be a hole where every sibling has a number.
maxBlockHeightRatio is inherited at 0.30 and no longer
decides anything about the size — a size the renderer may
shrink is not a stated size. It does mean a little more type
fits inside it here than on a panelled sibling, since there is
no card padding for the renderer to take out of the budget
first (see BLOCK_BUDGET in js/text.js).

id is this one because it is the unsuffixed show - the other two
