_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs it was cut from, which
is in the colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme sets its captions
in Telegraf on a hot pink card; beauty-hacks sets them in Proxima
Nova on a magenta one. This one takes beauty-hacks' type exactly and
puts it on a coral card, in sixteen pairings of a white, a black,
that coral and a violet-magenta.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, the shape of the card, its padding and corners and
shadow, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show, which is the whole of what a pack under this
heading should be.

_comment_face: Proxima Nova Bold. Which cut that is, why the full name rather
than 'Proxima Nova' is declared, and what the machine may already
know it by are written out in
content/faces/proxima-nova-bold.json rather than repeated here;
what capitals at the preset's 40px cost this face, which is
nothing, is written out in beauty-hacks.
The Bold and not the Black, so that a picked word has the heavier
cut to climb into - the argument, and what this pack did before
it, are in beauty-hacks with the measurements.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the four in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is
found by matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the coral card is the pairing this show opens on,
and it is a thin one, which is worth stating plainly rather than
leaving to be discovered: white on #FE6262 is 2.9 to 1, a shade
under even the 3:1 large-text threshold that a 700-weight grotesque
at 40px would otherwise sit comfortably inside. The coral is a
light colour and white on a light colour is always going to be
close. It is not the thinnest opening pairing under this heading -
hoodsiderz and rap-lore both open on white over an orange, at 2.5
and 2.7 - but it is in that company rather than in the company of
the packs it was cut from, which open at 3.7 and 3.2.
It opens on it anyway, because this is the show's own pairing and
the card is the brand - and because the whole point of `colors`
below is that the user is one button from the alternative. Black on
the same card is 7.1 to 1, the strongest pairing in the palette, so
a frame whose caption has to carry over a busy still has an answer
that costs one press. Anything that wants a guaranteed ratio out of
the box should change this value and the panel fill together; a
rule that forbade the brand pairing would be the pack overruling
the show.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does and for their reason: the point
is the PAIRING. Sixteen combinations of a white, a black, a coral
and a violet-magenta, and the ones worth having are the ones that
read. A palette that could only ever be used one way round would
be a palette of four cards, and this show's look is the pairing
rather than any one of them.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the two
neutrals, then the two brand colours - and the two defaults are
picked out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens
on the first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom
Hall of Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one
order.
The two brand colours are close enough in value that neither reads
on the other: #BB15D9 on the coral card is 1.7 to 1, and the coral
on the violet card is the same 1.7 the other way up. Those two are
the only pairings of DIFFERENT colours here that fail - the four
combinations of a colour with itself fail for the obvious reason.
All six are left available, for the reason the packs either side
give about white on white - the two lists are independent because
the pairing
is the feature, and a rule barring the combinations that fail would
cost the panel more explaining than an invisible caption costs a
user who can see it is invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Proxima Nova Black, in the same colour as
the rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and beauty-hacks' both. That the step climbs -
700 to 900, the way Hall of Femme climbs 200 to 800 - and that a
step this short makes a quiet highlight are measured out in
beauty-hacks, which is where that argument belongs and is not
repeated. This pack ran it the other way round until the seven
shows cut to that design were turned together.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Coral, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching
this value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be
written in the order the show states its colours in while the
channel still opens on white type and a coral card.
#FE6262 is a soft warm red, which is a lighter card than either of
the packs this was cut from carries - Hall of Femme's hot pink and
beauty-hacks' magenta are both mid-value colours and this is not.
The card is the shape that is a fifth of the frame and reads before
anything on it, so it is what carries the colour - and its being
this light is exactly what makes the note on `color` above
necessary.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.

channels.name: Crowned Ladies FR
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the
rewrite, the block at the foot of the frame and every number in it are
the same and are named here rather than restated. What makes this show
itself is one sentence long - it is set in Helvetica, in one magenta,
on the photograph itself with no card under it and with no highlight -
and everything below is that sentence.
The FR in the name is the account's, the way the DE in Hall of Femme
DE is and the FR in Soccer Stories FR and Inkjection FR: it says which
of the brand's feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What
lands on the frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying,
put through the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every
channel here; nothing in this pack changes that, and everything the app
itself says is English like the rest of it (see CLAUDE.md).
One thing this pack checked that its English-feed siblings had no
reason to, and that the two DE feeds and Inkjection FR checked before
it. The Helvetica file carries 2012 codepoints and covers what French
actually needs - the acute and the grave, the circumflex and the
diaeresis on the vowels that take them, the cedilla, the o-e ligature
in both cases, the angle quotes French sets speech in and the curly
apostrophe it elides with - so a caption is drawn from the file rather
than from whatever the browser substitutes for a missing glyph, which
would be a different face at a width nothing measured. Worth stating
because a face chosen for how it looks in English is not automatically
a face that can SET another language, and the check is two minutes
against a cmap.
A folder of its own rather than a second colourway of Hall of Femme,
for the reason oh-my-goal-news is a folder of its own: the person
picking a channel at the top of the app picks this one or that one and
never both, and these two do not merely disagree about colour - they
are set in different type, one of them has no card at all and one of
them has no highlight, which is as far as two packs under one heading
go.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Helvetica, in one magenta, straight onto the PHOTOGRAPH with no
card behind it, and every line of every caption is set the same way.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is
the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show, and then states the two keys the missing card forces:
`shadow`, which has to come back, and `panel`, which has to be said out
loud to go away.
Helvetica is the plainest thing a caption here has been set in, and
that is the brand rather than a shortage of ideas. Its siblings pick a
face with a voice - a hairline, a hand, a serif, a condensed display
cut - and then spend a card or a halo making that voice survive a
photograph. This one picks the face that has been the neutral of signage
for seventy years, which is the one kind of type that can stand on an
unknown picture without an argument: even strokes at a single weight,
closed apertures, no thins for a photograph to eat. What it needs from
this pack is not rescuing but separation, and that is the shadow below.
Uppercased, inherited, for the reason every one of its neighbours is:
at 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short
beats rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in.
It costs nothing here - Helvetica's capitals are the half of the face
the world knows it by.

_comment_color: A magenta, and it is the whole palette rather than the first of
several: this show is set in one colour. It is therefore also what
every frame is drawn in, since a frame stores no colour of its own
until it is given one and there is no swatch here to give it one
with (see state.textColorFor).
It is the loudest thing this heading has put on a photograph, and on
a channel with no card that is the point. A caption with no ground
under it is separated from the picture by two things only - its
colour and its shadow - and a colour that occurs in almost no
photograph is doing half of that work before the shadow is asked for
anything. Skin, hair, daylight, studio walls: none of them is this.
Which frame is the risky one follows from where the colour sits. Its
relative luminance is about 0.27, so it stands roughly six times
clear of a black and only three times clear of a white - a night
still holds it easily and a blown, sunlit one is where it thins out.
That is the still the shadow below is chosen for, and it is why the
shadow is a dark one.
_comment_colors: Absent, and that is the palette being stated rather than forgotten.
Hall of Femme, the pack this is cut from, offers rows of swatches
because its look IS the pairing - which of its colours is the card
and which is the type. This show has one colour and no card, so
there is no pairing to offer and nothing for a second button to be.
Left unstated rather than written as a list of one, which is the
answer Inkjection FR reached in the same position: a row of one
swatch is a control that cannot change anything - it draws the
colour already on screen, marked as chosen, and clicking it does
nothing a user can see. That is the one kind of control this panel
does not have anywhere (see the note on `alignable` in js/editor.js).
With no list the whole block of colour rows is hidden instead - see
editor.paletteOf, which hides a row whose colours have nothing to
recolour, and renderColorButtons, which drops the block when no row
survives.
Nothing counts these lists, so the day this show wants a second
colour it is one key in this file and the row appears.
_comment_shadow: An exception to the preset, and the first of the two keys the
missing card forces.
The preset states no shadow, and its reasoning is exact: there is a
solid slab under those letters in a colour the user picked, it
separates them from the photograph completely, and a shadow as well
would only smear the inside of the card. Take the card away and
every word of that stops being true - these letters are on a
photograph, with grain and edges and whatever was behind the subject
running through them.
A DARK shadow, which is the opposite of what Inkjection FR does with
the other cardless caption under this heading, and the two are the
same decision made about two different colours. That channel's navy
is nearly black, so a black shadow under it would be dark on dark
and it carries a white halo instead. This magenta sits in the middle
of the range and is in trouble at the light end rather than the dark
one (see `color` above): it is a bright still that swallows it, and
what a mid-tone letter needs on a bright ground is a dark edge.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow in
js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They are what
every channel in this app that sets type on a photograph uses, which
is the same job this is; a pack with no reason of its own should not
carry a number it merely agrees with, and where it has to state one
anyway it should state the one already in use.
_comment_highlight: None. Every line of every caption on this channel is set the same
way, and the highlight buttons stand where they stand everywhere
else and go dead with a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderHlButtons). A brand whose lines are all one treatment
says so here rather than being given a highlight nobody could tell
apart from the type - see `highlight` in js/channels.js.
All three things a highlight could be are unavailable to this show,
and they run out in order. A change of CUT is what most of this
heading picks its words out with, and the app carries one cut of
Helvetica; asking for a second weight of it would be the browser
emboldening the one file there is, and a synthesised weight is
measured as well as drawn. A recolour needs a second colour, and
this show has one. And a box needs a fill, which would be a second
colour again - and a graphic in the one frame under this heading
whose whole design is type lying directly on the picture.
Written as null rather than left out, for the reason `panel` below
is: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the preset's word-scope colour highlight arrives
whatever this pack says about it. Null is how a pack cut from that
preset declines the feature.
There is no `colors.highlight` either - there is no palette here at
all - so nothing draws a swatch row for words that cannot be picked
out (see editor.paletteOf, which hides that row on a channel with no
highlight).
_comment_panel: None, and its absence is half of this channel's design. Written as
null rather than left out, which is the opposite of what
laugh-society-snapchat does and is right for the opposite reason:
that pack inherits nothing, so a key restating the skeleton's own
null would read as a slab somebody had switched off. This one takes
the Snapchat caption preset, and the preset states a card - its
shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow. Null here is what
removes it, and it has to be said out loud.
Why drop it. On Hall of Femme the card and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the slab is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk.
Helvetica at 400 has no such problem, so a card under it would be a
fifth of the frame of flat colour spent on a difficulty this face
does not have - and it would cover the picture the captions exist to
show.
There is no `colors.panel` either, so the swatch row that fills a
card on most of its siblings is not drawn at all rather than drawn
dead (see editor.paletteOf).

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading - and like
Conspiracy Central this is a channel where the usual reason does not
apply, because its siblings say the gradient has nothing to do when a
title is on a card rather than on the photograph, and this title IS on
the photograph.
It still has nothing to do. The backend's gradient is a SIDE gradient -
full height, never past half the width, peaking on whichever side the
title column is (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient) - because it was
drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline set beside the subject.
There is no title column on a captured still: the block lies across the
width of the frame, and darkening one half of forty pictures would shade
half of every caption and leave the other half exactly as it was.
No `scrim` either, which is the tool that WOULD reach across the foot of
the frame. Laugh Society throws one and sets white type on it, and that
pairing is what a scrim is for. Under a magenta the trade is worse than
it looks: the shade would buy this colour a little at the light end of
the range, where the dark shadow is already helping, and cost it at the
dark end, where the caption and the shade are the same kind of dark.
What holds this type off the photograph is its own drop shadow, one
letter at a time, which leaves all forty pictures whole.

channels.name: Crowned Ladies NW
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame, the
palette handed to the user, the highlight that changes FACE and not
colour - all of it is Hall of Femme's and is named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long: it is set
in Cormorant Garamond with picked words in Great Vibes, on a plum
card, in a champagne the user can swap for the card's own colour. The
casing is the one further thing it changes, and it changes it because
the faces leave it no choice - see `uppercase` below.
The NW in the name is the account's, the way the FR is in Crowned
Ladies FR and the DE in Hall of Femme DE: it says which of the brand's
feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What lands on the
frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put through
the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel here,
and everything the app itself says is English like the rest of it (see
CLAUDE.md).
It shares a brand with Crowned Ladies FR and shares no design with it,
which is worth saying out loud because the two folders sort next to
each other and somebody will assume one was copied from the other.
That feed is Helvetica, one magenta, no card and no highlight, set
straight onto the photograph. This one was cut from Hall of Femme
instead, on the instruction that it follow that pack: it keeps the
card, keeps the palette and keeps the two-face highlight. They are two
accounts of one brand and not two colourways of one pack, and a change
to either is not a change to the other.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the pack it was cut from, which is
in the type and in the two colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme
sets its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline for the block,
the 800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card, in sixteen pairings
the user chooses between. This one is set in Cormorant Garamond with
picked words in Great Vibes, on a plum card, in four pairings of that
plum and a champagne.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the freeform text
box, the shape of the card, its padding and corners and shadow, where
the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the Snapchat caption
design and is stated once, in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
This pack states what makes it this show, and then states the one key
the faces force it to override.
The pairing is the idea. A Garamond and a copperplate script are what
an invitation is set in, and they are drawn to sit together: the serif
carries the sentence and the script is what a name or a title is
written in. That is the same division of labour Hall of Femme gets out
of one family's two ends, arrived at with two different kinds of
writing instead of two weights - see `highlight`.
Both faces are light, and on this heading that is normally the
argument for a card (Hall of Femme's own note makes it: a hairline
over an unknown photograph is the one thing a caption must never be).
The card is kept here for exactly that reason and not merely because
the pack it was copied from had one - a high-contrast serif has thins
that go to nothing over a blown-out still, and a joined script has
hairline joins that go first.

_comment_face: Cormorant Garamond Regular. Which cut of the family that is, why
the full name rather than 'Cormorant Garamond' is declared, and
what happens when the file is missing are all written out in
content/faces/cormorant-garamond-regular.json rather than repeated
here.
One consequence of the face reaches this pack, and it is worth
knowing before anybody changes the casing back. A Garamond has a
small lower case relative to its capitals - 386 units of the em
against 625 - so at the preset's stated 40px the x-height is 15.4px
where Hall of Femme's Telegraf gives 20.0px. Set in lower case, a
caption here reads a little smaller than the same caption on its
neighbours.
That is accepted rather than corrected. `fontSize` is 40 on every
channel under this heading and no pack has ever overridden it: the
preset's argument is that burned-in speech is ONE size, always, and
a pack that nudged it because its own face is delicate would be the
first crack in that. The capitals lose almost nothing by comparison
- 25.0px against 26.6px - so what the size costs is a consequence of
the casing below and not of the size.
_comment_uppercase: Off, and this is the one guideline of Hall of Femme's that this
pack breaks. It is the third channel under the heading to break it
- Killer Bites and Re-belle are the others, and Re-belle's note is
the one to read beside this, because the reason is the same reason
arriving from a different direction.
The preset's argument for capitals is that at 40px with twenty
characters to a line a caption is three short beats rather than a
paragraph, and beats are what capitals are for. That argument is
about grotesques. Neither face here is one, and the highlight face
is the one that settles it: Great Vibes is a copperplate script,
and a copperplate script has no capitals in the sense the preset
means. Its letters are drawn to JOIN, and the joins live in the
lower case. Set in capitals it comes apart into a row of
unconnected swash initials - not a louder version of the same hand
but a different and far harder object to read.
It is measurably worse as well as visually worse, which is why this
is not a matter of taste. Great Vibes' capitals are 44% wider than
Cormorant's for the same string, and they reach 34.4px above the
baseline and 16.0px below at 40px against its lower case's 25.2 and
14.0. A picked word in capitals would therefore be both the widest
thing on its line by a long way and the thing that sets the height
of every card in the block - two words swelling a caption in both
directions, which is the opposite of what picking a word out is
supposed to do.
The block's own face agrees for a quieter reason. A Garamond's
lower case is the half of it anyone recognises - the long
ascenders, the small round bowls, the descenders that hang - and set
in capitals it becomes a perfectly good inscriptional serif that
could be any of fifty others. The face was chosen for what it is;
capitals would spend it.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so turning it
off changes only what the canvas does: the text box held the user's
own casing all along, and the highlight buttons already offered the
words as the canvas would set them (see the `cased` note in
js/text.js and editor.renderWordButtons).
`uppercase` is the block's and there is one of it, so this reaches
the picked words too. That is the answer both faces wanted, which is
the whole of why it can be one key.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below, so the
champagne swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame.
Champagne letters on the plum card is the pairing this show opens
on, and with a palette of two the only decision here is which of
them is the CARD. It opened the other way round - plum type on a
champagne card - on the argument that the card is a fifth of the
frame and a shape that size in the plum is a dark slab over the
picture the stills exist to show. That is still true and it is no
longer the answer: this is the brand colour, and on a heading where
every other show puts its colour on the card, a caption that carried
it only in the letters read as the pale card belonging to nobody.
The slab is the plum and the type is the champagne on it.
Contrast is unchanged by the swap, which is what makes it free:
9.6 to 1 either way round, the widest margin any pack under this
heading carries and what a high-contrast serif with thin strokes
actually needs. What the swap does cost is the picture - a dark card
covers more of the still than a pale one appears to - and the
preset's shadow stops earning its keep, since it was written to
survive a pale slab thrown onto a pale wall and now falls from a
dark one. Neither is worth a number of this pack's own: the shadow
is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in the preset.
The other three pairings are a button away, the inverse among them.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and for
the card behind them - two buttons each in the title panel (see
editor.renderColorButtons).
The same two in both lists and in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is the
PAIRING. Four combinations of a plum and a champagne, and the two
worth having are the two that read. A palette that could only ever
be used one way round would be a palette of one card, and this
show's look is the pairing rather than either colour on its own.
Two colours rather than the four Hall of Femme offers, and that is
the brand and not an unfinished list - the two that were asked for
are the two the show has. Nothing counts these entries - the panel
draws a swatch per colour and the row wraps - so a third is one
string in this file the day the show has one.
Nothing stops the user setting plum on plum. That is not an
oversight either: the two lists are independent because the pairing
is the feature, and with a palette this short a rule barring the two
matching combinations would be a rule removing half the buttons. The
user can see the caption has gone and presses the other swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a different
FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type is has one
answer and not two. That matters more on a palette of two than on
one of four: with the block in champagne, a highlight left to pick
its own colour from the same list could only ever be plum, and plum
on plum is a picked word that vanishes into its card.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Great Vibes, in the same colour as the rest
of the block. The highlight here is the KIND OF WRITING: a Garamond
and a copperplate script on one line, which is the pairing an
invitation has used for three hundred years - the sentence is
typeset and the name in it is written.
It is Hall of Femme's highlight with the technique swapped. That
pack picks words out by weight, 200 against 800 of one family, on
the argument that at that contrast it is as loud as a box would be
and leaves the card one clean shape instead of a shape with a second
shape inside it. Both halves of that argument survive the swap: a
script in the middle of a serif is at least as loud as two weights
of one family, and it costs the card nothing.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated, and because a highlight that changed colour as well
as hand would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives - and it is
an argument this channel depends on more than most. What a script is
FOR is a word: a name, a place, the thing the clip turns on. A whole
line of it would be handwriting pretending to be a caption.
One consequence is worth knowing before picking many words at once.
Every box in the block takes one shared vertical band, and the band
is the union of what every row needs (see js/text.js), so a row
carrying a Great Vibes word makes every card in the caption as tall
as that word's ascenders and descenders ask for - about 43px at 40px
against the 27px a row of Telegraf capitals asks for on Hall of
Femme. A four-line caption here is therefore a visibly taller stack
than the same caption there. It is still inside the frame with room
to spare, since the block stands on the preset's 120px margin and
grows upward from it, and `maxBlockHeightRatio` does not pull it in:
at a stated `fontSize` there is no size left to shrink, which the
preset says where it states the size.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are on
a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts the one
shadow there is. A drop shadow under a script this fine would smear
the joins that make it a script.
_comment_panel: Plum, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are the
Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the first entry in `colors.panel` above and the type is the
second, which is the freedom Hall of Femme's note points out: the
swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching this value and not
by being listed first, so both rows stay written in one order
whichever way round the show opens.
The preset's shadow is half opaque and falls straight down, and its
note argues it from the hardest case a card can face - a white slab
thrown onto a white wall. A plum card is not that case and the
shadow does less here than it does next door. It is kept without a
number of this pack's own, because a card that casts no shadow at
all is a card printed on the photograph rather than lying on it,
and because the fill is the one thing about this card that is the
show's.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
There is a second reason here that its hot pink parent does not have.
This card is pale and the type on it is dark, so a gradient behind the
card would change nothing about the caption and would only darken the
picture the card already covers a fifth of.

channels.name: Determined
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack — the frame fetch,
the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the card the
caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in the same
numbers. What makes it a different show is the two things that are
visible from across a room: the face the words are set in, and the
colours they are set in.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and its siblings. Hall
of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline for
the block and the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card. Fitness
Story sets them in Hanken Grotesk, upright against italic, on an
electric blue one. This one sets them in Open Sans Italic, with the
Bold Italic for a picked word, on an acid yellow one.
The face is the plainest of the three, and that is what it is for.
Telegraf's hairline is a look before it is a text face and Hanken
Grotesk has enough drawing in it to be recognised; Open Sans is the
face people read without noticing they are reading it. On a show
whose graphic is the CARD — a slab of a colour nobody can ignore,
covering a fifth of the frame — that is the right division of labour:
the colour is the brand and the type is the sentence, and a face with
opinions would be a second thing arguing with the yellow.
The whole block is set in the ITALIC, not in the upright, which is
the one thing here that is a voice rather than a convenience. Every
other pack under this heading sets its captions upright and reserves
the slant, if it has one, for a picked word; this show leans the
entire sentence. On a caption that is three short beats of capitals
on a flat card, a slant across all of it reads as momentum — which
is what the show is called after — where the same slant on one word
in an upright line would only read as emphasis.
Fight Source, beside it, is set in the same family and shares this
pack's italic — one face pack, used by both, rather than two copies
of it, which is what faces/ is for. It is the upright that show sets
its blocks in, so the two are told apart twice over: this one leans
and that one does not, and the colours below are nothing like that
show's white and black on a black card.
Two consequences follow from the face, and both are the ones a
reader coming from the sibling packs will be looking for.
The first is that the slab is not holding the type up, exactly as it
is not on Fitness Story. Hall of Femme's card and its hairline are
one decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph
disappears, and the card is what makes that weight a choice rather
than a risk. A 400-weight humanist sans does not need rescuing that
way. The card is kept regardless, because it is the form this design
IS — a statement laid on the picture rather than words burned into it
— and because the colour pairing below is the show's look and there
is nowhere else to put it.
The second is what the highlight had to become once the block was
already slanted. Fitness Story can highlight with the italic because
its block is upright; here that door is shut, and weight is the only
axis left. So a picked word is the Bold Italic — the same slant, at
700 against the block's 400.
It went through the SemiBold on the way, and the reason it did not
stay there is worth keeping. 400 against 600 is a real step when you
are looking for it and a weak one when you are not, and NOT looking
for it is the condition this type is read under: a still scrolled
past on a phone, where the picked word has to be found before the
sentence is. Inside an all-italic block of capitals it had even less
to work with than it would upright, because the slant that would
otherwise set the word apart is already spent on every word around
it. 400 against 700 is the step that survives that.
The usual objection to the Bold applies and is accepted rather than
answered: this face was chosen for being the one people read without
noticing, and the Bold is where a plain face stops being invisible.
That is a price paid on one word in three lines, and it buys the
only signal the highlight has left. It is still short of Telegraf's
200 against its 800, which is the loudest a family gets, and the
block around it stays the quiet 400 the show is set in.
It also keeps the slant off the highlight's list of jobs, which is
worth stating because it looks like a loss and is not. A block where
the picked word is the only thing leaning tells the reader that word
is different; a block where everything leans and the picked word is
heavier tells them the same thing, and tells them the sentence has a
voice at the same time. One signal was spent on the show and the
other on the word.
Uppercased, for the reason every pack under this heading is: at 40px
with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in. It
does one thing more on a slanted block: capitals have no descenders
and few of the ambiguous shapes an italic lower-case leans into, so
the slant stays a property of the line rather than something the
reader has to work around.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the four in `colors`
below, so the black swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
Black letters on the yellow card is the pairing this show opens
on, and unlike the opening pairings of the three shows cut to this
same design there is nothing to weigh up about it. #EBFF00 is
the brightest colour in the palette by a distance, so black on
it is the largest contrast the four colours can produce in
either direction; it is the
pairing the grey and the white are both quieter versions of.
White on this yellow is the one combination here that genuinely
does not work, and it is a swatch the user can still press — see
the note on `colors`.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason
hall-of-femme states at length: the point is the PAIRING.
Sixteen combinations of an acid yellow, a mid grey, a white and a
black, and the ones worth having are the ones that read — black
on yellow, yellow on black, white on grey, yellow on grey, grey
on white. A palette of four colours that could only ever be used
one way round would be a palette of four cards, and this show's
look is the pairing rather than any one of them.
This palette is built differently from either sibling's, and it
is worth saying how. Hall of Femme and Fitness Story each pair
two brand colours with the two neutrals, so their sixteen
combinations are four loud ones and twelve quiet ones. Here there
is ONE colour and three values of grey — yellow, #626262, white,
black — which makes the palette a brightness ladder with a single
chromatic rung. What that buys is a show that can go from
shouting to almost sober without leaving its own colours: the
yellow card is the brand at full volume, the grey card is the
same design for a frame that should not shout, and the yellow is
still there as the ink on it.
#626262 is the rung that makes that work, and it is a mid grey on
purpose rather than a dark one. It has to be a ground the white
and the yellow both read on AND ink that reads on the white, and
those two jobs pull in opposite directions — anything darker
stops being distinguishable from the black card, anything lighter
stops holding white type. At this value it does both, and the one
thing it does not do is carry black type, which is a pairing the
eye rejects on sight.
Absolute black rather than a soft near-black, and it is the one
colour here whose exact value matters. It is the ink the yellow
is loudest against and the ground the yellow is loudest on, and a
#111 that reads as black on a monitor turns into a grey slab
beside a genuinely black picture on a phone — which on this
palette would also put it within touching distance of the #626262
and turn two rungs of the ladder into one. There is nothing for
it to be too harsh against: the card is a flat shape, not a
photograph seen through it.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or white on the
yellow. That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent
because the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the
combinations that do not read would cost the panel more
explaining than an illegible caption costs the user, who can see
it is illegible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in the Bold Italic, in the same colour as
the rest of the block. The colour it names is the block's, so the
recolour draws exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the
face is the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated — and moved to black with
it, since a highlight that changed colour as well as weight would
be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from snapchat-caption, which is also
where the argument for word scope is written down. Nothing here
disagrees with it; what this pack adds is which face the picked
word is set in, and the note above on why it is a weight.
The two faces are the same slant at the same size, which makes
this a gentler form of the two-face highlight than an upright
against an italic: the run boundaries fall between letters that
lean identically, so the join a run costs its kerning at is not
somewhere the eye is already looking. What is measured across it
is still two sets of metrics — see `styleFor` in js/text.js — and
the Bold Italic is the wider of the two by about 5% on a word of
capitals, so a picked word makes its line longer as well as
darker. Under this heading's stated `fontSize` that costs the
line its length and nothing else: there is no fit left to
retrigger, so a highlighted word cannot resize the block around
it the way it could under a size fit.
_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on, in whichever of the four colours
the frame is wearing. Every number in it is hall-of-femme's, and
the long argument for each is there rather than repeated here:
one box per LINE and `joined`, so the background is a single
shape that steps in and out with the sentence instead of a
rectangle the width of its longest line; 12 of padding, which is
a highlighter's margin and not a card's; no border, because a
keyline would make the slab read as a box drawn over the picture
rather than as a card lying on it; 13 of corner radius, the
number every background under this heading is rounded by; and a
soft shadow falling straight down, which has to survive being
thrown by a white slab onto a white wall.
The fill is the one line here that is this show's own. The yellow
is the brand and the card is the bigger surface — a fifth of the
frame, read before anything set on it — so the yellow is the card
and not the letters. This and `color` above are also the only
place the opening look is stated: the two lists in `colors` are
written in one order so the two rows of buttons read as the same
palette twice, which means neither of them can decide what an
untouched frame wears.
The shadow earns its keep more here than on either sibling. This
yellow is brighter than most of what a photograph contains, so
the card does not separate from the picture by being darker than
it the way a blue or a pink slab does — the shadow under it is
most of what says the card is lying ON the frame rather than
having been cut out of it.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, for hall-of-femme's reason: it exists to hold a
title legible against the photograph, and this title is not against
the photograph at all — it is on a slab of its own. A scrim over
every still would darken forty pictures to solve a problem the card
has already solved.

makes it this show.

round O and a tall x-height, and set in capitals at 40px it is the
blunt, even, poster-like line that sports captions have always been
set in. The app carries one cut of it and one only (see the face
pack), which is no shortcoming at caption size on a card - a geometric
face is at its most legible exactly where it is least decorated - but
it is what decides the highlight below.

Two colours rather than Hall of Femme's four, and that is the

Nothing counts the lists - the panel draws a swatch per entry and

_comment_highlight: None, and this is the one place the pack parts company with the
Snapchat caption design. The preset gives its channels a
word-scope highlight in colour mode; this one switches it off
outright, and the reason is the face.
Every sibling under this heading picks a word out by changing its
CUT and keeping its colour. Hall of Femme sets its captions in
Telegraf UltraLight and a picked word in UltraBold, Determined and
Fight Source swap an Open Sans for its bold, Fitness Story runs
Hanken Grotesk's two ends against each other. That is why the
preset chooses colour mode over box mode in the first place - the
words are already on a solid ground of their own, so a rectangle
behind them would be a shape inside a shape, and the change of cut
is loud enough without one.
This channel has no second cut to change to. The app carries one
weight of League Spartan, the show is set in League Spartan, and
that is the whole of the family available to it. Neither way round
that is worth having:
- A synthesised bold is a stroke laid over letters drawn without
one, and it is MEASURED as well as drawn - the caption would be
laid out against a face nobody chose, which is the failure
fontguard exists to catch, only self-inflicted.
- A picked word in the palette's other colour is the CARD's
colour, and on the card that is a picked word nobody can see.
- A box behind the picked word would work, but it is a second
shape inside the card and a second thing for the user to
colour, and this channel is deliberately two questions wide.
So the pack says so in as many words rather than shipping a
highlight nobody could tell apart from the type. `null` is how
that is said, and it is a stated position rather than a key left
out (see `highlight` in js/channels.js): every line of every
caption on this channel is set the same way.
What the user sees is the highlight buttons still standing where
they stand on every other channel and going dead, with a tooltip
saying whose decision that was (see editor.renderHlButtons). That
is the point of leaving them there. A control that vanished on
some channels and not others would read as the panel rearranging
itself; one that is present and locked reads as a channel that
does not do this, which is exactly what it is.
Noisy Dish is the other pack under this heading that says null,
and it says it for its own reason. This one is worth knowing
before the palette is ever touched, because it is not permanent:
the day a second weight of League Spartan is dropped into fonts/
this channel can have Hall of Femme's highlight exactly - a second
face pack, `highlight.face` naming it, and nothing else changes.

_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the pack it was cut from, which is
in the face and the colours and nowhere else. Hall of Femme sets its
captions in Telegraf on a hot pink card, in sixteen pairings of four
colours. This one sets them in Kallisto on a navy card, in nine

_comment_face: Kallisto Medium. Which cut that is, why the full name rather than
'Kallisto' is declared, and what the machine may already know it
by are written out in content/faces/kallisto-medium.json rather
than repeated here.
It is a wide squarish techno sans, and the width is the one thing
about it worth knowing before a caption is set on it. Its capitals
average 0.753em, which makes it the widest block face under this
heading, and at the preset's 40px on a 540-wide frame that is
about 27px a character against the 486px a line has. So the lines
break at roughly eighteen characters and the preset's `maxChars`
of 20 is never what stops them: of the two ceilings the preset
states, the width is the one this face runs into first.
That is a fact to know rather than a problem to fix. The two
ceilings exist to ask different questions - what the frame holds,
and what a viewer reads at a glance (see `maxChars` in
js/channels.js) - and a face wide enough to answer the first more
strictly than the second is a face whose lines are already inside
what a glance reads. Hall of Femme is the other way round at
0.660em, where twenty characters fit the width and the character
ceiling is what breaks the line.
A 500-weight face is legible over a photograph for the reason Hall
of Femme's 200-weight one is: it is not over the photograph at
all, it is on a card in a colour somebody chose. On this show the
argument is barely needed - the Medium is a solid mid weight with
squared, closed forms and would hold its own on a still - but the
card is what makes the weight a choice instead of a risk taken
forty times a run.

Which ones read is unusually lopsided here, and it is worth having
written down rather than discovered: the navy is the only dark
colour of the three, so it is one half of every pairing that
works. Yellow on navy is 16.7 to 1, white on navy 18.9, and both
of those the other way up. The two light colours against each
other are 1.1 to 1 - a yellow caption on a white card is not a
weak pairing, it is an invisible one.
That is not an oversight either, and it is Hall of Femme's
argument applied to a palette that happens to be two lights and a
dark. The two lists are independent because the pairing is the
feature, and a rule barring the combinations that do not read
would cost the panel more explaining than an invisible caption
costs a user, who can see it is invisible and presses another
swatch.
The absolute white is meant as written: #FFFFFF, not an off-white
pulled towards either of the others. It is the show's second way
of setting type on the navy and the only alternative to the
yellow, so what it is for is being the neutral - a white with a
cast in it would be a third brand colour nobody chose.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the brand
yellow, the neutral, the ground - and the two defaults are picked
out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens on the
first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom Hall of
Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one order.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Kallisto Heavy, in the same colour as the
rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and rap-lore's both.
500 against 900 is nearly the whole of what this family has, and
it is a loud highlight - closer to Hall of Femme's 200 against 800
than to rap-lore's single step of Montserrat. It can be, because
these two cuts are within two percent of each other in width
(0.753em against 0.768em): the picked word arrives heavier without
arriving wider, so the sentence keeps the rhythm it was wrapped
with and the card keeps its shape. Hall of Femme's two cuts are
ten percent apart on that measure and the highlight works there
too - this is the same gesture with less of that cost, not a
quieter one.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Navy, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching
this value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be
written in the order the show states its colours in while the
channel still opens on yellow type and a navy card.
#0C0938 is the darkest card under this heading, where the
neighbours run to pinks, magentas, reds and one orange, and that
is what makes this show itself at a glance: the card is the shape
that is a fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it, so
it is what carries the colour, and the type is what has to stay
legible against it. A near-black navy is also the one ground both
of the show's other colours read on, which is why the note on
`colors` above can be so short about which pairings work.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.

channels.name: Expulsion Science
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's
and is taken from the same presets rather than restated: the frame
fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite
that turns speech into report, the stated 40px, the twenty characters
to a line, the freeform text box, the drag.
What makes it a different show is the face and the colour. It is set
in Montserrat Bold, in one purple, with picked words in Montserrat
ExtraBold - and with no card under any of it, which is the one place
it parts company with the pack it was cut from and the one place that
costs more than a value. That is argued below.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and Hall of Femme.
Set in Montserrat Bold, in #665282, with picked words in Montserrat
ExtraBold and no card behind the block. Everything else - the size,
where the lines break, the capitals, the freeform box, the drag, the
margin off the foot of the frame - is the Snapchat caption design and
is stated once, in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
Two things this pack overrides in that preset, and the second follows
from the first. The card is dropped, so the type is over the
photograph; therefore the drop shadow comes back, because that is
what holds type legible over a photograph nobody chose the contrast
of. The highlight is NOT promoted to a box along with it, and that is
a deliberate departure from what Conspiracy Central did on dropping
its own card - see the highlight note, which is where the cost of it
is written down rather than hidden.
Uppercased, inherited, for the reason every pack under this heading
is: at 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is three
short beats rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are
set in. Montserrat has no lower case anybody would call the brand,
and its capitals are geometric enough to carry a line of them.

_comment_color: The one colour this show is set in, on every frame, for good.
Unlike Hall of Femme it offers no palette (see below), so this is
THE colour rather than the colour a frame opens on.
It is a mid-dark purple, which on a card would be an unremarkable
choice and over a photograph is the reason the shadow below is
stated. Nothing else in the frame is this show's: no card, no
box, no second colour at a picked word. One purple and a weight
step is the whole of the brand, so the purple has to be the
purple - it is not adjusted to suit a background, because there
is no background for it to be adjusted against.
_comment_shadow: Back, and this is the one sentence in the preset this pack
contradicts. Every channel under this heading sets `shadow` to
null, on the argument that a drop shadow is what keeps type
legible over a photograph nobody chose the contrast of and there
is no photograph under those letters - there is a solid card
doing the job completely.
The argument is right, and it is exactly why dropping the card
means picking the shadow back up. There IS a photograph under
these letters, on all forty stills. A purple this deep is worse
off than the near-white Conspiracy Central hangs over its frames:
white only disappears into the bright end of a picture, where
#665282 has a dark end and a bright end to lose itself in, and a
captured still is whatever the video happened to be showing.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow
in js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They
are what every channel that sets type on a photograph in this app
uses, which is the same job this is; a pack with no reason of its
own should not carry a number it merely agrees with, and where it
has to state one anyway it should state the one already in use.
_comment_colors: Absent, and worth the note because the pack this one was cut from
is the pack that INVENTED the feature - sixteen pairings of four
colours in two rows of swatches - and anyone reading the two side
by side will look for it here.
Two of the three rows could not be drawn even if somebody wanted
them. `colors.panel` needs a panel and there is none (see the
note on `colors` in js/channels.js), and `colors.highlight` needs
a highlight that IS a colour, where this one is a weight.
That leaves `colors.text`, and a list with one colour in it is a
row holding a single swatch that is already the answer: a button
that visibly does nothing, which is the one kind of control this
panel does not have anywhere (see the note on paletteOf in
js/editor.js). This show has one colour, so it states it as its
colour and not as its only option. If it is ever given a second,
the row is one line here and costs nothing to bring back.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Montserrat ExtraBold, in the same colour
as the rest of the block. The highlight here is WEIGHT, exactly
as it is on Hall of Femme: the colour it names is the block's, so
the recolour draws what its neighbours are drawn in and the face
is the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated - a highlight that
changed colour as well as weight would be two highlights.
What is worth being plain about is how much smaller the step is
here than the one it is copied from. Hall of Femme picks out
words at Telegraf 200 against 800, which is a family's two ends
and is as loud as a box; this is 700 against 800, one cut apart
in a text sans, and it is quieter than any other highlight under
this heading. On Hall of Femme's card that would still read,
because a card is a controlled ground. Over a photograph it is
the smallest signal this app draws.
It is still what the brand asked for, and it is left as asked
rather than rescued with a box. Conspiracy Central dropped its
card and promoted its highlight to a box in the same breath, on
the argument that a recolour of two words in a block of one
colour is two words in that same colour to anyone scrolling. The
argument applies here too - but a box needs a fill colour, a fill
colour is a second brand colour, and this show has one. Inventing
the second to make the first louder would be the pack deciding
what the brand is.
So the entry to change, the day this show wants a highlight that
carries at a scroll, is a `fill` beside a `mode` of box - not the
face, which is the part that was specified.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, and the scope is
worth keeping in view: word rather than line, because a caption's
line breaks are wherever the sentence ran out of width, so
picking a LINE out picks out a fragment rather than a thought.
The shadow is the third thing dropping the card costs, and it is
stated for the same reason `shadow` above is. The preset sets the
highlight's to null because its letters are on a card; these are
not, and a picked word over a photograph needs exactly the lift
its neighbours have. So it takes the block's own numbers rather
than a second set - a picked word here differs from the words
either side of it in weight, and in nothing else. Conspiracy
Central, the other pack under this heading with no card, does the
same.
_comment_panel: No card. This is the decision the rest of the pack is downstream
of, and the two consequences are the `shadow` above and the size
of the highlight beside it.
Stated as null rather than left out, because it cannot be left
out: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the card's shape, padding, corners and shadow
arrive from snapchat-caption.json whatever this pack says about
them. Null is how a pack cut from that preset declines the one
part of it that is a whole shape rather than a number.
One thing changes quietly with it and is easy to miss, and it is
not the margin. `bottomRatio` is measured to the block's own box
rather than to what is drawn (see blockTop0 in js/text.js), so
the box still bottoms out 120px off the foot of the frame here,
exactly as it does on a panelled sibling.
What changes is the box. Under a line-scope panel the card's
padding is inside the band the rows are stacked by, so dropping
the card makes the block SHORTER and the letters come down with
it: measured at two lines of twenty characters, this pack sets
the same sentence twenty pixels lower on the frame than Hall of
Femme does. It also stops anything hanging below the margin,
where the card used to put twelve pixels of padding and a shadow
of its own - so what is drawn ends higher even though the block
sits lower.
The margin is inherited unchanged all the same: 120px off the
foot of a 960-tall frame is measured against the player's own
furniture along the bottom edge, and that furniture does not move
because a card went away.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading - and like
Conspiracy Central this one needs its own sentence, because the usual
reason does not apply. Its siblings say the gradient has nothing to
do: their titles are on a card and not on the photograph. This one's
titles ARE on the photograph.
It still has nothing to do. The backend's gradient is a SIDE gradient
- full height, never past half the width, peaking on whichever side
the title column is (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient) - because it
was drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline set beside the
subject. There is no title column on a captured still: the block lies
across the width of the frame, and darkening one half of forty
pictures would shade half of every caption and leave the other half
exactly as it was. What holds this type off the photograph is its own
drop shadow, which is the tool for the job at this scale.

channels.name: FeedDrama
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite that turns speech into report, the stated
40px, the twenty characters to a line, the freeform text box, the
block at the foot of the frame and the drag are all the same and are
named here rather than restated. Where it parts company with Hall of
Femme is in three places, and all three are subtractions: a different
face, no card behind the type, and nothing picked out of it. For that
half of it the packs to read are buzzer-beater-de and
conspiracy-central, which are the other channels here that set their
captions straight onto the photograph.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to. It is written as one word because the
brand is - FeedDrama is a closed compound and not two words, so
'feed-drama' would be this file inventing a seam the name does not
have. The name itself is the brand, capitals and all.
_comment_order: Last under the heading, which is where a new show goes: the numbers
are a running order rather than a ranking, and new feeds have been
landing at the end of it since Hall of Femme DE took 920.
930, and the number had to be re-read twice while this one file was
being written. The heading ended at 927 when the pack was drafted, at
928 by the time it was first saved (Expulsion Science), and at 929 a
minute later (Crowned Ladies NW). That is the third and fourth
instance of what buzzer-beater-de's order note records happening at
924 and 926, and at this point it is the normal case rather than the
surprise: several packs are written against the same heading at once.
930 is in fact SHARED with Crowned Ladies NW, which moved onto it in
the seconds after this file was saved onto it. That is left standing
rather than chased, and the chase is the reason: two packs each
taking last-plus-one against a heading the other is also editing will
trade the number indefinitely, and the next read is as stale as the
last. A shared number is not an error - the server breaks the tie
alphabetically by name (see serve.py) - so Crowned Ladies NW sorts
above FeedDrama and this show is still last under the heading, which
is all the number was ever asked to say.
The rule buzzer-beater-de draws is still the right one and is worth
repeating because it is now cheap to get wrong: read the heading's
last number at the moment of SAVING, not at the moment of writing.
What this pack adds is the second half of it - when the read comes
back changed twice over, the collision is cheaper than the race.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in ITC Avant Garde Std Medium, in one bone white, straight onto the
photograph, with no card behind it and nothing picked out of it.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show and then declines two whole shapes that preset draws, which
is what buzzer-beater-de does and for the same reason.
Why no card. On Hall of Femme the slab and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the card is what turns that weight from a risk into a choice.
This show does not have that problem to solve. A geometric sans at
Medium is a real text weight with closed, circular counters and a cap
height of 740 - the letterforms are large and solid at 40px, and what
carries them is their shape rather than a ground behind them. A fifth
of the frame of flat colour under a face like that buys legibility it
already has and costs the footage the space. What is left is a
sentence lying on the picture: no graphic, no second shape, nothing
between the words and the frame.
The face is wide, which is the thing to know before editing the
layout. Twenty mixed capitals measure 500px against the 486px a line
has, so unlike most packs under this heading the frame's width and
the preset's twenty-character ceiling land in the same place rather
than the characters binding first - an unusually wide line breaks at
nineteen instead of twenty, which the wrapper does on its own and
nobody sees. Ordinary prose measures between 426px and 490px and
fits, though the top of that range is close enough to the line that
a sentence of round capitals is worth looking at rather than
assuming. The
measurements are in content/faces/itc-avant-garde-std-md.json, along
with the cap height and what it means for how large this reads next
to a sibling at the same stated size.
Uppercased, for the reason every one of its neighbours is: at 40px
with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in. It
costs this face nothing - Avant Garde's capitals are geometric
constructions on a circle and a triangle, and they are the half of
the face everybody recognises. Its lower case is the more unusual
half, so `uppercase: false` is the one line this pack would change if
the show ever decides that is the brand; Killer Bites is the pack
that has made that call.

_comment_color: Bone white, and it is what every frame is set in for good: this
channel offers no palette (see `_comment_colors` below), so this
is the colour rather than the colour a frame opens on.
#F3F3ED and not #FFFFFF, which is a real decision and not a value
to be tidied towards a round one. It is a white pulled a few
points off in all three channels and pulled furthest in blue, so
it reads as paper or bone rather than as screen white. Against
footage that is what keeps it from looking like a player's own
burned-in subtitle track, which is flat #FFFFFF everywhere it
appears - the caption is meant to read as something the show put
there. It is the same argument conspiracy-central makes for
#FEFEFD, one step further along.
There is no card for it to be read against, so what it is read
against is the footage, and a near-white sits near the top of the
lightness range: on night footage it is the brightest thing in
the frame, and on a blown-out sky or a white wall it is nearly
gone. That is what the shadow below is for, and it is the half of
the problem a shadow can actually solve.
If the show ever wants the other half solved, the two honest
remedies are the ones that change the brief rather than patch it:
a card, which is the decision `panel` declines, or a second
colour in a `colors` list for the user to switch to on a bright
still. Both are one edit to this file.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because most of its
siblings under this heading have one and the next person to copy
this folder will wonder where it went.
Two of the three could not be offered even if somebody wanted
them: `colors.panel` needs a panel and there is none, and
`colors.highlight` needs a highlight and there is none either -
the rows are hidden rather than drawn dead (see
editor.paletteOf).
The third is the decision fight-source-de argues and
buzzer-beater-de inherits, and this pack inherits it in turn. The
brief here names one text colour. One colour is one swatch, and a
row of one swatch is a button that is already pressed - the one
kind of control this panel does not have anywhere, because a
button that visibly does nothing reads as the app ignoring the
click. So the colour is stated as the channel's own answer, at
`color` above, which is where a decision the channel makes
belongs. A palette is for a channel where the CHOICE is part of
the look, which is what Hall of Femme's sixteen pairings are; it
is not a way of showing that a pack has a colour. The day this
show has a second colour the list is two strings in this file,
and it becomes a palette by being one.
_comment_shadow: Back, and this is the one place this pack contradicts a sentence
the preset writes. Every channel with a card sets `shadow` to
null on the argument that a drop shadow is what keeps type
legible over a photograph nobody chose the contrast of and there
is no photograph under those letters. The argument is right, and
it is exactly why dropping the card means picking the shadow back
up: there IS a photograph under these letters, on all forty
stills.
It works here for the reason it works on conspiracy-central and
buzzer-beater-de and does not on fight-source-de: a drop shadow
separates type from a picture by putting darkness behind it,
which does nothing for near-black type and everything for a
near-white.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow
in js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They
are what every channel that sets light type on a photograph in
this app uses, which is the same job this is; a pack with no
measurement of its own should not carry a number it merely
guessed at. This face takes them more happily than most - a 3px
hard offset was chosen under a heavy condensed grotesque, and
these terminals are cut square and thick enough to carry it.
_comment_highlight: None. Not a highlight that happens to look like the rest of the
block - none: `null` is how a channel says it has no highlight
FEATURE, and the word buttons in the title panel go dead with it
rather than offering a treatment nobody could see (see the note
on `highlight` in js/channels.js and editor.renderHlButtons).
It is in the brief, and it is also the answer this pack would
have arrived at. Every other channel under this heading picks
words out by changing something it has a second of: Hall of Femme
changes weight, 200 against 800 of one family; Conspiracy Central
changes colour and puts a box under it. This show is one weight
of one family, in one colour, on no card - so a highlight would
have to introduce a second face or a second colour, and either
would be the show acquiring a feature rather than the sentence
gaining an emphasis.
Worth naming what it would cost, so that it is declined on
purpose rather than by omission. ITC Avant Garde Gothic has real
drawn Demi and Bold cuts, and one of them beside this Medium
would be Hall of Femme's highlight exactly - weight against
weight on one family, which is the version of this that needs no
box and no second colour. It is not here because it is not in the
brief and because it is a second file in fonts/ and a second face
on one block (see `highlight.face` in js/channels.js, and what
two faces on one block cost in metrics). The day the show wants
it, that is the price.
_comment_panel: No card. The argument is in `_comment_title` above, and the
consequences are the `shadow` and the `highlight` beside it.
Stated as null rather than left out, because it cannot be left
out: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the card's shape, padding, corners and shadow
arrive from snapchat-caption.json whatever this pack says about
them. Null is how a pack cut from that preset declines the one
part of it that is a whole shape rather than a number.
The preset's `layout` survives intact and is what puts the block
at the foot of the frame, 120px up, where Hall of Femme's card
stands. That margin is measured to the first thing DRAWN, which
on a pack with no card and no box is the capitals themselves - so
this show's type sits a padding's worth lower than a panelled
sibling's does, exactly as Buzzer Beater DE's and Fight Source
DE's do. It is the one visible difference the missing card makes
to where the words are, and it is small enough to be worth
leaving rather than correcting with a number nobody measured.
`maxBlockHeightRatio` is inherited at 0.30 and no longer decides
