than on a panelled sibling, since there is no card padding for
the renderer to take out of the budget first (see BLOCK_BUDGET in
js/text.js).

channels.name: Fight Source
_comment_group: One of the shows under the Snapchat heading cut to Hall of Femme's
design, sitting between Fitness Story and Determined. Placed by its
neighbours rather than by an ordinal, because packs under this
heading arrive, are renumbered and go: 'the fifth show' is a number
nothing checks, wrong the first time one is added above it and
silently so. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack —
the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite,
the card the caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in
the same numbers. What makes it a different show is the two things
that are visible from across a room: the face the words are set in,
and the colours they are set in.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs cut to the same design.
Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline
for the block and the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card.
Fitness Story sets them in Hanken Grotesk, upright against italic, on
an electric blue one. Determined sets them in the Open Sans italic
with the Bold italic for a picked word, on an acid yellow one. This
one is set in exactly those two cuts, on a card that is black or white
and nothing else.
That last sentence is the thing to be honest about rather than to
write around: this pack and Determined are set identically, and the
palette is the whole of what tells them apart. Both arrived at the
same two cuts from different directions — that show wanted momentum
under a colour nobody can ignore, this one wanted a sentence said in
motion with no colour in the way — and one face pack serving both is
what faces/ is for. Two packs agreeing is not two copies of anything.
What they agree on is worth stating in this pack's own words. A block
set entirely in the italic is the same sentence said leaning forward
— the thing italic does before it means emphasis, which is why it
stops meaning emphasis once every word is in it. On a show cut from
footage of people fighting, that lean is the show: the caption is not
a label under a picture, it is a line said in motion.
Which is what settles the highlight, and it is the pack's other
decision. With the slant spent on the block there is nothing left for
a picked word to lean into, so the emphasis has to be WEIGHT: the
Bold italic, 700 against 400 — the same slant, at the family's bold.
It is not the family's loudest pair — the SemiBold at 600 sits between
them and was where this pack started — and 700 is what it settles on
because a highlight has to be visible from the distance the caption is
read at rather than under inspection. At 40px capitals on a flat
ground, 600 against 400 is a difference a reader finds after being
told there is one; 700 is one they see. It is still short of Hall of
Femme's 200 against 800, and deliberately: that pack changes voice at
a picked word, and this one presses the same voice harder.
Two things follow from the face that a reader coming from any of the
sibling packs will be looking for.
The first is that the slab is not holding the type up here, where on
Hall of Femme it is. That pack's card and its hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown
photograph disappears, and the card is what makes that weight a
choice rather than a risk. A 400-weight humanist sans does not need
rescuing that way. The card is kept regardless, because it is the
form this design IS — a statement laid on the picture rather than
words burned into it — and because with a palette this plain the card
is the only place the look lives at all.
The second is that an all-italic block is the one setting here where
the card is doing real work beyond the look. Slanted stems make a
ragged left edge of a stack of lines, and the same slant against an
unknown photograph makes the ragged edge look like an error. Against
a flat rectangle it looks like a decision — which is a second reason
this pack keeps the joined line boxes below rather than reaching for
a single card round the block: each box is cut to its own line, so
the shape steps with the sentence instead of leaving the lean sitting
in a rectangle of air.
What is this show's own, then, is the palette, and it is the one pack
under this heading whose colours are neutrals and nothing else. Every
other one owns a hue — a hot pink, an electric blue, an acid yellow, a
red — and offers it both ways round against the neutrals, so that the
PAIRING is the look. Killer Bites opens on the same white-on-black
this does and is the pack to compare against rather than the ones with
loud cards: it keeps a red in the list, and that one swatch is the
difference between a show that can go quiet and a show that has
nowhere else to go. Here what the user picks is not which of sixteen
combinations to use, it is which way round to read the same card. See
`colors` below, which is honest about what that costs.
Uppercased, which is snapchat-caption's answer rather than this
pack's, and is argued there. It costs this pack a little more than it
costs the others, and the trade is still the right way round: italic
capitals lose the descenders and the single-storey letterforms that
make a slanted lower case obviously italic, so what survives is the
slant itself. That is enough at 40px on a flat ground, and a caption
in lower case would be a different show — which is a live option under
this heading and not a hypothetical one, since Killer Bites overrides
the same key for exactly that reason.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below,
so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the black card is the pairing this show opens
on, and it is the louder of the two the palette can make. Black
is the bigger surface here — a fifth of the frame, read before
anything set on it — and a black card on a photograph reads as
something laid deliberately on the picture rather than as a gap
in it; white type is what is unambiguously legible against it at
every size, in a way that does not depend on the still
underneath. The other way round is one swatch away.
_comment_colors: The two colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — two buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists, so a
row of two is a row of two; see `colors` in content/README.md.
The same two in both lists, which on its siblings is the whole
point and here is closer to a consequence. Their palettes are
four colours offered both ways round because sixteen pairings of
a brand hue and three neutrals are sixteen different cards. Two
colours make four combinations, of which two are a caption and
two are an empty rectangle, so what this panel really offers is
one switch: white on black, or black on white.
That is the brand and not a shortfall. A show called Fight Source
is cut from footage that is already loud — a palette that added a
colour to it would be a third thing shouting, and the one thing a
caption on a fight clip has to do is read. Black and white is the
pairing that reads over any still ever cut, which is exactly what
the three hues its siblings own cannot promise: a hot pink card
in a red corner, an acid yellow one under yellow lighting.
It also leaves the italic somewhere to be the loudest thing on
the card. On a coloured slab the colour is what is read first and
the type is what is read second; with the colour gone the lean is
the only thing left with a voice, which is the arrangement this
show wants.
Absolute black and absolute white, and here both of those exact
values matter rather than just the black. Hall of Femme's note
explains the black: a #111 that reads as black on a monitor turns
into a grey slab beside a genuinely black picture on a phone, and
there is nothing for a true black to be too harsh against because
the card is a flat shape, not a photograph seen through it. The
white is the same argument in the other direction — an off-white
card that is a card on a monitor is a dirty one against a blown
highlight, and the whole of this palette's job is to be the two
ends of the range rather than two greys near them.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or black on black.
That is not an oversight, and it is not worth a rule either: the
two lists are independent because the switch between them is the
feature, and an invisible caption is something the user can see
is invisible and fixes by pressing the other swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two, which is what
makes a palette this short usable at all; see `_comment_highlight`
below.
_comment_highlight: The two things the preset leaves to a pack: the face a picked word
is set in, and the colour it keeps. Everything else about the
highlight — word scope, colour mode, what a mixed row costs to
draw — is snapchat-caption's and is argued there.
The face is the Bold italic, 700 against the block's 400. The
argument for the weight is in `_comment_title` above: the slant
is the block's, so the emphasis has nowhere to go but weight, and
700 is the step a reader sees at the distance one of these frames
is actually looked at. Two slanted cuts also make the run joins
easier to get away with than an upright-to-italic pair does —
nothing changes angle across the space between two runs, so the
eye has no vertical stem to measure the gap against.
The colour is the block's. The recolour therefore draws a picked
word in exactly what its neighbours are drawn in, and the face is
the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated — and moved to white with
it, since a highlight that changed colour as well as weight would
be two highlights.
That is not merely the tidier of two options on this pack, it is
the only one: with two colours in the palette, a highlight that
changed colour could only ever be the card's own fill, which is a
hole in the sentence rather than an emphasis.
_comment_panel: The card is snapchat-caption's, in whichever of the two colours
the frame is wearing, and `fill` is the one thing that preset
leaves to a pack because it is the one thing about the card that
IS the brand. Here it is black.
This and `color` above are also the only place the opening look
is stated: the two lists in `colors` are written in one order so
the two rows of buttons read as the same palette twice, which
means neither of them can decide what an untouched frame wears.
Two of the shared numbers land differently on an all-italic block
than they do on the packs the preset was written against, and
neither is worth overriding. The padding of 12 is measured from
the ink, and slanted ink reaches further right at the cap line
than an upright's does, so a line sits a hair closer to the right
edge of its box than to the left — which reads as the slant, not
as a mistake, and is the reason not to go looking for a smaller
number. And the shadow has to survive being thrown by a white
slab onto a white wall, which on a palette that is half white is
a case this pack produces rather than imagines.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, for hall-of-femme's reason: it exists to hold a
title legible against the photograph, and this title is not against
the photograph at all — it is on a slab of its own. A scrim over
every still would darken forty pictures to solve a problem the card
has already solved.

channels.name: Fight Source DE
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more
folder under it rather than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
It is cut to Hall of Femme's design, and that pack is the one to read
first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite that turns speech into report, the stated
40px, the twenty characters to a line, the freeform text box and the
drag are all the same and are named here rather than restated. Where
it parts company with Hall of Femme is the card - there is none - and
for that half of it the pack to read is conspiracy-central, which is
the other channel here that sets its captions straight onto the
photograph.
The DE in the name is the account's, the way the DE in Hall of Femme
DE and Fitness Story DE is: it says which of the brand's feeds this
is and not what language the app is in. What lands on the frames is
whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put through the
transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel here;
nothing in this pack changes that, and everything the app itself says
is English like the rest of it (see CLAUDE.md).
The glyph check the two DE feeds before this one made a habit of, and
this face passes it with one footnote. Korolev Bold carries 365
codepoints, the umlauts, the eszett and the low quotes German sets
speech in among them, so a caption is drawn from the file rather than
from whatever the browser substitutes for a missing glyph - which
would be a different face at a width nothing measured. The footnote is
the capital eszett: U+1E9E is not in the file, and is never asked for,
because the preset's `uppercase` goes through toUpperCase (see `cased`
in js/text.js) and JavaScript maps a lower-case eszett to SS rather
than to its capital. A face chosen for how it looks in English is not
automatically a face that can SET another language, and the check is
two minutes against a cmap.
A separate folder rather than a second colourway of Fight Source, for
the reason Hall of Femme DE is a folder of its own: the person picking
a channel at the top of the app picks this or that one and never both,
and these two do not merely disagree about colour. Fight Source is
white or black type on a card in the other colour, set in an italic;
this is one dark plum, in an upright display bold, with no card at
all. That is further apart than any two packs under this heading that
could ever have shared a folder.
_comment_order: Last under the heading, which is where a new show goes: the numbers
are a running order rather than a ranking, and the foreign feeds have
been landing at the end of it since Hall of Femme DE took 920. 924
was taken by Re-belle between this pack being written and being
saved, which is the one thing a shared number costs - the server
breaks a tie alphabetically by name (see serve.py) and would have put
this above it for no reason anybody chose.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading, and like
conspiracy-central it is not only a swap of face and colour: it is set
in Korolev Bold, in one dark plum, straight onto the photograph, with
no card behind it and nothing picked out of it.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is the
Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show and then declines two whole shapes that preset draws, which
is the most a pack under this heading has ever had to say.
Why no card. On Hall of Femme the slab and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears, and
the card is what turns that weight from a risk into a choice. Korolev
Bold is at the other end of that axis - a bold display sans whose
capitals are the whole of what it is for - so it has no need of
rescuing, and a card under it would be a fifth of the frame of flat
colour spent on a problem this face does not have. What is left is a
sentence in one colour lying on the picture, which is what this show
is: no graphic, no second shape, nothing between the words and the
footage.
It also costs nothing in shape. Korolev Bold is narrow for its weight
- twenty capitals come out around 389px of the 486px a line has (see
content/faces/korolev-bold.json, which measures it) - so the preset's
twenty characters, and not the width of the frame, is still what
decides where a line breaks. That is the arithmetic the whole heading
is built on: one rewritten caption of eighty characters is four lines
of twenty, and one screen of the account fills one block.
Uppercased, for the reason every one of its neighbours is: at 40px
with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short beats
rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in. This
face has a lower case and nobody would call it the brand - Korolev's
capitals are what the family is drawn around, which is the same thing
that makes it safe to drop the card.

_comment_color: The dark plum, and it is what every frame is set in for good: this
channel offers no palette (see `_comment_colors` below), so this is
the colour rather than the colour a frame opens on.
It is the show's one colour and the show is one colour, which is as
far from its siblings' sixteen pairings as a pack here goes. There
is no card for it to be read against, so what it is read against is
the footage - and that is the one thing about this design worth
knowing before changing anything in it, because it cuts both ways.
On daylight, on a canvas, on skin, a near-black plum is the most
legible thing in the frame. On a dark still - night footage, a
black canvas, a shadowed corner - it is dark type on a dark picture
and it will lose.
Nothing in this pack can fix that half, and the two things that
look like they could are worse than the problem. A drop shadow is
black and would be invisible exactly where the type is (see
`shadow` below). A light outline would read as a second colour and
this show has one. The honest remedies are the ones that change the
brief rather than patch it - a card, which is the decision `panel`
declines, or a second colour in a `colors` list for the user to
switch to. Both are one edit to this file the day the show wants
them.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because most of its
siblings under this heading have one and the next person to copy
this folder will wonder where it went.
Two of the three could not be offered even if somebody wanted them:
`colors.panel` needs a panel and there is none, and
`colors.highlight` needs a highlight and there is none either - the
rows are hidden rather than drawn dead (see editor.paletteOf).
The third is a decision. One colour is one swatch, and a row of one
swatch is a button that is already pressed - the one kind of
control this panel does not have anywhere, for the reason the note
beside paletteOf gives: a button that visibly does nothing reads as
the app ignoring the click. A palette is for a channel where the
CHOICE is part of the look, which is what Hall of Femme's sixteen
pairings are; it is not a way of showing that a pack has a colour.
The day this show has a second colour the list is two strings in
this file, and it becomes a palette by being one.
_comment_shadow: None, which is what the preset already says - and it is restated
here because the preset's REASON is not this pack's, and a null
inherited under an argument that is false where it lands is a trap
for whoever reads it next. Its siblings have no shadow because
there is no photograph under their letters, only a card doing the
job completely. There is a photograph under these letters, on all
forty stills, which is exactly the case conspiracy-central picks
the shadow back up for.
It does not work here, and the difference is the colour. A drop
shadow separates type from a picture by putting darkness behind it,
which is why it rescues conspiracy-central's near-white capitals.
Behind a near-black plum it is darkness behind darkness: on a bright
still the letters already read and the shadow is a smudge nobody
asked for, and on a dark still the two go together. On the
mid-tones in between it is actively the wrong way round - it darkens
the ground immediately around letters that are themselves dark,
which is contrast spent rather than bought.
So the shadow is declined on its own terms rather than by
inheritance, and what this design does about a dark still is
written in `_comment_color` above: nothing, on purpose, with the two
edits that would change that named there.
_comment_highlight: None. Not a highlight that happens to look like the rest of the
block - none: `null` is how a channel says it has no highlight
FEATURE, and the word buttons in the title panel go dead with it
rather than offering a treatment nobody could see (see the note on
`highlight` in js/channels.js and editor.renderHlButtons).
Every other pack under this heading picks words out, and all of
them do it by changing something this show has no second of. Hall
of Femme changes weight, 200 against 800 of one family. Fight
Source changes weight inside an italic. Conspiracy Central changes
colour and puts a box under it. This show is one face, in one
colour, on no card - so a highlight would have to introduce a
second face or a second colour, and either would be the show
acquiring a feature rather than the sentence gaining an emphasis.
What is left is a caption that reads as one voice throughout, which
on footage this loud is the point: the frame is already shouting
and the words are the one flat thing in it.
_comment_panel: No card. The argument is in `_comment_title` above, and the
consequences are the `shadow` and the `highlight` beside it.
Stated as null rather than left out, because it cannot be left out:
`use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the card's shape, padding, corners and shadow
arrive from snapchat-caption.json whatever this pack says about
them. Null is how a pack cut from that preset declines the one part
of it that is a whole shape rather than a number.
The preset's `layout` survives intact and is what puts the block at
the foot of the frame, 120px up, where Hall of Femme's card stands.
That margin is measured to the first thing DRAWN, which on a pack
with no card and no box is the capitals themselves - so this show's
type sits a padding's worth lower than a panelled sibling's does.
It is the one visible difference the missing card makes to where
the words are, and it is small enough to be worth leaving rather
than correcting with a number nobody measured.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading - and like
conspiracy-central this needs its own sentence, because the usual
reason does not apply. Its siblings say the gradient has nothing to
do: their titles are on a card and not on the photograph. This one's
titles ARE on the photograph.
It still has nothing to do. The backend's gradient is a SIDE gradient
- full height, never past half the width, peaking on whichever side
the title column is (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient) - because it
was drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline set beside the
subject. There is no title column on a captured still: the block lies
across the width of the frame, and darkening one half of forty
pictures would shade half of every caption and leave the other half
exactly as it was.
And darkening is the wrong direction for this pack in particular.
Where conspiracy-central's near-white type would be helped by a darker
ground if the gradient ever fell in the right place, this show's dark
plum would be hurt by it - see `_comment_color`.

channels.name: Fitness Story
_comment_group: The fourth show under the Snapchat heading, and the second one cut to
Hall of Femme's design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack —
the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite,
the card the caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in
the same numbers. What makes it a different show is the two things
that are visible from across a room: the face the words are set in,
and the colours they are set in.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its sibling,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and Hall of Femme.
That pack sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline for
the block and the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card. This
one sets them in HK Grotesk, which the files themselves call Hanken
Grotesk, on an electric blue card: an ExtraLight Italic block, with a
picked word climbing to the ExtraBold Italic — the same two ends of a
weight axis, spent the same way round, in another typeface and on
another colour.
Four consequences follow from the face, and all four are worth
stating because they are what a reader coming from one of the
sibling packs will be looking for.
The first is that the card is doing the same job here that it does
next door, and has to. Hall of Femme's card and its hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the card is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk.
A 250 is the same bet and gets the same answer. It would be kept
regardless, because it is the form this design IS — a statement laid
on the picture rather than words burned into it — and because the
colour pairing below is the show's look and there is nowhere else to
put it.
The second is that the whole block leans, and that is the show
rather than an emphasis. It is what separates this pack from the two
Open Sans shows next door, which set an upright block and pick a
word out by slanting it — here the slant is spent before the
highlight is reached, so the highlight has to be something else.
The third follows straight from the second: what is left is weight,
and this pack spends all of it — 250 against 800, the widest gap the
family has, which is Hall of Femme's 200-against-800 in a different
typeface. It is also the ONLY thing that changes across the card:
same slant, same colour, same size, flat ground, nothing else
moving. A cut that changed colour as well would be two signals
saying one thing.
The fourth is which END of that axis the block sits on, and this
pack has had it both ways round, so the reason is written down rather
than left to look arbitrary. It opened in the ExtraBold with a picked
word dropping to the ExtraLight, on the argument that the contrast is
exactly as loud either way because it is the same two ends. It is.
The two directions are still not symmetrical, and that is what
settled it: a 250-weight capital is the one setting in this family
with no stems to spare, and the frame opens on black type over
#0040FF, the darkest of the four cards. Run the other way, the
thinnest thing on the card was the picked word — the least legible
thing on the frame, which is an odd place for the word that was worth
picking out, and backwards from every other pack under this heading
(Hall of Femme 200 to 800, Fight Source and Determined 400 to 600).
The hairline is the block now, where the card is already there to
hold it up, and the emphasis climbs into the cut with stems to
spare.
An italic block is a real cost anywhere the type sits on a
photograph, and it is not one here. These letters are on a solid
card in a colour somebody chose, at 40px capitals, so the slant
costs nothing it would cost over an unknown picture — the same
argument the card already makes for the hairline the block is set
in.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the four in `colors`
below, so the black swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
Black letters on the blue card is the pairing this show opens
on. The blue is the brand, so it is the CARD — the shape that is
a fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it — and the
type is what has to stay legible against it.
Worth being honest about, because it is the one number here that
is not comfortably the best of its four options: #0040FF is a
dark blue, so black on it is a contrast of tone rather than of
brightness, and it is a smaller gap than black on the pink its
sibling opens on. It is the BLOCK this costs, since the block is
the 250: a hairline capital cut out of the card by a difference
of tone alone. That is the same bet Hall of Femme makes with its
own 200, and the reason both packs keep the card at all — the
argument is in `_comment_title` rather than twice here. The
picked words are the 800 and have stems to spare.
White on the same card is the louder pairing and is one swatch
away, and the other fourteen are beside it — which is the point
of handing the colours over at all.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason
hall-of-femme states at length: the point is the PAIRING.
Sixteen combinations of an electric blue, an acid yellow, a white
and a black, and the ones worth having are the ones that read —
yellow on blue, blue on white, white on blue, black on yellow. A
palette of four colours that could only ever be used one way
round would be a palette of four cards, and this show's look is
the pairing rather than any one of them.
The blue and the yellow are picked to be each other's opposite
rather than each other's neighbour, which is what makes both of
them work in both roles. #0040FF is dark enough to be a ground
for the yellow and saturated enough to be ink on the white;
#FFF736 is bright enough to be ink on the blue and to be a card
the black sits on. Two colours of similar brightness would have
given eight pairings that are all the same pairing.
Absolute black rather than a soft near-black, and it is the one
colour here whose exact value matters. The other three are ink on
a card either way round; black is what the blue and the yellow
are loudest against, and a #111 that reads as black on a monitor
turns into a grey slab beside a genuinely black picture on a
phone. There is nothing for it to be too harsh against — the card
is a flat shape, not a photograph seen through it.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or black on
black. That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent
because the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the four
matching combinations would cost the panel more explaining than
an invisible caption costs the user, who can see it is invisible
and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.

_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and its siblings.
Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight hairline
for the block, the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink card.
Fitness Story sets them in HK Grotesk Italic on an electric blue
one. This pack sets them in Acumin Pro, upright, on a card that is
either plain white or plain black and is never anything else.
Three things follow, and all three are worth stating because they
are what a reader coming from one of the sibling packs will be
looking for.
The first is that there is no brand colour here, and that is the
design rather than a gap in it. Every other pack under this heading
puts its show's colour on the card, because the card is a fifth of
the frame and reads before anything set on it. This one has two
absolutes and the card is one of them, so what identifies the show
is not a hue at all — it is the maximum contrast a screen can draw,
which is the one thing a two-colour palette buys and the one thing
a coloured card can never quite have.
The second is that the face is doing more work than it does next
door. A hot pink card is recognisable at a glance whatever is set on
it; a white card is not, so Acumin has to be the difference. It is a
neo-grotesque — Akzidenz bones, large x-height, flat terminals — and
upright, which puts this pack between the two Open Sans shows
(upright block, slanted highlight) and Fitness Story (slanted
throughout). Set in black on white at 40px capitals it reads as
plain rather than as styled, which is the register this show is in.
The third is the highlight, and it is the one to argue with. Hall of
Femme spends 200 against 800 and Fitness Story 250 against 800 —
both of them the two ends of a weight axis, which at caption size is
as loud as a box would be. Acumin Pro is carried here in two cuts
and they are the Regular and the Bold, so this pack spends 400
against 700. That is the narrowest gap under the heading: a real
difference, and not a dramatic one.
It is also the only one available, which is why it is stated rather
than apologised for. The palette rules out a colour change, the
block is already upright so there is no slant left to spend, and the
preset's highlight mode is colour rather than box because the words
are already on a solid ground of their own. Widening it means a
third cut of Acumin in fonts/ and a face pack beside it; nothing
else here would have to change.
Everything else — the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame, what a picked word
does — is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.

_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading. The heading names the
network these frames are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are
cut from, so another show cutting for the same network is one more

than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.

first: the frame fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the block at the foot of the frame and
every number in it are the same and are named here rather than
restated. What makes this show itself is one sentence long - it is set
in Century Gothic Bold, in one cream, on the photograph itself with no
card under it and with no highlight - and everything below is that
sentence.
The NW in the name is the account's, the way the DE is in Fitness
Story DE and the NW in Crowned Ladies NW: it says which of the brand's
feeds this is and not what language the app is in. What lands on the
frames is whatever the video's own voice track was saying, put through
the transcription and the rewrite exactly as on every channel here;
nothing in this pack changes that, and everything the app itself says
is English like the rest of it (see CLAUDE.md).
It shares a brand with Fitness Story and Fitness Story DE and shares
almost no design with either, which is worth saying out loud because
the three folders sort next to each other and somebody will assume one
was copied from another. Those two are Hall of Femme's card: a
coloured slab at the foot of the frame, a palette of four colours
handed to the user for the type and four more for the slab, and a
picked word that changes CUT. This one keeps the block where they put
it and drops all three - no card, no palette, no highlight - which is
as far as two packs under one heading go.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme and
at crowned-ladies-fr wherever the reasoning is the same, and states
its own only where this pack actually decides something.

the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has

that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this heading
captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken, because the
folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Century Gothic Bold, in one cream, straight onto the PHOTOGRAPH
with no card behind it, and every line of every caption is set the
same way.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform text box, where the block stands on the frame, the drag - is
the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show, and then states the two keys the missing card forces:
`shadow`, which has to come back, and `panel`, which has to be said out
loud to go away.
Century Gothic is a geometric sans built on circles - Monotype's
answer to ITC Avant Garde - and the Bold is the weight that lets it
stand on a photograph without a card under it. That is the whole
argument for the cut rather than the Regular: a 400-weight geometric
has thin joins where the circles meet the stems, and a thin join is
the first thing a busy still eats. At 700 the stems are even and heavy
the whole way round, which is the same property that makes the face a
signage face.
It is also WIDE, which is the one thing to know before writing for it
and is measured in content/faces/century-gothic-bold.json rather than
here: twenty capitals can run past the 486px a line has, so the
occasional round sentence breaks at nineteen characters instead of the
preset's twenty. The wrapper does that on its own and nobody sees it
(see the two ceilings in js/caption.js) - it is noted because a caption
here takes a line more often than the same sentence on a narrower
sibling, and four lines is what the block is written to.
Uppercased, inherited, for the reason every one of its neighbours is:
at 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is three short
beats rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are set in.
It costs nothing here - a geometric sans is a face whose capitals are
the circles and the straight lines it was drawn from, and this one's
round O and pointed A are what it is recognised by.

_comment_color: A cream, and it is the whole palette rather than the first of
several: this show is set in one colour. It is therefore also what
every frame is drawn in, since a frame stores no colour of its own
until it is given one and there is no swatch here to give it one
with (see state.textColorFor).
#FEEECA is a warm off-white and not a white, and on a channel with
no card that is a decision about the photograph rather than about
the brand palette. A caption with no ground under it is separated
from the picture by two things only - its colour and its shadow -
and against skin, hair and daylight, which is what these stills
are, a pure white is the one light colour that turns up in the
picture as well: a blown highlight, a white wall, a studio
backdrop. A cream sits just off all of them.
Which frame is the risky one follows from where the colour sits.
Its relative luminance is about 0.86, so it stands 18 times clear
of a black and only 1.15 times clear of a white - a night still
holds it with room to spare and a blown, sunlit one is where it
disappears entirely. That is the still the shadow below is chosen
for, and it is why the shadow is a dark one. It is the opposite
end of the range from Crowned Ladies FR's magenta, which is in
trouble at the light end too but has some tone of its own to fall
back on; this colour has none, and leans on the shadow harder than
any caption under this heading.
_comment_colors: Absent, and that is the palette being stated rather than
forgotten. Hall of Femme, the pack this is cut from, offers rows
of swatches because its look IS the pairing - which of its colours
is the card and which is the type - and Fitness Story and Fitness
Story DE carry that over with palettes of their own. This show has
one colour and no card, so there is no pairing to offer and
nothing for a second button to be.
Left unstated rather than written as a list of one, which is the
answer Inkjection FR and Crowned Ladies FR both reached in the
same position: a row of one swatch is a control that cannot change
anything - it draws the colour already on screen, marked as
chosen, and clicking it does nothing a user can see. That is the
one kind of control this panel does not have anywhere (see the
note on `alignable` in js/editor.js). With no list the whole block
of colour rows is hidden instead - see editor.paletteOf, which
hides a row whose colours have nothing to recolour, and
renderColorButtons, which drops the block when no row survives.
Nothing counts these lists, so the day this show wants a second
colour it is one key in this file and the row appears.
_comment_shadow: An exception to the preset, and the first of the two keys the
missing card forces.
The preset states no shadow, and its reasoning is exact: there is a
solid slab under those letters in a colour the user picked, it
separates them from the photograph completely, and a shadow as well
would only smear the inside of the card. Take the card away and
every word of that stops being true - these letters are on a
photograph, with grain and edges and whatever was behind the
subject running through them.
A DARK shadow, and on this colour it is not a close call the way it
is for the other two cardless captions under this heading. Crowned
Ladies FR weighs a mid-tone magenta and Inkjection FR carries a
white halo because its navy is nearly black. A cream at 0.86
luminance is a light colour with nothing behind it: black is the
only side of it there is contrast on, so the shadow is the whole of
what holds it off a bright still.
The numbers are the skeleton's own (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE.shadow in
js/channels.js) rather than a fresh set invented here. They are
what every channel in this app that sets light type on a
photograph uses, which is the same job this is; a pack with no
reason of its own should not carry a number it merely agrees with,
and where it has to state one anyway it should state the one
already in use.
_comment_highlight: None. Every line of every caption on this channel is set the same
way, and the highlight buttons stand where they stand everywhere
else and go dead with a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderHlButtons). A brand whose lines are all one treatment
says so here rather than being given a highlight nobody could tell
apart from the type - see `highlight` in js/channels.js.
All three things a highlight could be are unavailable to this show,
and they run out in order. A change of CUT is what most of this
heading picks its words out with - both of this show's own siblings
included, which spend the two ends of a weight axis on it - and the
app carries one cut of Century Gothic; asking for a second weight
of it would be the browser emboldening or thinning the one file
there is, and a synthesised weight is measured as well as drawn. A
recolour needs a second colour, and this show has one. And a box
needs a fill, which would be a second colour again - and a graphic
in a frame whose whole design is type lying directly on the
picture.
Written as null rather than left out, for the reason `panel` below
is: `use` merges the preset UNDER this pack (see `expand` in
js/channels.js), so the preset's word-scope colour highlight
arrives whatever this pack says about it. Null is how a pack cut
from that preset declines the feature.
There is no `colors.highlight` either - there is no palette here at
all - so nothing draws a swatch row for words that cannot be picked
out (see editor.paletteOf, which hides that row on a channel with
no highlight).
_comment_panel: None, and its absence is half of this channel's design. Written as
null rather than left out, which is the opposite of what
laugh-society-snapchat does and is right for the opposite reason:
that pack inherits nothing, so a key restating the skeleton's own
null would read as a slab somebody had switched off. This one takes
the Snapchat caption preset, and the preset states a card - its
shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow. Null here is what
removes it, and it has to be said out loud.
Why drop it. On Hall of Femme the card and the hairline are one
decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown photograph disappears,
and the slab is what makes that weight a choice rather than a risk.
The two Fitness Story feeds keep the card without needing it, on
the argument that the colour pairing is their look and there is
nowhere else to put it. This feed has no pairing to place - one
colour, no palette - so the card would be a fifth of the frame of
flat colour buying nothing, over pictures the captions exist to
show.
There is no `colors.panel` either, so the swatch row that fills a
card on most of its siblings is not drawn at all rather than drawn
dead (see editor.paletteOf).

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, like every pack under this heading - and like
Conspiracy Central and Crowned Ladies FR this is a channel where the
usual reason does not apply, because its siblings say the gradient has
nothing to do when a title is on a card rather than on the photograph,
and this title IS on the photograph.
It still has nothing to do. The backend's gradient is a SIDE gradient -
full height, never past half the width, peaking on whichever side the
title column is (reframe_engine.apply_dark_gradient) - because it was
drawn for a landscape thumbnail with a headline set beside the subject.
There is no title column on a captured still: the block lies across the
width of the frame, and darkening one half of forty pictures would
shade half of every caption and leave the other half exactly as it was.
No `scrim` either, which is the tool that WOULD reach across the foot
of the frame, and this is the pack under this heading with the best
case for one: Laugh Society throws a scrim and sets white type on it,
and a cream at 0.86 luminance is the same pairing. It is still not
taken. A scrim is a band of shade across the bottom fifth of all forty
pictures whether or not the caption on any given one needed it, which
is the card's cost paid in grey instead of in colour; the drop shadow
buys the same separation one letter at a time and leaves the pictures
whole. If this show ever finds the shadow is not enough, a scrim is the
next thing to try and laugh-society-1 is the pack to read for it.

that can SET another language, and the check is two minutes against a
cmap.
A folder of its own rather than a second colourway of Hall of Femme,
for the reason oh-my-goal-news is a folder of its own: the person
picking a channel at the top of the app picks this one or that one
and never both, and these two do not merely disagree about colour -
they are set in different type and one of them has no card at all,
which is as far as two packs under one heading go.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: What separates this show from the others under the heading: it is set
in Texturina Regular, in one navy, with a picked word in Texturina
Bold - and it is set on the PHOTOGRAPH, with no card behind it.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals,
where the block stands on the frame, what picking a word covers - is
the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states what makes it
this show, and then states the two keys that the missing card forces
(`shadow` here and `shadow` inside `highlight`), each of which says
why it is an exception rather than a preference.
The face is the brand and the ground is what makes it difficult. A
serif at caption size over a still nobody chose the contrast of is
the hardest thing this app asks of a typeface: the hairlines that
make it a serif are exactly the strokes a photograph eats, and at
40px there is not much of them. Two things answer it. The file is the
18pt optical cut, which is the drawing of Texturina made for reading
rather than for a headline and therefore the one whose thins have
some body to them (see texturina-18pt-regular.json). And the type
carries a halo instead of a drop shadow, which is the `shadow` key
below.
Compare the three ways this heading has held a caption legible, since
this is now the third. Hall of Femme and most of its neighbours put
the words on a solid card, which is a ground somebody chose. Laugh
Society throws a dark scrim up from the foot of the frame and sets
white type on it. This channel does neither - the picture is left
whole, and the separation is bought one letter at a time.

_comment_color: A dark navy, and it is the whole palette rather than the first of
several: this show is set in one colour. It is therefore also
what every frame is drawn in, since a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one and there is no swatch here to give
it one with (see state.textColorFor).
Navy and not black, and on a channel with no card the difference
is not decoration. Black type on a photograph reads as something
punched out of the picture; a navy this deep is still
unmistakably dark at a glance, and carries a colour the eye can
name once it looks - which is what makes the caption belong to a
brand rather than to the player.
_comment_colors: Absent, and that is the palette being stated rather than
forgotten. Every other pack under this heading offers rows of
swatches because its look IS the pairing - which of its colours
is the card and which is the type. This show has one colour and
no card, so there is no pairing to offer and nothing for a second
button to be.
Left unstated rather than written as a list of one, because a row
of one swatch is a control that cannot change anything: it draws
the colour already on screen, marked as chosen, and clicking it
does nothing a user can see. That is the one kind of control this
panel does not have anywhere (see the note on `alignable` in
js/editor.js). With no list the whole block of colour rows is
hidden instead - see editor.paletteOf, which hides a row whose
colours have nothing to recolour, and renderColorButtons, which
drops the block when no row survives.
Nothing counts these lists, so the day this show wants a second
colour it is one key in this file and the row appears.
_comment_shadow: An exception to the preset, and the first of the two the missing
card forces.
The preset states no shadow, and its reasoning is exact: there is
a solid slab under those letters in a colour the user picked, it
separates them from the photograph completely, and a shadow as
well would only smear the inside of the card. Take the card away
and every word of that stops being true - these letters are on a
photograph, with grain and edges and whatever was behind the
subject running through them.
So a shadow, and it is a LIGHT one, which no other pack here has.
The dark drop shadow every channel uses works because its type is
white: a dark edge under a light letter is contrast. This type is
navy. A black shadow under a navy letter is dark on dark - it
adds nothing on a bright still and is invisible on a dark one,
which is precisely the frame where the caption is already in
trouble. What dark type needs is a light ground, and with no card
to put one on, the ground is carried by the letters themselves: a
white halo, tight enough to read as a glow around the type rather
than as a shape behind it.
It is also why this channel throws no scrim (see `branding`
below). A scrim darkens the foot of the frame, which is the right
answer for white type and exactly the wrong direction for this.
No offset, in either axis. An offset shadow is cast by something
standing off a surface, and these letters are not standing off
anything; centred, it is light coming off them, which is what
holds a letter on all four sides rather than on two of them. 18px
of blur is what it takes to find an edge under a serif's thins at
40px without the halo becoming a visible white smudge - a couple
of pixels would show around the stems and nowhere else, and the
stems are not the strokes that go missing.
0.9 rather than 1: a hard white would put a second outline round
every letter and the caption would read as a sticker. Just under
opaque is a glow.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Texturina Bold, in the same navy as the
rest of the block. The highlight here is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's answer rather than Laugh Society's: one family, two cuts,
the change of voice being a change of volume and nothing else.
400 against 700 is the ordinary text pairing, and it is the right
one for this face - Texturina's Bold is drawn as the emphasis its
own Regular takes, and the two set on one line at the same cap
height with about five percent between their widths (both
measured in texturina-18pt-bold.json). That the cap heights are
identical matters more here than on a channel with a card: there
is no slab edge to measure the line against, so a picked word
riding even slightly high would be visible as a fault in the
sentence rather than as emphasis in it.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the weight is the whole of
the difference. Stated all the same, for the reason `color` above
is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as weight
would be two highlights, and this show has one navy.
The shadow is the second key the missing card forces, and unlike
the first it would be a bug rather than a weakness if it were
left out. The skeleton's own highlight shadow is a dark halo
meant to sit under a filled box (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE in
js/channels.js), and the preset overrides the block's shadow
without touching it - so a picked word would come out carrying a
BLACK halo while every word either side of it carried a white
one. Restated here to the number, so the whole sentence lifts off
the photograph the same way whether a word is picked out or not.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: None, and its absence is this channel's whole design. Written as
null rather than left out, which is the opposite of what
laugh-society-snapchat does and is right for the opposite reason:
that pack inherits nothing, so a key restating the skeleton's own
null would read as a slab somebody had switched off. This one
takes the Snapchat caption preset, and the preset states a card -
its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow. Null here is
what removes it, and it has to be said out loud.
There is no `colors.panel` either, so the swatch row that fills a
card on every sibling is not drawn at all rather than drawn dead
(see editor.paletteOf).

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, which is what every pack under this heading says,
but not for their reason - they have a card between the type and the
photograph and this one does not.
The reason here is the direction. The backend's gradient is a dark
ramp baked into the picture to hold LIGHT type legible, and this
channel's type is navy: darkening the frame under it closes the one
gap the caption is relying on. The whole of this pack's answer to
legibility is the white halo in `title.shadow`, which works by making
the letters lighter at their edges rather than the picture darker
behind them - and a shade thrown over the foot of the frame would
fight it on every still.
No `scrim` either, and for the same sentence: Laugh Society's shade
is the right answer for white type on a photograph and the wrong one
for dark type on the same photograph.

channels.name: Justice O'Clock
_comment_group: One of the shows under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack - the frame fetch,
the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the card the
caption is set on - comes from the two presets below. What makes it a
different show is what is visible from across a room: the faces the
words are set in, the colours they are set in, and the corners of the
card they are set on.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in.
The id is `justice-oclock` and the name is `Justice O'Clock`. The id
is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the key
everything else refers to; the name is the brand and keeps its
apostrophe.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not. It matters
here for the reason it matters on all of them and one reason more:
these frames are read alone, on a card that reads as a statement
ABOUT the person on screen rather than as their own speech, and a
still captioned in the first person is a caption of nobody.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs cut to the same design.
Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline
for the block, the 800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card. This
one sets them in Forma DJR Display Extra Bold, with ITC American
Typewriter Bold for a picked word, on a deep blue one, and it is the
only pack under this heading whose card has square corners.
The two faces are the decision the rest of the pack follows from, and
the pairing is a kind no sibling has: every one of them picks a word
out with another cut of the SAME family - a weight, or a slant. This
one changes family outright, from a display grotesque to a slab
serif.
It is not a free choice, and the constraint is worth stating because
it is what a reader will otherwise try to relax. A highlight here has
only three languages available - colour, weight, or face. Colour is
spent: `colors` below hands both colours to the user, and `text`
reaches the highlight along with the block, so a highlight that
recoloured would be recoloured out from under itself. Weight is spent
too, and that is the part that is new: the block is already an Extra
Bold, so there is no heavier cut of it to reach for. Hall of Femme
could go 200 to 800 precisely because it started at the bottom of its
family; a pack that starts at the top has to change something else.
What is left is the face, and a slab serif against a display
grotesque is the loudest version of that there is. It changes the
shape of every letter rather than its weight, so a picked word reads
as a different KIND of statement - stamped, typed, on the record -
which is the register a show about charges and verdicts wants. It is
the technique laugh-society-2 uses under the Binge heading, where a
picked line in an upright face reads as somebody else speaking,
applied to a word instead of a line.
It costs what a second face always costs, and the cost is documented
rather than absorbed: everything about a picked word is measured in
its OWN face (`styleFor` in js/text.js), both faces are loaded and
verified before the channel is drawn with, and a missing one is named
in the fontguard banner by itself. See the `highlight.face` section of
content/README.md.
The card is kept, as it is on every pack under this heading, and here
it is not doing the job it does on Hall of Femme. There the card and
the hairline are one decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown
photograph disappears, and the card is what makes that weight a choice
instead of a risk. An Extra Bold display face needs no such rescuing.
The card stays because it is the form this design IS, a statement laid
on the picture rather than words burned into it, and because the six
colours below are the show's look and there is nowhere else to put
them.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the six in `colors` below,
so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the deep blue card is the pairing this show opens
on: the blue is the brand, so it is the CARD - the shape that is a
fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it - and the type
is what has to stay legible against it.
White rather than black, which is where this pack parts company
with the siblings that open dark on a bright card. #021A91 is not
a bright card. It is a very dark blue, nearer to black than any of
the other five colours here, so black on it is barely a contrast
at all - it is the one pairing in this palette that fails outright
rather than merely reading quietly. Of what is left, white is the
loudest and the most neutral; #FFD400 on the same card is the
louder-still alternative and is one swatch away, along with the
other thirty-four.
_comment_colors: The six colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - six buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists and the
row wraps, so a palette is as long as a pack wants it; four is
what the first packs under this heading happened to want, not a
number the feature has.
The same six in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason Hall
of Femme states: the point is the PAIRING. Thirty-six combinations
of a black, a white, a pale grey, a deep blue, a red and a yellow
- and unlike a palette of four, this one is not an argument that
every pairing is worth having. It is an argument that which ones
are worth having is not knowable in advance, because it depends on
the photograph the card is lying on.
The six are three pairs rather than six colours. Absolute black
and absolute white are the ends, and the exact values matter for
the reason every pack under this heading gives: a near-black that
reads as black on a monitor becomes a grey slab beside a genuinely
black picture on a phone, and an off-white card is a dirty one
against a blown highlight. The card is a flat shape, not a
photograph seen through it, so there is nothing for either extreme
to be too harsh against.
#DBDBE6 is the quiet one - a pale grey with just enough blue in it
to belong to #021A91 rather than to sit beside it - and it is here
so the show has a card that is not shouting, which is what a long
caption over a busy still wants.
#021A91, #DB051F and #FFD400 are the loud three, and they are
spaced across the wheel rather than around one hue, which is what
makes each of them work in both roles: a blue dark enough to be a
ground for the other two, a red at full saturation and middling
brightness which is the one colour here that works better as ink
than as a card, and a yellow bright enough both to be ink on the
blue and to be a card the black sits on. Three colours of similar
brightness would have given a great many pairings that are all the
same pairing.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or blue on blue.
That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent because
the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the six matching
combinations - or the several more that are near enough to
matching to be unreadable - would cost the panel more explaining
than an invisible caption costs the user, who can see it is
invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type
is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in ITC American Typewriter Bold, in the same
colour as the rest of the block. Why the face and not the weight
is argued in `_comment_title` above: the block is already an Extra
Bold, so there is nothing heavier to reach for, and the slab serif
changes the shape of the letters instead.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as face
would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
One consequence is this pack's own, and it is why the preset's
stated `fontSize` matters more here than on a single-family pack.
The Typewriter is the wider of the two faces at the same size, so
a picked word makes its line longer. At a stated size that is all
it does - the line breaks one word earlier and nothing is resized.
Under a size fit it would have retyped the block around the word
being emphasised, and worse than on a sibling: a block takes one
size, from whichever line needs the smallest one, so a picked word
in the wider face could have set the size for every line including
the ones it is not on (see content/README.md). Stating the size is
what makes two families on one block safe, as well as what makes
forty stills one set.
_comment_panel: Deep blue, and square. The fill is what every pack under this
heading states for itself - it is the one thing about the card
that IS the brand - and the radius is this pack's exception, which
the preset asks to be explained where it is taken.
The blue is the card and not the letters because it is the brand
and the card is the bigger surface: a fifth of the frame, read
before anything set on it. This and `color` above are also the
only place the opening look is stated, since the two lists in
`colors` are written in one order so the two rows of buttons read
as the same palette twice - which means neither of them can decide
what an untouched frame wears.
The radius is 0 against the preset's 13, and it contradicts a
sentence written for every other channel here: that a
square-cornered slab reads as a crop or a letterbox, something the
player did, while a rounded one reads as a graphic somebody made.
That argument is right and this show takes the other side of it on
purpose. A rounded corner is a soft, conversational, social shape;
a square one is a document. This is a show about charges and
verdicts, set in a display grotesque and picked out in a typewriter
face - the whole look is paperwork read aloud, and a card with
rounded corners is the one part of it that would read as a chat
bubble.
The letterbox risk the 13 protects against is also much smaller
here than it is there, because it is a risk for a card in a
NEUTRAL colour and five of these six are not neutral. A square
block of #DB051F across the foot of a still is not something
anybody mistakes for the player. It is a real risk for the two
that are neutral, and the honest version of this note is that a
black card with square corners on a dark still can look like a
crop - which is a pairing the user chose and can leave in one
press, and a smaller cost than rounding the other four.
Nothing else about the card is stated. Its shape, its padding, its
border and its shadow are the Snapchat caption design and come
from the preset, including the border colour that is never drawn -
and which, at radius 0, has one less thing to do: it is there to
stop the outer rectangle blending into a pale rim along a ROUNDED
edge. Left in place regardless, because it is the preset's answer
and this pack has no reason of its own to hold a copy of it.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.

channels.name: Karens Unleashed

title._comment_shadow: No drop shadow on the type: the glow below is what lifts it.
_comment_highlight: Highlighting recolours the line and nothing else — no box, no
texture. The outline and the glow belong to every letter, so a
highlighted line keeps both: only the fill changes.

_comment_branding: Title left, subject right — what the automatic framing already
produces, so neither flip is needed.

channels.name: Killer Bites
_comment_group: The seventh show under the Snapchat heading, and the fifth one cut to
Hall of Femme's design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack —
the frame fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite,
the card the caption is set on — is Hall of Femme's and is stated in
the same numbers. What makes it a different show is what is visible
from across a room: the face the words are set in, the colours they
are set in, and — this pack alone under the heading — whether they
are shouted.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of its siblings,
for the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that
gets dropped in. The prose below therefore points at hall-of-femme
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the four packs cut to the same
design. Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight
hairline for the block, the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink
card. Fitness Story uses HK Grotesk on an electric blue one,
Determined uses Open Sans on acid yellow, Fight Source uses Open Sans
on black or white. This one is set in Arial Bold, with the bold
italic for a picked word, on a card that is black, white or a single
muted red — and it is the only pack under this heading that does not
uppercase what the user typed.
Arial is the decision the rest of the pack follows from, and it is a
deliberately unglamorous one. The four siblings each reach for a
typeface with a voice — a hairline, a humanist sans, a geometric —
because their captions are the only graphic in the frame. A show
about food is looking at the food: the caption's job is to name what
is on screen and then get out of the way, and Arial Bold at 40px is
about the most legible way to put a short sentence over a picture
that anybody has shipped. It is also on every machine that will ever
open this app, which is what makes the next paragraph possible.
It is declared inline and with no file, because it is not a font
this app ships. `file` is null and `css` false to say so outright —
nothing is registered for it (see channels.registerFace, which skips
a face with no file) and it is reached by name. fontguard still
verifies that something real answers to that name before a single
line is measured, so a machine that somehow lacks Arial says so
instead of quietly laying the block out against a fallback.

_comment_face: Arial at bold, which is a WEIGHT of the family rather than a
family of its own — the opposite of the case a face like Arial
Black presents, which has to be asked for by NAME because it is
its own family and asking Arial for 900 would only invite a
browser to synthesise one. Here the cut genuinely
exists: every machine that has Arial has Arial Bold, and `bold`
is how you reach it.
The stack falls back through Helvetica before the generic, which
is the one fallback in this codebase that is not merely damage
limitation. Helvetica is metrically compatible with Arial — the
same advance widths, glyph for glyph — so a machine that somehow
had one and not the other would lay this block out to the same
numbers rather than to Impact's. It is still a fallback and
fontguard still refuses to draw against one; it is just the only
one here that would not be a lie.
_comment_uppercase: Off, and this pack is the only one under the Snapchat heading
where it is. What the user types is what the canvas sets, capital
for capital.
The argument every sibling makes for capitals is a real one, and
it is an argument about their faces rather than about captions in
general. Hall of Femme is set in a 200-weight hairline, and a
hairline lower-case at caption size is the one setting where it
genuinely disappears — capitals give it stems the eye can find.
Arial Bold has no such problem: it is a 700-weight grotesque
whose lower-case is as solid as its capitals, so uppercasing it
would buy nothing and cost the two things below.
The first is that a food show's captions are full of names that
carry their own casing — a dish, a restaurant, a chef, a place —
and a name flattened into capitals is a name the reader has to
reconstruct. Those names arrive from the rewrite rather than from
somebody typing them (see backend/narrator.py), so the casing in
the text box is information that was produced on purpose, and
throwing it away at the draw would be throwing away the more
considered of the two.
The second is reading speed, which is the whole job here. A line
of capitals is a rectangle; a line of mixed case has ascenders
and descenders sticking out of it, and word shape is most of how
a sentence is read at a glance on a phone. Twenty characters is a
glance either way, and mixed case is the faster glance.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so turning
it off changes only what the canvas does: the text box held the
user's own casing all along, and the highlight buttons already
offered the words as the canvas would set them (see the `cased`
note in js/text.js and editor.renderWordButtons). Which is why
nothing downstream of this key needed to know it had changed.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the three in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the black card is what this show opens on. Black
is the bigger surface — a fifth of the frame, read before
anything set on it — and against food, which is what every still
on this channel is going to be warm and bright with, a black card
is the one ground that neither competes with the plate nor gets
lost in it. White is what is unambiguously legible on it at every
size. The red, and the same card the other way round, are a
swatch away.
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — three buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists, so a
row of three is a row of three; see `colors` in
content/README.md.
The same three in both lists, in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is
the PAIRING, and two rows written the same way read as one palette
