offered twice rather than as two unrelated sets.
Two of the three are the ends of the range and the third is the
brand. Fight Source's note explains why the black and the white
are absolute rather than a #111 and a #FAFAFA, and every word of
it applies here: a near-black that reads as black on a monitor
becomes a grey slab beside a genuinely black picture on a phone,
and an off-white card that is a card on a monitor is a dirty one
against a blown highlight. The card is a flat shape, not a
photograph seen through it, so there is nothing for either extreme
to be too harsh against.
The red is what makes this a show rather than a default. It is a
muted one and not a signal red — nearer a brick than a warning —
which is the only kind that can be BOTH ink and card, and being
both is the whole of what this palette asks of a colour. At Fight
Source's contrast a hot red as type on white would vibrate and the
same red as a card would fight the food; at this one it is dark
enough to carry white letters and light enough to be read as
letters on the white. It is also, on a channel whose frames are
cut from cooking footage, the one hue that belongs to what is on
screen rather than being laid over it.
Six of the nine combinations are worth having and three of them
are a rectangle — black on black, white on white, red on red.
Nothing stops the user choosing one, and that is not an oversight:
the two lists are independent because the pairing is the feature,
and a rule barring the three matching combinations would cost the
panel more explaining than an invisible caption costs the user,
who can see it is invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Arial Bold Italic, in the same colour as
the rest of the block. The colour it names is the block's, so the
recolour draws exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the
face is the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated — and moved to white with
it, since a highlight that changed colour as well as slant would
be two highlights.
The slant rather than a heavier cut, as on Fitness Story and
Fight Source, and here there is no second option to weigh: the
block is already bold, and this family's next step up is Arial
Black, which is a different family with different proportions
rather than a heavier weight of this one. Leaning the word is the
change this face can make cleanly, and at 40px on a flat ground
with nothing else moving it is enough.
It reads harder here than on either sibling, for a reason that is
this pack's alone: with `uppercase` off, an italic lower-case
carries a change of letterform as well as of angle — Arial's
italic a and e are drawn differently, not merely slanted — so a
picked word is doing two things at once where a picked word in
capitals could only ever lean.
Word scope, the same as all six of its neighbours, and for their
reason: a caption's line breaks are wherever the sentence happened
to run out of width, so picking a line out picks out a fragment
rather than a thought. The words are what carry meaning, and the
one worth leaning — a dish, a number, the verb the clip turns on —
sits in the middle of a line as often as it fills one. A row whose
picked words are in another face is built out of runs, each
measured and drawn in its own face at the pen the runs before it
reached (see `runRows` in js/text.js), which is what lets the face
change at a word and costs the kerning across each join.
Mode is colour rather than box because there is nothing to box
against — the words are already on a solid ground of their own —
so the highlight here is the SLANT, on a card that stays one clean
rectangle.

_comment_face: The italic cut of the same family, and the one place in this
pack where the data is doing something that needs explaining
rather than merely stating.
There is no `style` key on a face, and adding one would be a
worse answer than this. Every measurement and every draw in
the renderer builds one CSS font shorthand out of two fields —
`${weight} ${size}px ${stack}` — at the raw canvas (the four
measuring contexts in js/text.js) and through fabric, which
prepends its own `normal` font-style in front of the same
weight. Nothing reads a third field. So a `style` key invented
here would reach the drawn text and not the measurements, or
the reverse, and a block laid out against one cut and painted
in another is precisely the failure fontguard exists to catch
— self-inflicted this time, and invisible until somebody
notices the boxes are the wrong width.
So the slant travels in `weight`, as `italic bold`. That is
not a trick played on the shorthand, it is the shorthand: CSS
lets font-style, font-variant, font-weight and font-stretch
appear in any order in front of the size, and a leading
`normal` from fabric is skipped rather than fighting the
`italic` behind it. Both strings therefore parse to the same
font — and, which is the actual point, they are the SAME
string, so what is measured and what is drawn cannot come
apart.
It is worth the paragraph because it looks like a mistake. A
field called `weight` holding two words is the kind of thing
somebody tidies up on a quiet afternoon. The alternative is a
`style` field, four call sites in text.js and a fabric
property to keep in step with them, for one channel — against
content/README.md's whole claim, which is that a channel is a
folder that gets dropped in.
The family is `Arial` and not `Arial Bold Italic`, unlike rift
or hanken-grotesk-italic, and the difference is that those
ship a FILE holding one cut, which has to be named exactly or
another cut of the family answers to it. Arial arrives with
the machine as a family and its cuts are reached by weight and
style rather than by name, so asking for `Arial Bold Italic`
as a family would find nothing at all.
One consequence, and it is the right one: because both faces
are family `Arial`, text.titleFaces collapses them into a
single face to verify and fontguard caches its answer under
that one family. That dedup was written for a pack that named
the same face twice, and it is correct here for a better
reason — `is Arial on this machine` has one answer, and asking
it twice would not make it two.

_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on, in whichever of the three colours
the frame is wearing. Every number in it is hall-of-femme's, and
the long argument for each is there rather than repeated here:
one box per LINE and `joined`, so the background is a single shape
that steps in and out with the sentence instead of a rectangle the
width of its longest line; 12 of padding, which is a highlighter's
margin and not a card's; no border, because a keyline would make
the slab read as a box drawn over the picture rather than as a
card lying on it; 13 of corner radius, the number every background
under this heading is rounded by; and a soft shadow falling
straight down, which has to survive being thrown by a white slab
onto a white wall — a case this pack can actually produce, since
white is a third of its palette.
One thing the line boxes do that no sibling has had to think about,
because this is the first pack under the heading with descenders
in it. Every box in a block takes ONE shared vertical band, the
union of what every row needs, so the boxes differ in width and in
nothing else — a line ending in a g does not get a taller box than
the line above it (see the band in js/text.js). What the band does
do is grow for the block as a whole, so a caption containing a
descender is carried on a card a few pixels deeper than one that
happens not to. That is the one price mixed case pays and capitals
do not; it is smaller than the shadow under the card, and it buys
the reading speed `uppercase` above is about.
The fill is the one line here that is this show's own, and it is
black. This and `color` above are also the only place the opening
look is stated: the two lists in `colors` are written in one order
so the two rows of buttons read as the same palette twice, which
means neither of them can decide what an untouched frame wears.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, for hall-of-femme's reason: it exists to hold a
title legible against the photograph, and this title is not against
the photograph at all — it is on a slab of its own. A scrim over every
still would darken forty pictures to solve a problem the card has
already solved.

channels.name: La Parenthèse Inattendue

_comment_shadow: A hard shadow, not a soft one: no blur at all, so what lands
behind every letter is a second, solid black copy of it. That
crispness is the channel's look — a blurred version of the same
numbers reads as a printing fault rather than as a deliberate
second layer.
1.5px, which is close enough to the letterform to read as weight
on the type rather than as a shape behind it. The fractional half
is deliberate and survives: nothing rounds an offset, and at 1px
the shadow lands exactly on the pixel grid and comes out as a
hard hairline instead of a shoulder.
It is thrown to the LEFT and DOWN. Every other channel here that
carries a shadow throws it down and to the right; this one is the
exception, and the sign on offsetX is the whole of it.
_comment_layout: The line breaks are the user's, typed into one block, and the
renderer reproduces them exactly — see `freeform` in channels.js.
This channel's titles are written as sentences that break where
the writer wants them to break, which the three fixed line slots
cannot express.
One size for the whole block follows from that. Fitting each line
to the full width would make a line's size a function of how many
characters happen to be in it, and with the breaks in the user's
hands that is a lever they would be pulling on constantly without
meaning to: adding a word to line 2 would resize line 2. At one
shared size a break moves words and nothing else.
_comment_highlight: Per WORD, not per line — the user clicks the words themselves in
the panel, and each one gets its own green box. Two words picked
side by side get ONE box spanning both, the space between them
filled in (see pickedSpans in text.js).
A picked word gives up its own hard shadow — the green box is
what lifts it off the photo, and shadowed letters inside a
shadowed box read as a printing fault. The words beside it keep
theirs, which is why a line with both kinds in it is drawn twice
(see the two-copy note in text.js).
The box's own shadow is Supermission's letter shadow, to the
number: the same soft dark that lifts white type off a photo
there is what lifts this box off one here.
_comment_glow: The Karens halo, offered rather than applied: `toggle` makes it a
button in the panel instead of part of the channel, off until the
user turns it on for a frame.
Shared with Karens Unleashed through the preset on purpose. It is
one design used in two places — the same light, at the same
radius, stacked the same number of times — so a change to it is
meant to reach both. See superlove's glow for the opposite case,
where the overrides ate the preset and it was written out in full.
_comment_movable: The one channel whose title is placed by hand. Everywhere else the
block sits where the guidelines put it, which is the point of
having guidelines; here the photo is part of the composition and
the title is moved and sized around whatever is in it.

_comment_branding: Title left, subject right — what the automatic framing already
produces, so neither flip is needed.
No dark gradient. This channel's type carries its own contrast: a
hard black shadow on every letter, and a green box under whatever is
picked out. A gradient under all that is a dark smear across the
photo doing a job already done — and this is the one channel whose
title is placed against what is IN the photo, so anything that
changes the photo's own values fights the placement. Per frame it is
still a button away.

channels.name: Laugh Society 1
_comment: The one channel whose thumbnail is not the photograph.
Every other channel here takes a frame of the video, crops it to
1280x720 and sets a title over it. This one takes the frame apart: the
person is cut out of it, the rest is thrown away, and what they stand
on is a stage picture that is the same on every thumbnail the channel
ever makes. The video is where the subject comes from, not where the
picture comes from.
Four things follow from that, and they are why this pack states more
than any other one does:
- the frames are CHOSEN differently (`framing`), because a close-up
of a face is the wrong thing to cut a standing figure out of;
- the background is stated (`background`), because there is no photo
left to be one;
- the subject is placed (`cutout`), because nothing else puts them
anywhere;
- the title sits on the right (`branding.flipText`), and is set
against that margin, because the left half is where the person
starts out.
_comment_selection: Which frames count as the same moment, for the pass that narrows the
video down to candidates. The default measure is a colour histogram
of the face region; this channel asks for the face DESCRIPTOR
instead.
The histogram has a kind of footage it cannot read, and it is exactly
this channel's: one performer, one costume, one lighting setup, a
camera that does not move. What it measures then is skin under an
unchanging light, so it reports every frame as a copy of every other.
Measured on a stand-up special, 100% of candidate pairs inside every
character cluster cleared the duplicate threshold — including the two
most different frames in eight and a half minutes, at 0.965 against a
threshold of 0.95. The pool collapsed to ONE frame per character, the
emergency floor topped each back up to four, and the grid came out
with 12 thumbnails instead of the 20 it asks for. Twelve was not a
number anybody chose; it was three characters times a floor of four.
The descriptor separates the same footage about five times as well —
pairwise spread 0.13 to 0.17 against the histogram's 0.03 — because
what moves it is the shape of a face rather than its colour, and the
shape of a face is what an expression is. Same video, same threshold
logic: 34 candidates pooled, all 20 slots filled.
It is not asked for globally. On a video with cuts, locations and
wardrobe changes the histogram answers the same question more cheaply
and has never been the thing that failed. See SelectionRequest in
backend/api.py.
Quality still comes first and this does not touch that: deduplication
runs in SCORE order and the sharp frames are offered the budget before
the soft ones (see api._build_pool). This decides only which frames
are redundant, never which are good.
_comment_cleanup: The two inpainting passes that clean burned-in overlays off a frame —
the channel bug in a corner, the captions across the bottom — are off
for this channel, and this is the pack that has to say so because it
is the only one with a reason.
Every other channel composites the PHOTOGRAPH, so an overlay left in
is an overlay in the finished thumbnail and there is no later stage
that could take it out. This one composites a person cut out of the
photograph and standing on a backdrop of its own: every pixel those
passes could clean is a pixel that gets thrown away anyway. The
upside is exactly zero.
The downside is not. Both passes are inpainters, and an inpainter
aimed at something that is really part of the set paints over
whatever is standing in front of it. Measured on this channel's own
footage — a stage with neon signage on the back wall — the text
detector read the signage as captions and declared a band from 0.297
to 0.611 of the frame height, a third of the picture straight through
the middle. The subtitle remover then erased 30% of the frame, the
performer's head and shoulders included. What reached the canvas was
a flat grey wall with an arm beside it, and the face the pipeline had
correctly found on the original frame now pointed at nothing, which
is what took the cutout apart everywhere downstream.
Two of the twenty thumbnails in that run were destroyed this way. See
CleanupRequest in backend/api.py.
_comment_framing: How the video's frames are chosen for this channel — read once, when a
run starts, from the channel picked above the link box. See
backend/framing.py, and `framing` in js/channels.js for why this one
key cannot be changed after the fact the way the rest of a pack can.
What is being kept: expressions. The selector's whole job is finding
sharp, well-lit, eyes-open moments and keeping the varied ones (the
per-character deduplication in api._build_pool), and none of that
changes here. What is being changed is the SHOT those expressions are
wanted in.
faceAreaRatio 1/45 is a medium shot, arrived at from the head rather
than from the face: in a waist-up shot a head takes about a quarter of
the frame's height, which on a 720px canvas is ~165px, and the box a
face detector draws is roughly 0.8 of that and square — ~130px a side,
or a forty-fifth of the canvas. The pipeline's own 1/6 puts a 390px
face in a 720px frame, which is a head and shoulders and nothing else:
cut out, it is a floating head.
In practice this mostly stops the framing zooming IN. compute_scale
never goes below cover scale, so on ordinary footage a target this
small means the frame is taken as shot, which is exactly right — the
person's own distance from the camera is what decides whether they are
a usable cutout, and no amount of cropping can add the rest of them.
anchorX 0.5 centres the subject instead of putting them on the
right-hand third. The thirds rule is there to leave a text zone beside
the face; there is no text going in this photo, and a subject pushed to
one edge is a subject whose arm is outside the frame — which the cutout
then ends at.
minTextSpace 0 follows: the clear space that rule demanded was for text
that is not going there, so a frame lacking it is not unusable here,
and refusing those frames would throw away most of the video.
left_space 0 is the same statement made to the scorer. It measures edge
density in the left 40% of the frame — how clean the photo is behind
the title — and this channel deletes that region before anyone sees it.
The 0.22 it carried is shared out over the criteria that still mean
something (see quality_scorer.weights), which is how sharpness and
exposure — the two that actually decide whether a cutout looks like a
person or like a smear — end up counting for more.

_comment_faceFill: The scorer normally penalises a frame whose face would fill much
more of the CROP than the ratio above intends, because on a channel
that composites the photograph an inherently close shot really is a
worse thumbnail — it blows past the target with no way to zoom out.
This channel never shows the crop. The subject is cut out of the
whole photo and rescaled onto a backdrop of its own, so a close shot
is not a composition failure here — it is more pixels on the only
part of the frame that survives. The penalty is multiplicative and
reaches zero, so it does not demote those frames, it deletes them.
Measured on a stage set with two camera positions: with the penalty
on, the sharpest frames of two of the five character clusters scored
0.000 and the grid came out with 7 of its 20 thumbnails below the
sharpness floor — soft, motion-blurred, eyes unreadable. With it off,
2 of 20, and the median sharpness rose from 49 to 59.

_comment_background: The same stage on every thumbnail, by design — it is the set this
channel is shot on as far as a viewer is concerned, and a channel whose
backdrop changed per video would not read as one channel.
Drawn to cover the canvas, never stretched to it. The file is 1672x941,
which is 16:9 to within a pixel, so in practice nothing is cropped.
_comment_stamp: The channel mark, 10px from the top of the canvas and 10px from its
left, at the file's own size. Exact pixels rather than a ratio: a
lock-up is a measurement, and 'about ten pixels' is not one.
Drawn above the subject, so a tall figure standing at the left cannot
end up in front of the logo, and below the title and the user's own
overlays, which are the things they are here to place.
_comment_cutout: The person, cut out of the frame whole by the backend (see
/cutout-frame and backend/background_remover.py) and stood on the
backdrop.
Every number here describes where the subject ARRIVES, and nothing
here describes where they may go. That distinction is the whole design
of this feature: the channel proposes a composition and the user is the
one composing, so the subject can be dragged anywhere on the canvas —
across the middle, off an edge, behind the title — and zoomed over a
range far wider than their starting size. The only rule they cannot
escape is that enough of them stays on screen to be grabbed again (see
compose.clampCutout).
fitWidthRatio 0.5 is the left half: they arrive standing in it, so the
title has the other half. fitRatio 0.92 fits them to most of it rather
than all of it, which reads as a person standing in their half with air
around them instead of one wedged into it.
bottomRatio 1 stands them on the bottom edge. A cutout floating with a
gap under it reads as a sticker; standing on the frame's own edge reads
as a person on a stage, which is what the backdrop is a picture of.
minZoom/maxZoom are the ends of the zoom control, as multiples of that
arrival size. Wide on purpose and bounded by nothing on the canvas: a
subject blown past the frame and cropped to a face is a thumbnail
somebody may well want.
copiesBySlot is what makes the grid a set of OPTIONS rather than
twenty versions of one idea. Ten slots show the subject once; five
show them twice and five show them three times, which is a look this
kind of channel leans on and which nothing else in the app can
produce. It is a property of the slot and not of the photo in it, so
option 12 is a two-figure arrangement whatever video is loaded — the
user learns where in the grid to look.
Each of those figures is a DIFFERENT MOMENT of the video, not a second
print of the same photograph, and not a neighbouring frame either:
they are cut from points at least 5% of the running time apart (see
vary.MOMENT_SEPARATION_FRAC), because two seconds of a person talking
is one pose from three angles and a thumbnail showing the subject
three times wants three things they DID. That is the whole point of
showing them more than once, and it is why each figure costs a
restoration of its own photo.
Variation walks ONE figure onward through those moments rather than
re-rolling the whole arrangement, for the same reason the zoom and the
flip act on one: the arrangement is the user's.
copyScale 1 and copyOffsetGap 0.62 are how they ARRIVE, and only that.
Same size, standing on the same ground line, and set apart by getting
on for two thirds of their own drawn width — which leaves each figure
showing about two thirds of itself and overlapping the next by the
rest. Far enough apart to be three people; close enough to be one
group rather than three separate pictures.
This started at thirty pixels, on the reasoning that a neat stack is
easier to drag apart than a spread one is to gather up. That was
wrong, and wrong in a way only visible on the canvas: thirty pixels on
a figure three hundred wide is not a stack, it is one person with a
sliver of a second showing past their shoulder. Nothing about it says
there is anybody behind them, so a three-figure option looked like a
one-figure option that had gone wrong — and the user had no reason to
go looking for the other two.
A fraction of the figure rather than a number of pixels, because the
figures are not one size: a full-length shot arrives about a third as
wide as a head-and-shoulders, and any fixed step that spreads one of
those properly buries the other. Every one of them is draggable,
resizable, flippable and reorderable on its own from wherever they
land.
The shadow began as Supermission's letter shadow at double strength —
24px of blur and a 6px throw — and the throw has since been opened to
24, four times over, while the blur stayed exactly where it was.
Only one of the two moved, because they answer different questions.
BLUR is how far away the light is: wide is an overcast sky, tight is a
lamp, and this backdrop is a lit stage — so 24 is right, and opening it
further only turns the shadow into a smudge with no edge left to read.
THROW is how far the person is from what they are standing against, and
that is what was wrong: at 6px the figure was pressed flat to the
backdrop. At 24 there is air behind them.
The alpha stays at 0.8, the value this started at. A letter stroke is
thin and loses most of a shadow to its own antialiased edge, so type
needs the higher number; a figure is a solid shape and does not.
Computed from the CUT-OUT, never from anything before it. A fabric
shadow follows the image's own ALPHA, and by the time this is drawn the
image IS the person with the background taken away (see
compose.addLogoOverlay, which hands the shadow to the figure itself) —
so what falls on the stage is their silhouette, hair and fingers and
the gap under an arm included. Thrown from the frame as it arrived it
would be a rectangle, and at a 24px offset a rectangle is not a subtle
mistake. Measured on a real cutout rather than assumed: of the pixels
the shadow darkens, none lie in the corners the person does not reach.

_comment_face: Rift, and specifically the cut in fonts/Rift.otf, which is its
Bold Italic — the slant is drawn into the letterforms rather than
leaned on by the browser. The face pack says why it is registered
under the full name and not under 'Rift'.
Laugh Society 2 is set in the same face, because the two channels
are one show. What separates them is what happens to a picked
line: here it changes colour and nothing else, there it changes
voice as well.
_comment_shadow: Heavier than the skeleton's, which is Supermission's. This type is
set over a stage backdrop with hot lights and bright curtain in it,
not over a photograph that has already been darkened by a gradient
— nothing else here is lifting the letters off what is behind them,
so the shadow is the whole of what does it.
Same geometry as the shadow the cutout throws (Supermission's,
doubled), so the type and the figure sit at the same apparent
distance off the backdrop rather than at two. The alpha is higher
than the figure's: a letter stroke is thin, and a thin shape loses
far more of its shadow to its own antialiased edge than a person
does.
_comment_layout: Four lines, which is one more than any other channel here has, and
the reason the slot count became a number a pack states rather than
a fact about the markup.
Set RIGHT, which is two decisions and needs both of them.
uniformSize true is the first: one font size for the whole block,
so a line is however long its words make it. Every other channel
with a straight right edge gets it the other way, by fitting each
line to the full width at its OWN size — which produces two
straight edges and, with four lines, makes a line's size a function
of how many characters happen to be in it. AT ALL set to the same
width as AND NOBODY comes out two and a half times the height of
it, and the block stops reading as one voice.
align right is the second: with one shared size the short lines are
genuinely short, and this is what says which end they are short
AT. The right-hand margin, because that margin is the frame's own
edge — a real straight edge on screen, where the left of the block
is only an edge the eye infers from whichever line is longest.
maxBlockHeightRatio 0.6 — three fifths of the frame, against the
0.8 every other channel takes. Four lines at four fifths is a wall
of type from the top of the canvas to the bottom, with the subject
beside it looking like something the type is stacked around. Pulled
in to three fifths, the block reads as a caption standing next to a
person, which is what it is.
_comment_highlight: Highlighting recolours the line and nothing else — no box, no
texture. Yellow against the white, which is the whole of the
difference: with the type set on a backdrop this channel controls,
a box would be a second surface competing with a stage that is
already one.
The shadow is stated rather than inherited, and it is stated as
the same one the unhighlighted lines carry above, to the number.
Every line of this channel's titles lifts off the backdrop the same
way whether it is picked out or not, and the skeleton's own
highlight shadow (a wider, centred, softer one meant to sit under a
filled box) would make a highlighted line sit differently from its
neighbours.

_comment_branding: Title on the RIGHT, and not as a matter of taste: the left half of the
canvas is the subject's and the title cannot be there. `flipText` is
what moves the block across.
`flipImage` is not read here at all. There is no photograph on screen
to mirror, so on this channel the Flip image button means the FIGURE:
it mirrors whichever cut-out subject is selected, on the canvas, one
at a time — which is what a thumbnail carrying three of them needs it
to mean, and what makes it useful for a subject facing off the canvas
instead of into the title.
No dark gradient. It is applied to the photo by the backend, and this
channel does not show the photo — so all it could do is darken pixels
that are thrown away, and darken the cutout's own edge with them.

channels.name: Laugh Society 2
_comment: Laugh Society 1's second look, and the word that matters is SECOND: it
is the same show shot on a different set, not a different show. The
frames are chosen the same way, the person is cut out the same way and
stood in the same half of the canvas, the title is set in the same
face on the same right-hand margin over the same four lines. Anyone
who can use one of these packs can use the other without being told
anything.
Four things are new, and every one of them is something the user can
reach for rather than something the channel simply is:
- two stages instead of one, with a button between them, so a
subject who disappears into the first is not stuck there;
- a second brand mark, the FULL SPECIAL badge, hung off the right
edge opposite the logo;
- the highlight is a spotlight — a warm off-white core falling
away into yellow — rather than a flat yellow;
- the cut-out figures can wear a thin coloured rim light inside their
own edge, blue or gold or none.
Read laugh-society-1 first. Everything this pack restates without
changing is explained there, and it is restated rather than shared
through a preset for one reason: these are two brands that currently
agree, not one brand written twice. A preset would make every future
change to either of them a change to both, and the whole point of a
second channel is that it is allowed to move.
_comment_selection: Laugh Society 1's, for its reasons exactly: one performer in one
unchanging setup is the footage the colour histogram cannot read, and
the face descriptor is what separates two expressions of the same
person. That pack argues it at length, with the numbers.
_comment_cleanup: Laugh Society 1's, for its reasons exactly: this channel composites a
cut-out person on a backdrop of its own, so the overlay and subtitle
inpainters have nothing to gain on it and a performer to lose. That
pack argues it at length, with the numbers.
_comment_framing: Laugh Society 1's, unchanged, and it has to be: `framing` is the one
key read before the frames exist (see the note in that pack and in
js/channels.js), so it is what decides whether there is a standing
figure in the shot to cut out at all. A medium shot with the subject
centred, no text zone demanded, and the clear-space criterion switched
off because this channel deletes the photograph it would have measured.

_comment_faceFill: The scorer normally penalises a frame whose face would fill much
more of the CROP than the ratio above intends, because on a channel
that composites the photograph an inherently close shot really is a
worse thumbnail — it blows past the target with no way to zoom out.
This channel never shows the crop. The subject is cut out of the
whole photo and rescaled onto a backdrop of its own, so a close shot
is not a composition failure here — it is more pixels on the only
part of the frame that survives. The penalty is multiplicative and
reaches zero, so it does not demote those frames, it deletes them.
Measured on a stage set with two camera positions: with the penalty
on, the sharpest frames of two of the five character clusters scored
0.000 and the grid came out with 7 of its 20 thumbnails below the
sharpness floor — soft, motion-blurred, eyes unreadable. With it off,
2 of 20, and the median sharpness rose from 49 to 59.

_comment_background: Two stages, and which one a given thumbnail is shot on is the user's,
one frame at a time, from the Change background button (see
editor.cycleBackground). The pack owns the set; the button walks it and
wraps, so on a two-entry list the second click is the way back.
This is the one place this channel disagrees with Laugh Society 1,
which states flatly that a channel whose backdrop changed per video
would not read as one channel. That still holds, and it is why there
are two here and not twenty: two sets are a venue with two rooms, which
is a thing a real show has. What the choice is FOR is contrast — a
subject in a dark jacket vanishes into one of these and reads cleanly
on the other, and no amount of care over the cutout fixes that.
Stage 2 is listed first, so it is the one a frame arrives on.
Both files are 1672x941 and 1672x940 — 16:9 to within a pixel — and are
drawn to cover the canvas, so in practice nothing is cropped from
either and the two crops match each other.
_comment_scrim: A shade thrown up from the bottom edge, over the backdrop AND over
the figures standing on it.
Over the figures is the whole of it. A gradient painted into the
backdrop, or drawn under the subject, leaves them lit from the
ankles up and floating an inch off the stage — the plate goes dark
and the person does not. The same shade falling ACROSS their legs
is what makes the two read as one photograph taken in one light.
Bottom to top, because that is the direction it is thrown in: it is
the floor going dark under them, not a vignette. `at` runs 0 at the
canvas floor to 1 at the top of the scrim's own span, so the stops
read in the order the eye travels.
0.6 of the canvas, which is as far up as it can go before it starts
eating the curtain the stage is recognisable by. It ends on a fully
transparent stop rather than on an opacity of its own, so there is
no line anywhere across the picture where the scrim stops.
Under the brand marks and the title, which are the two things that
have to stay legible whatever is behind them: a scrim over the logo
is a dimmed logo, and over the type it is the drop shadow the type
already carries, laid on twice.
_comment_stamp: Two marks, in opposite corners, and they are two different kinds of
thing wearing the same mechanism.
The logo is Laugh Society 1's, to the pixel: 10px from the top and 10px
from the left, at the file's own size. Exact numbers rather than
ratios, because a lock-up is a measurement.
The FULL SPECIAL badge is the other half of the lock-up, and it is
anchored to the RIGHT edge — `right: 0` puts the end of the image on
the frame's own edge. Stated as a right inset and not as a computed
`left` on purpose: the badge has to stay against that edge whatever the
artwork turns out to measure, and a `left` worked out by hand from
today's file is a number that quietly stops being true the first time
the badge is re-exported a few pixels wider. compose.addStamp does the
arithmetic from the width it actually draws.
`right: 0` and not a 10px inset to match the logo, because the file is
not tight: the artwork is 2124x740 with the yellow ticket sitting
inside about 87% of that width and starting some way down from the top.
The transparent margin the badge was exported with IS its inset, and
adding another one on top would push it visibly further in than the
logo on the other side.
width 400 sizes it against the reference thumbnails: at that width the
visible ticket comes out about 350px across and 85px tall on a 1280x720
canvas — a badge that reads at grid size without competing with the
title under it. `top: 10` is the logo's own inset, said again, so both
marks are hung from the same line even though only one of them starts
its ink there.
The shadow is strong on purpose and stronger than anything else in this
pack: 8px of throw where the type and the figure take 6. It is the
largest solid shape on the canvas, it is a flat yellow slab, and it is
sitting over a lit stage with bright curtain behind it — at this size a
shadow that merely separates it reads as a printing artefact, and one
that lifts it reads as a sticker somebody put there, which is what a
ticket stub is. Like the cutout's, it follows the image's ALPHA rather
than its bounding box, so what it throws is the torn edge of the ticket
and not the rectangle of the file.
_comment_cutout: Laugh Society 1's placement, restated in full — the left half, standing
on the bottom edge, the same twenty-slot spread of one, two and three
figures, the same arrival gap of two thirds of a figure's own width, and
the same doubled Supermission shadow thrown by the person's own
silhouette. That pack explains every one of these numbers and why it is
the number it is; nothing here disagrees with any of it.
What is new is `glow`: a band of light lying inside the figure's outline
and drawn over them. Blue when a frame arrives, with a button that walks
blue, gold, off and round again (see editor.cycleFigureGlow). It applies
to every figure on the frame at once, which on the two- and three-figure
slots is two or three of them: they are one subject cut from three moments
of the same shot, and lighting them in three colours would make them three
people.
What it is FOR is the one problem this channel has that no other one does.
A cut-out person has a hard edge by construction, and standing on a stage
that was photographed without them, that edge is the single thing saying
they were never there. Light on it does not hide it; it makes it
deliberate.
Two properties define the band, and both were arrived at the hard way.
It never goes OUTSIDE the cutout. This was built the other way twice — a
halo behind the figure, and a stroke around it, the way a layer style does
them — and both times it read as a sticker with a border, because any
colour past the outline is a margin between the person and the stage where
the photograph had none.
And it FADES INWARD: depth measured perpendicular to the outline, full
strength at the pixel touching the cut edge, falling away monotonically
into the body. The brightest pixel is always the one on the edge. A band
of even alpha has a second edge — the inner one — and that second edge is
what reads as drawn rather than as light.
The numbers, as fractions of the figure's own longer side, so the band
holds its proportion at every zoom:
edgeRatio   0.044 — the ramp is 29px long on a figure at its arrival
size, and about 12px of that is visible. Those are
two different numbers and the gap is `edgeFalloff`
doing its job: at a falloff of 5 the last half of
the ramp is below anything a screen can show, so
moving the band 5px further into the person means
lengthening the ramp by nearly 10. Anyone tuning
this by the stated reach alone will be surprised by
how little moves; it is a number to set by looking.
A fraction rather than a pixel count, so those
numbers hold only at the arrival size: the band
keeps its proportion as the figure is zoomed, which
is why every number in this block is a fraction.
edgeAlpha   0.7   — the opacity at the outline, and literally that: the
band is normalised to peak at 1 before the falloff
is applied, so this is not quietly scaled by the
shape of the fade.
edgeFalloff 5     — and it fades hard. Half the strength is gone within
a quarter of the reach and four fifths within half
of it, so the light dies into the shoulder instead
of holding and then trailing off.
The colours are mid-tone on purpose, and this is the one number here that
took a measurement to settle rather than an eye.
Screen adds light, so what a pixel of the photograph comes out as is
d + a(screen(d, s) - d), and the slope of that against the photograph's own
value is exactly 1 - a*s/255. In plain terms: the BRIGHTER the glow
colour, the less of the picture underneath survives it — per channel, and
regardless of the blend being screen at all. A channel at 255 is the worst
case and it is absolute: screen(anything, 255) is 255, so that channel of
the photograph is gone.
That is what killed the first pair. #35AFFF is a fine neon blue and its
blue channel is 255, so at 0.7 it kept 57% of the luminance under it and
none of the blue detail at all — hair, fabric and the fold of a sleeve all
flattened into one bright rim. #FFB300 was worse: red at 255, and 50%.
#2E6FA8 and #9C6B26 keep 72% and 69%. They read as a lit edge rather than
as neon, which is the trade being made: under screen, luminosity and the
survival of the photograph are the same dial turned in opposite
directions, and there is no colour that is both. What is NOT the answer is
dropping the opacity instead — that dims the light everywhere rather than
only where it was destroying detail, and 45% of #35AFFF was measured at
73%, no better than this and a good deal fainter.
Blue first because it is the one that works on the most footage: these
stages are warm — hot lights, red curtain, wood — and a cool light is a
colour the backdrop does not already contain, so it separates on every
frame rather than on the ones that happen to be dark. Gold is second
because it does the opposite: it agrees with the stage, and on a subject
already lit warm it reads as the spill off the lamps. Off is third, for
the frames where the subject already separates cleanly and light would be
an effect for its own sake.

_comment_face: Laugh Society 1's, and for its reason: the two channels are one
show and the type they are set in is the first thing that would
give it away if they were not. Rift Bold Italic — the slant is
drawn into the letterforms; see the face pack.
It is the UNHIGHLIGHTED voice here, which is the difference. On
that channel it is the only one.
_comment_shadow: Laugh Society 1's, and for its reasons: this type is set over a lit
stage rather than over a photograph a gradient has already darkened,
so the shadow is the whole of what lifts it. Same geometry as the
one the figure throws, at a higher alpha, because a letter stroke is
thin and a thin shape loses far more of its shadow to its own
antialiased edge than a person does.
_comment_layout: Laugh Society 1's, unchanged: four lines at one shared size, set
hard against the right margin — which is a real edge on screen,
where the left of the block is only one the eye infers from the
longest line — and held to three fifths of the frame so the block
reads as a caption standing beside a person rather than as a wall
the person is stacked against. That pack argues each of these at
length.
_comment_highlight: The one thing about the type that is not Laugh Society 1's.
Still a recolour and still nothing else — no box, no second surface
competing with a stage that is already one — but the picked lines
are filled with a ramp instead of a flat yellow.
It is a SPOTLIGHT: one pale core with the yellow falling away
around it, which is a radial ramp read the way a lamp actually
works rather than the way a gradient tool defaults to.
Both halves of that took a wrong turn first, and both are worth
recording because each looks reasonable in the file and wrong on
the canvas.
The COLOURS were the wrong way round. The ramp used to start at
the yellow and travel out to the pale, which is the negative of a
light: the one point that should be brightest was the only point
that was not. A spotlight is pale in the middle and darker at the
edges, so #fdfce9 is at the centre now and #fff701 is what it
falls away into.
The ORIGIN was on an edge. It sat at [0.5, 1] — the middle of the
block's bottom edge — on the reasoning that a stage is lit from
the footlights, so the light should come from below. That is true
about the stage and false about the type: an origin ON a boundary
has no rings inside the block, only two arcs opening away from it
left and right, so the change reads as happening in two directions
at once. Moved inside the block, at [0.5, 0.38], the rings close
and there is a single bright spot with everything around it darker
— which is the whole of what makes it read as a lamp.
Above the middle rather than at it, because a title is read from
the top and a light that lands slightly high sits where the eye is
already going. 0.38 puts the core across the upper picked line and
the head of the lower one.
A LINEAR ramp was tried and is not this. It changes along one axis
only, so every line gets whichever band its height happens to fall
in — and the gap between two picked lines is wide enough that the
crossover lands in it whatever the stops say. Measured: six
different stop pairs between 0.20 and 0.55 gave the identical
picture, each picked line one flat colour and no transition
anywhere. It also means a title arriving three lines long instead
of four is a different picture, which a spotlight is not.
Mapped across the WHOLE block rather than per line, exactly as the
foil texture is on Best of Supermission and for the same reason:
two highlighted lines are two windows onto one lamp. Per line,
each would carry its own copy of it and the block would band.
The radius is a fraction of the block's LONGER side. Measured
against the longer side and not the height so that a title
arriving three lines long does not tighten the whole light — the
longer side is the one the eye measures the block by and the one
that barely moves when a line is added or lost.
Four stops, not two, and the middle pair is the shape of the
light. 0.22 is how far the core holds before it begins to fall;
0.66 is where it has finished falling. Between them is the
falloff, and its width is what separates a lamp with an edge from
a wash: measured on a four-line title with two lines picked, this
pair gives 19% core, 35% falling and 46% yellow. Two independent
knobs, and worth knowing which is which — WHERE the pair sits
decides how big the lit area is, how far APART they sit decides
how soft its edge is.
A plain two-stop ramp was the first attempt and it never arrived:
on a block this size the far end came out at blue 130 of the 233
it was aimed at, so none of the type was ever actually the second
colour. The whole highlight was one long crossover and the pale
existed only in this file.
#fdfce9 is not white. It is an off-white carrying the ramp's own
yellow, so the brightest point of the light is still the same
light: a core of pure #FFFFFF arrives somewhere the eye can name,
and the picked line stops looking lit and starts looking like two
inks.
Nor is the yellow Laugh Society 1's. That channel picks its lines
out in a flat #fbfb0d, colder and greener; this one falls away
into #fff701, warmer and a shade brighter, because it has
somewhere to fall from and a flat colour does not. The two
channels are one show and they no longer say so through the
highlight — Rift is what they share, and what a picked line DOES
is what tells them apart. Nothing in the code ties the three
values and nothing should; matching them again is a hand edit.
The FACE changes too, which is the other half of what a picked
line does here. The block is set in Rift, which is slanted; a
picked line is set in Sharp Grotesk Bold 20, which is upright.
Not a second weight of the same family and not the same face
recoloured — a different voice, so the line reads as somebody
else speaking rather than as the same voice under a light.
Upright against slanted, and that way round on purpose: the
slant is the channel's running voice and the picked line is what
it stops on, so the picked line is the one that stands still.
Everything about that line is measured in ITS face — the width
fit, the ink bounds, the cap band — because two faces on one
block means two sets of metrics, and a line laid out against the
wrong one is the failure the font guard exists to catch, only
self-inflicted. See `styleFor` in js/text.js.
One consequence worth stating, because it is visible and is not a
bug: the block is set at ONE size (`uniformSize`), taken from
whichever line needs the smallest one to reach the width. A
picked line is measured in Sharp Grotesk, so it is that face's
widths that decide the shared size whenever the picked line is
the widest — and the whole block, Rift lines included, follows
it. That is what one size for the block means; the alternative
is two sizes and a title that no longer reads as one.
This is not a switch. There is no button and no default to be off:
the ramp is what this channel's highlight IS, in the way the flat
yellow is what the other one's is, and a highlight that could be
turned back into a flat colour would just be two channels wearing
one pack.
The shadow is stated rather than inherited, and stated as the same
one the unhighlighted lines carry above, to the number — so every
line lifts off the backdrop the same way whether it is picked out
or not. The skeleton's own highlight shadow is a wider, softer,
centred one meant to sit under a filled box, and it would make a
highlighted line sit at a different depth from its neighbours.

_comment_branding: Laugh Society 1's, with one difference. The title is on the right because
the left half of the canvas is the subject's; `flipImage` is not read on a
channel with no photograph on screen, so the Flip image button mirrors
whichever FIGURE is selected instead, one at a time.
`gradient` is true, and on this channel it means the scrim above rather
than the backend's dark gradient. Laugh Society 1 sets it false and says
why: that gradient is applied to the photo, and a channel that never draws
the photo has nothing for it to darken — which also left its Gradient
button doing nothing at all. Here the same button switches the scrim, so
one control still means one thing, and it arrives on because the shade is
part of how this channel looks rather than an effect to go and find.

channels.name: Laugh Society
_comment_id: The folder is `laugh-society-snapchat` and the name is plain 'Laugh
Society', and the two disagreeing is deliberate. The name is the
brand and is what this show is actually called. The id is a key on a
filesystem, and there are already two folders under the Binge heading
beginning laugh-society- that are a DIFFERENT show with a similar
name: one more of them would read as its third look, which is exactly
the thing somebody would edit by mistake. The heading it belongs to
is the one fact that separates them, so the id says it.
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, and the same kind of thing
every one of them is: the heading names the network these frames are
cut FOR and the channel is the show they are cut from, so another
show cutting for the same network is one more folder under it rather
than a heading of its own.
Like all of its neighbours it is a frame fetcher rather than a
thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of vertical
stills comes out, each carrying the sentence that was being said at
the moment it was cut from.
It follows Hall of Femme, which is the pack to read first: the frame
fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the block
at the foot of the frame and every number in that block are that
pack's, stated here in the same numbers. The prose below points at it
wherever the reasoning is the same, and states its own only where
this pack actually decides something.
It decides three things, and all three are about the words. There is
NO CARD - the type is set straight onto the photograph, which no
other pack under this heading does. It is set in Open Sans with a
picked word in Garet, which is a change of face and a change of
COLOUR at once. And the shade that holds it legible is the channel's
own, laid over the bottom third of the picture.
_comment_capture: The same frame fetch every channel under this heading runs, stated in
the same numbers, because it is the same job: the slider opening at
forty and running to two hundred, delivered at the 540x960 vertical
full-screen frame Snapchat is cut for, transcribed, and rewritten
from speech into reported information before anything is set.
What each of these keys does, and what the rewrite refuses to do, is
written out at length in content/README.md, and pointed at from
hall-of-femme/channel.json. Nothing here disagrees with any of it.
`captions` is on: this channel writes on its frames, so the run has
to transcribe the video's voice track for there to be anything to
write - and everything below about the type is about how those words
are set.
_comment_framing: The picture is the product, so it is fitted to the canvas centred and
left alone, exactly as it is on every channel beside this one.
min_text_space is zero because it asks how much room is clear BESIDE
the subject for a title to go in, and this title does not go beside
anybody - it lies across the foot of the picture. No frame should be
rejected for failing to leave a column nothing is ever set in.
_comment_scrim: The one piece of furniture this channel has, and the piece that pays
for everything else about it: a shade thrown up from the bottom edge,
over the photograph, reaching a third of the way up the frame.
Every other pack under this heading sets its caption on a solid card,
and the card is what makes the type legible over a photograph nobody
chose the contrast of. This one has no card. Take the shade away and
the same white letters are laid straight onto whatever the still
happens to contain - a blown-out sky, a white shirt, a strip light -
and a drop shadow does not save them, because a shadow separates type
from a background it already contrasts with rather than creating the
contrast. The shade is what creates it, and it does so without
putting a shape between the viewer and the picture: it darkens the
photograph rather than covering it, which is the whole difference
between this look and the card.
A THIRD of the frame, and it is measured rather than chosen. The
block stands 120px off the foot of a 960-tall frame, and a full four
lines of 40px type with the renderer's own 10px between them is 190px
tall, so the top of the longest caption this channel can produce
lands at 310px - just inside the 320px the scrim reaches. Every
caption is therefore covered end to end, and a shorter one is covered
with room to spare. Less than a third and a four-line caption has its
first line hanging in clear picture; much more and the shade stops
reading as the foot of the frame going dark and starts reading as the
picture having been dimmed.
Bottom to top, because that is the direction it is thrown in. `at`
runs 0 at the canvas floor to 1 at the top of the scrim's own span,
so the stops read in the order the eye travels. There is no way to
aim it at an angle and that is deliberate - see `scrim` in
js/channels.js.
It ends on a fully transparent stop rather than on an opacity of its
own, so there is no line anywhere across the picture where the scrim
stops. The middle stop is what keeps the ramp from being a straight
fade: most of the darkening is spent in the bottom half, where the
type actually is, and the top half is the long tail that hides the
join.
It is drawn on the canvas, under the title and over the photograph -
see compose.addScrim - and it is switched by the Gradient button,
which arrives ON because the shade is part of how this channel looks
rather than an effect to go and find. See `branding` at the foot of
this file for why that button does not also reach the backend.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs cut to Hall of Femme's
design. They set their captions on a coloured slab; this one sets
them on the photograph, under the shade above.
That decides the face. A card is a flat ground somebody chose, and it
is what lets Hall of Femme set a 200-weight hairline at caption size
at all. There is no such ground here: the letters are on a
photograph, darkened but still a photograph, with grain and edges and
detail running through them. What that ground asks for is a face with
solid stems and open counters at 40px, which is what Open Sans is -
a humanist sans drawn to be read small, and the same family two of
its neighbours are already set in.
It also decides the shadow. Hall of Femme states none, because a card
does that job completely and a shadow as well would only smear the
inside of it. Here the shadow is half of what holds the type: the
scrim gives the letters a dark ground to sit on and the shadow gives
them an edge against it, and neither is enough alone on a frame that
happens to be dark already.

_comment_face: Open Sans, in the cut this app carries: `open-sans-italic`, which
is the face Determined and Fight Source are also set in. The
family ships as a set of files each carrying its own full name,
and a channel names the exact cut rather than the family - see
the note in the face pack for why 'Open Sans' on its own is
deliberately not a name anything asks for here.
The slant is drawn into the letterforms and the face is
registered at style normal, which is what `family` and `weight`
between them have to say; there is no third field in the font
shorthand this renderer builds, and inventing one would let the
measurement and the draw come apart. See the face pack, and the
long note in killer-bites/channel.json where the same ground is
covered for a family reached by weight instead.
_comment_uppercase: Off. What the user types is what the canvas sets, capital for
capital, and this is the second pack under the heading to say so
- Killer Bites argues it at length and every word of that
argument holds here.
The short version, because the reasons are this pack's as much as
that one's. The captions arrive from the rewrite rather than from
somebody typing them (see backend/narrator.py), so the casing in
the text box is information produced on purpose, and flattening
it at the draw throws away the more considered of the two. And a
line of capitals is a rectangle where a line of mixed case has
ascenders and descenders sticking out of it - word shape is most
of how a sentence is read at a glance on a phone.
There is a reason of this pack's own on top of those. This is the
only channel here whose type is on the photograph rather than on
a card, and mixed case is what makes that survivable: capitals
are one solid band of ink across the frame, which reads as a
graphic laid on the picture, while a mixed-case line has holes in
it that the picture shows through. The scrim is what makes the
letters legible; the casing is what keeps them from looking
stuck on.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so the text
box held the user's own casing all along and the highlight
buttons already offered the words as the canvas would set them
(see the `cased` note in js/text.js).
_comment_color: Pure white, which is the channel's own answer and therefore what
every frame is set in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame
stores no colour of its own until it is given one, and this is
what it falls back to (see state.textColorFor). It is one of the
three in `colors` below, so the white swatch is the one that
shows as chosen on an untouched frame - the swatch is found by
matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White is the default and not one of the two warm colours for the
reason the scrim exists: the shade is a black one, and white is
what is unambiguously legible on it at every size and over every
photograph underneath. The red and the orange are legible on it
too, and are a swatch away, but a caption whose colour has to be
checked against the frame is not a default.
Pure white rather than an off-white, and it is the one colour
here whose exact value matters. An off-white that reads as white
on a monitor is a grey caption on a phone held next to a bright
still, and there is nothing for a true white to be too harsh
against - it is sitting on a deliberately darkened band.
_comment_shadow: Stated, where every other pack under this heading states null,
and the difference is the card. Those channels put their type on
a solid slab in a colour the user picked, which separates it from
the picture completely and leaves a shadow with nothing to do but
smear the inside of the slab. This channel's type is on the
photograph.
So the shadow is doing the job it was invented for, and it is the
second of the two things holding these letters: the scrim gives
them a dark ground and this gives them an edge against it. Both
are needed. On a still that is already dark the scrim buys
little and the shadow is the whole of the separation; on a bright
one the shadow alone would be a soft grey halo round white
letters on a white wall.
It falls straight down rather than diagonally. A diagonal throw
is a shadow cast by an object standing off a surface, which is
what the cards on the other packs are; these letters are not
standing off anything, and at 40px an offset in both axes reads
as an emboss rather than as depth. Three pixels down and sixteen
of blur is enough to find an edge under every stem without the
blur becoming visible as grey.
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered TWICE - once for
the letters and once for the words picked out of them (see
editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists, so a row of
three is a row of three.
This is the first pack anywhere to state `highlight`, and the
reason it needs it is the reason `colors` in js/channels.js is
worth reading first. On every other palette here the picked words
are a different CUT of the same face in the same colour, so
`text` reaches them too and there is one question. Here the
picked words are a different colour as well as a different face,
and which one is the user's - so there are two questions, and a
pack that states the second list is saying exactly that. Left
unstated, the highlight would follow the block and a picked word
would come out the same white as its neighbours in a face most
people would not notice at a glance.
The same three in both lists, in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is
the PAIRING, and two rows written the same way read as one
palette offered twice rather than as two unrelated sets. What it
is FOR here is one step more literal than usual - the highlight
is meant to be whichever of the three the block is not, so the
second row is the first row asked again.
The two warm colours are the brand and the white is the ground
they are read against. #FF3131 is the hot one and #FF914D the
warm one, and they are far enough apart to be told apart at
caption size on a phone while both being legible on the same dark
band - which is the whole of what this palette asks of a colour,
since either can be the block or the picked word.
Nine combinations, and three of them set a picked word in exactly
the colour of its neighbours, which leaves the change of face as
the only difference. Nothing stops the user choosing one and that
is not an oversight: the two lists are independent because the
pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the three matching
combinations would cost the panel more explaining than a quiet
highlight costs the user, who can see it is quiet and presses
another swatch.
There is no `panel` list, because there is no panel. That row of
buttons is simply not drawn rather than drawn dead - see
editor.paletteOf, which hides a row whose colours would recolour
something the channel never puts on the canvas.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Garet Book, in a colour of its own that
the user chooses from the second row of swatches.
Two changes at once, where every sibling makes one. Those packs
put their captions on a card, and a card is a flat ground where a
change of weight or of slant alone is as loud as anything needs
to be. This one puts them on a photograph under a shade, and a
photograph is busy: a picked word that differs only in the shape
of its letters is a word most viewers will not notice, because
there is grain and edge and detail competing with exactly that
signal. Colour is what carries across a busy ground, and the face
is what makes the change deliberate rather than a recolour
somebody applied.
Garet against Open Sans is a geometric against a humanist - one
built on circles with a single-storey a, the other drawn from
handwriting with a two-storey one. That is a change of VOICE and
not a change of emphasis, which is the right relation here for
Laugh Society 2's reason: the picked word reads as somebody else
speaking rather than as the same voice under a light. It is also
why it is not simply a bolder Open Sans - a weight is the same
voice louder, and on a busy ground it is the change least likely
to survive.
The default is #FF3131 while the block's is white, and the two
differing is the point rather than an accident of listing. The
same colour in both rows would leave a picked word separated by
the face alone on an untouched frame, which is the one case this
channel is careful not to produce - and it would make the second
row of swatches look like a copy of the first rather than a
question with its own answer. Red on white is also the pairing
this show opens on; the other eight are a button away.
Word scope, the same as every neighbour, and for their reason: a
caption's line breaks are wherever the sentence happened to run
out of width, so picking a line out picks out a fragment rather
than a thought. The words are what carry meaning, and the one
worth setting apart - a name, a number, the verb the clip turns
on - sits in the middle of a line as often as it fills one. A row
whose picked words are in another face is built out of runs, each
measured and drawn in its own face at the pen the runs before it
reached (see `runRows` in js/text.js), which is what lets the
face change at a word and costs the kerning across each join.
Mode is colour rather than box, which on this channel is not the
usual argument. Elsewhere it is that the words are already on a
solid ground and there is nothing to box against; here it is that
a box would be the card this channel deliberately does not have,
drawn one word at a time.
The shadow is stated rather than inherited, and stated as the
same one the unhighlighted words carry above, to the number - so
every word lifts off the picture the same way whether it is
picked out or not. The skeleton's own highlight shadow is a
wider, softer, centred one meant to sit under a filled box, and
it would put a picked word at a different depth from the words
either side of it on the same line.
_comment_panel: There is none, and its absence is this channel's whole design -
see `_comment_title` and `_comment_scrim` above. Left out rather
than written as null, because the skeleton's answer is already
null and a key restating it would read as a slab somebody had
switched off rather than as a channel that never had one.
_comment_movable: The block starts at the foot of the frame and the user moves it
from there. Same reasoning as on every channel beside this one:
the bottom of a captured still is only where a caption usually
belongs, and it lands over somebody's face often enough that
being able to drag it clear is part of the job.
One thing is different, and it is worth knowing before dragging
far. On those channels the caption carries its own ground with it
- the card moves where the words move, so a block dragged to the
top of the frame is as legible there as it was at the foot. Here
the ground is the scrim, and the scrim does not move: it is a
shade on the bottom third of the picture, not a shape behind the
type. A block dragged above it keeps its drop shadow and nothing
else. That is a real limit rather than a bug - the drag is there
to clear a face by a line or two, and a caption that has to live
at the top of the frame is a frame this channel is the wrong one
for.

_comment: Hall of Femme's block, stated in its numbers: nearly the full
width, standing on a margin off the bottom edge that clears a
player's own furniture, at a stated 40px so that forty stills
cut from one video are one set rather than forty type sizes.
What each of them is doing there, and what a stated
`fontSize` switches off, is written out in that pack and in
`fontSize` in js/channels.js.
Keeping them unchanged is the point rather than laziness.
This channel differs from its neighbours in how the words are
SET - the face, the colours, the ground under them - and not
in where they sit or how big they are, which are facts about
Snapchat's frame rather than about any show. It is also what
makes the scrim's third of the frame the right third: those
numbers are what the arithmetic in `_comment_scrim` is done
against, so changing one of them means recomputing the shade.
`maxChars` is the second ceiling on where the lines break -
the width asks what the frame holds, this asks what a viewer
reads at a glance, and a line has to be under both. It is the
same twenty every pack under this heading states, and it is
the ceiling that usually binds here: Open Sans's lower-case
is narrower than the capitals most siblings break against, so
twenty characters of it sit well inside the column and
without this the lines would run past thirty.
`freeform` on, and four lines, because a caption is a
sentence rather than three typed beats - it arrives already
broken (see js/caption.js) into one text box the user rewraps
by hand. Four is a count of slots and a freeform channel has
none, so it does nothing here; it is stated because four
lines is what the scrim was measured against.
lineGap is not stated, so the lines are spaced by the
renderer's own 10px (see BASE_TITLE_STYLE in js/channels.js).
On the panelled packs that number has to be read twice over,
because a joined slab changes what it measures between; with
no slab here it is simply the gap between two lines of type,
which is what it says.
maxBlockHeightRatio no longer decides the caption's size, and
no longer pulls a block in either - a size the renderer may
shrink is not a stated size. It is left where every sibling
leaves it, and on this channel it is the one number in the
block genuinely doing nothing: those packs at least spend it
on the card's padding (see BLOCK_BUDGET in js/text.js), and
there is no card here to spend it on.

_comment_branding: `gradient` is true, and on this channel it means the SCRIM above
rather than the backend's dark gradient - the same thing it means on
Laugh Society 2, and the reason the two are one button is that they
are one idea: the shade that holds the title legible. It arrives on
because the shade is part of how this channel looks rather than an
effect to go and find, and the button turns it off for the frame
whose picture is already dark enough to carry white type unaided.
Every other channel under this heading sets `gradient` false, and
each of them says why: the backend's gradient exists to hold a title
legible against the photograph, and their titles are on a slab of
their own. This channel's title IS on the photograph, so it needs
that job doing - and does it itself.
This is also the first pack that both draws the photograph and
states a scrim, and it is what forced state.backendPresentation into
existence. The two gradients are not alike: the backend's is a
full-height ramp down the SIDE the title sits on, put there to clear
a column for a headline beside a subject, and baked into the pixels
it returns. Asked for on top of the scrim it would darken a vertical
still down one edge as well as up from the foot - two shades, in two
directions, for one press of one button. So a channel with a scrim
is now never asked for the backend's; Laugh Society 2 was covered by
accident before, since a channel that never draws the photograph
cannot show what was done to it.

channels.name: Look Rewind
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, and another pack cut to
Hall of Femme's design. The heading names the network these frames
are cut FOR and the channel is the show they are cut from, so another
show cutting for the same network is one more folder under it rather
than a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
Two packs to read before this one, and in this order. Hall of Femme
is the design: the frame fetch, the vertical output, the
transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot of the frame and
every number in that card are its, reached here through the same two
presets it reaches them through. Stars Dans Le Retro is the pack that
already sets a caption in these two faces, and it is where the
argument for pairing them lives - measured, at length, and not
repeated here.
What is left for this pack to decide is therefore small, and it is
the whole of what makes it this show: the face the words are set in,
the face a picked word changes to, and the four colours the two of
them and the card are drawn in.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs beside it, and it is one
sentence long: it is set in Neue Montreal Bold, with picked words in
Anton, on a violet card, in colours the user picks per frame.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame, what a picked word
does - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show.
The pairing of faces is Stars Dans Le Retro's, and its pack is where
the case for it is made: Neue Montreal has a Bold in this app and
nothing else, so the weight highlight the older siblings use is
closed off here, and Anton replaces it with a change of WIDTH -
around a quarter to a third narrower at the 40px the preset sets
every caption at. Three consequences follow from that, and all three
are written out there: a picked word can only ever shorten its own
line, a caption carrying one wears a vertical band about six pixels
taller than the same caption without one, and the highlight survives
only while the block is set in capitals, because Anton is a display
capital with no lower case anybody would call the face.
None of it is restated here. Two packs holding two copies of one
argument is how the copies come to disagree, and the numbers in it
are facts about the two faces rather than about either show.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the four in `colors` below, so
the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame - the swatch is found by matching this value rather than by
being listed first.
White letters on the violet card is the pairing this show opens
on, and it is the strongest of the sixteen: white on #5B12B6 is a
contrast ratio of about 9.5 to 1, the widest gap in this palette
that is not black on white. The violet is the brand, so it is the
CARD - the shape that is a fifth of the frame and reads before
anything on it - and the type is what has to stay legible against
it.
Pure white rather than an off-white, for fitness-story's reason:
there is nothing here for a true white to be too harsh against,
because the card is a flat shape somebody chose and not a
photograph seen through it, and an off-white that reads as white
on a monitor is a grey caption on a phone.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason
hall-of-femme states at length: the point is the PAIRING. Sixteen
combinations of a deep violet, a light violet, a white and a
black, and the ones worth having are the ones that read.
Brand colours first, then the white and the black, which is the
order every palette under this heading is written in. It is a
convention rather than a requirement - no swatch is found by its
position, and what shows as chosen on an untouched frame is
whichever entry matches `color` and `panel.fill` - but two rows
written the same way read as one palette offered twice, which is
what a palette built on the pairing needs them to read as.
This palette is two violets rather than a violet and its opposite,
which is what makes it this show and also what has to be said
plainly. #5B12B6 and #A855F7 are one hue at two brightnesses, so
the pairings that carry are the ones with the white or the black
in them: white on the deep violet is about 9.5 to 1, black on the
light violet about 5.3 to 1, white on the light violet about 4 to
1, and black on the deep violet about 2.2 to 1 - legible at 40px
capitals on a solid card, and not much more than that. The two
violets against EACH OTHER are about 2.4 to 1 either way round,
and that is the one pairing here to treat as an effect rather than
as a caption: it reads as a tone-on-tone card at a glance and the
words arrive second.
It is offered all the same, and the packs beside it are the
precedent. Nothing stops the user setting white on white or black
on black on those either. The two lists are independent because
the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the combinations
somebody should think twice about would cost the panel more
explaining than a quiet caption costs the user, who can see it is
quiet and presses another swatch.
Absolute black and absolute white rather than a soft near-black
and an off-white, and they are the two values here that have to be
exact: the violets are the brand and are ink or card either way
round, and the black and the white are what both of them are
loudest against.
One thing about the deep violet is worth saying out loud so that
nobody later 'corrects' it. Stars Dans Le Retro, the pack this one
shares its two faces with, is built on #5B21B6, and this show's
violet is #5B12B6 - the same six characters with two of them the
other way round, and a colour the eye cannot tell from it: the two
are about 1.06 to 1 apart, which is no difference at all. It is
written here as the show gave it, and every contrast figure above
is computed against THIS value rather than copied from that pack.
