A hex that looks like a slip of the folder next door is exactly
the kind of thing somebody tidies up in passing; it is the brand,
and it stays.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type
is has one answer and not two, and a user who picks black gets a
black caption with black picked words in Anton rather than one
word left behind in white.
_comment_highlight: Word scope, colour mode and what a second face costs are the
preset's - see snapchat-caption.json, which explains all three.
What this pack states is the two things that are its own: the face
a picked word changes to, and the colour it keeps.
The face is Anton, reached through the shared pack in
content/faces/ rather than by a second copy of it - the same face
Stars Dans Le Retro picks its words out in, Conspiracy Central
sets its whole block in, and Karens Unleashed sets its titles in.
Anton and not anton-bold: that pack is the same file asked for at
a weight it does not contain, and a synthetic bold of an already
heavy condensed face is a refinement rather than a highlight - its
own comments say so, and say to reach for it only where the weight
is the third thing that changes. Here the width is doing all of
the work and there is nothing for a stroked outline to add.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws a picked
word in exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is
the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback
reason `color` above is stated - a highlight that changed colour
as well as face would be two signals saying one thing, and this
one is loud enough on the face alone.
The shadow is the preset's, which is null, and the argument for
it is written there rather than here now. It used to be this
pack's to make: the skeleton's highlight shadow is a wide, soft,
centred one meant to sit under a filled box, and it reached every
colour-mode highlight under this heading that did not refuse it by
name. Refusing it is the design and not this show's opinion, so it
is stated once where the design is.
_comment_panel: Violet, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset, which argues
each of them.
The deep violet and not the light one, because the card is the
bigger surface - a fifth of the frame, read before anything set on
it - and the deep one is the brand. It is also the only one of the
two with a comfortable colour to be read against: white on it is
the pairing this show opens on, where the light violet's best ink
is black at about 5.3 to 1.
It is the first entry in `colors.panel` above as well, so the
swatch that shows as chosen on an untouched frame is the one at
the start of the row. Nothing requires that - the swatch is found
by matching this value rather than by being listed first - and the
type's own colour is deliberately NOT first in its row, which is
the same freedom used the other way round.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient, for hall-of-femme's reason: it exists to hold a
title legible against the photograph, and this title is not against
the photograph at all - it is on a card of its own. A scrim over
every still would darken forty pictures to solve a problem the card
has already solved.

channels.name: Noisy Dish
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, built to Hall of Femme's
brief. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's and
is stated in the same two references: the frame fetch, the vertical
output, the transcription, the rewrite, and how the caption is set.
Where it parts company with its neighbours is not the type at all, it
is the PICTURE. Every other channel under this heading delivers the
still edge to edge and puts a card of type on it. This one delivers
the still as a card of its own, lying on a ground the channel paints
- see `photo` below - and then sets the caption in nothing but white
letters, because the picture is now carrying all the graphic the frame
can hold.
Written as its own folder rather than as an override of a sibling, for
the reason content/README.md gives: a channel is a folder that gets
dropped in. The prose below points at hall-of-femme wherever the
reasoning is the same and states its own where this pack decides
something.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into report.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a pack
that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a piece of
it.
_comment_photo: The still, resized and laid on a painted ground. This is the whole of
what makes the channel look like itself, and the three parts of it are
one composition rather than three effects - see `photo` in
js/channels.js for what each key means and why the geometry is stated
the way it is.
85% of the frame, centred. Both dimensions by the same fraction, which
is the only scaling that leaves the picture the picture: the still
arrives already cut to 540x960 (see snapchat-capture), so 0.85 is
459x816 and the crop the backend chose survives it intact. What the
margin is for is the ground: 41px of it down each side and 72px top
and bottom, which is a band of the gradient rather than a field of it
- enough to read as the frame's colour and as a deliberate edge, and
not so much that the still stops being the thing on screen.
13px of corner radius, the same 13 the caption cards elsewhere under
this heading are rounded by (see snapchat-caption). Same reason, too:
a square-cornered picture inset on a coloured ground reads as a
letterbox, something the player did, and a rounded one reads as a
graphic somebody made.
The backdrop runs on the diagonal: crimson in the bottom-left corner,
amber in the top-right. [0,1] to [1,0] is that corner to that corner,
measured across the canvas - the ramp is stated as the two ends of the
line it travels along and nothing about the size of what it crosses,
so it is the same statement whatever the card is sized to.
A diagonal rather than a fall down the frame, and it is what makes the
margin worth having at 85%: a band this narrow crossed by a top-to-
bottom ramp is two flat stripes, one down each side, because the sides
are where nearly all of it is and each side is a single height. Run
corner to corner, every edge of that band travels through the whole
ramp instead, and the frame reads as one field of colour with a
picture lying on it.
The tint is one colour and it is the join between the two halves of
the composition: a brick that is what the crimson and the amber have
in common, laid over the picture so the card looks lit by the ground
it is lying on instead of pasted onto it. Full strength along the
bottom edge of the card and gone by the top, which is the direction
every shade in this app is thrown in (see `scrim`) and the one that
puts the deepest colour where the picture meets the caption. It is a
treatment OF the photograph and is clipped to it, corners included -
that is what `tint` is for and what separates it from a scrim, which
would run out across the ground.
To wash the whole picture evenly instead, give both stops the same
alpha; the direction and the fade are these two stops and nothing
else.
_comment_title: Bebas Neue, white, and nothing else. Every other decision about how a
caption is set under this heading - the size, where the lines break,
the capitals, where the block stands, that the user can drag it off a
face - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
Bebas has no lower case of its own, so the preset's capitals are the
face's own answer rather than a transformation laid over it (see
content/faces/bebas-neue.json).
At the preset's 120px bottom margin the block sits inside the card,
48px up from its bottom edge, and grows upward from there however
long the caption runs. That is the deepest part of the tint, which is
what makes a card of its own unnecessary: the letters are on the one
band of the picture this channel has already painted a known colour,
rather than on an unknown photograph - which is the whole of the
argument the preset makes for a card in the first place.
It is a margin the card can lose, though, and that is worth knowing
before either number is touched. The block is measured off the FRAME
and not off the card, so shrinking the picture moves the card's foot
up while the type stays where it is: at 0.70 the same caption crossed
the bottom edge and stood half in the ground. Nothing breaks when it
does - the amber below is the palest thing in the frame and the type
carries an opaque black shadow - but the two numbers are related and
the relation is not in either of them.

_comment_color: Pure white, on every frame, with no palette offered beside it.
That is a brand decision rather than a missing feature: the
colour in this channel is the ground and the tint, and a second
colour in the type would be a third thing competing with them.
Hall of Femme hands two of its colours to the user because the
PAIRING of card and letters is what that show is; here there is
no card, so there is no pairing to offer.
_comment_shadow: Absolute black, at the app's own shadow geometry, and it is doing
real work rather than decorating. The preset drops the shadow
because its caption sits on a solid card in a colour somebody
picked; this one has no card and stands on the amber foot of the
gradient, so white letters need something under them again.
Opaque rather than the 0.8 black everywhere else in this app: the
ground it has to hold the type against is a bright warm colour of
known contrast, not an unknown photograph, and against amber a
translucent shadow reads as a muddy edge instead of as a shadow.
_comment_panel: None. The preset's card is exactly what this channel does not
have: the still has already been shrunk to make room for a
coloured ground, and a slab of a third colour laid over that
ground would be a background in front of a background.
Stated as null rather than left out, because the preset states
one and a pack that says nothing inherits it whole.
_comment_highlight: None either, and it follows from the two decisions above rather
than being a decision of its own. A highlight under this heading
is one of three things: another colour, another cut of the face,
or a box. The type here is always pure white, so a colour is out;
Bebas Neue ships as a single cut, so a second weight is out; and
a box is a background, which is the one thing this channel does
not have.
The word buttons in the panel stay where they are and go dead,
with a tooltip saying whose decision that was (see
editor.renderWordButtons) - a live button that produced no
visible change would read as the app ignoring the click.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not over the photograph at all - it is
below the card, on the channel's own ground. Left on, the backend
would darken the foot of every still to solve a problem that is not
in the picture, and darken the exact part of it the tint is already
spoken for.

channels.name: Oh My Goal
_comment_group: Another show under the Snapchat heading, and the same kind of thing
every one of them is: the heading names the network these frames are
cut FOR and the channel is the show they are cut from, so another show
cutting for the same network is one more folder under it rather than a
heading of its own.
Like all of its neighbours it is a frame fetcher rather than a
thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of vertical
stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said over it.
It is one of the four packs set in League Spartan, and dr-football-us
is the one to read: this pack's face, its two-question palette and its
absent highlight are all that pack's, argued there at length, and the
argument is about the FACE rather than about either show. Behind that
sits Hall of Femme, whose design all four are cut to - the frame
fetch, the vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the card
at the foot of the frame and every number in it.
What this pack decides is its two colours. Oh My Goal News is the
other half of this brand and decides the same two; the two files sit
next to each other in the list on purpose (see `order`).
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: Set in League Spartan on an electric blue card, in two colours the
user picks per frame. Everything else about how the words are set -
the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the shape of the card,
where it stands on the frame - is the Snapchat caption design and is
stated once, in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
Why League Spartan suits a caption at this size, and why its single
cut leaves this channel with no highlight, is written out in
dr-football-us. Nothing about it is different here.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the two in `colors` below, so
the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame - the swatch is found by matching this value rather than by
being listed first.
Absolute white, and on this card the exact value matters more than
it does anywhere else under this heading. #312ED5 is a strong,
fully saturated blue and it is dark enough to carry white type

Signature, a joined signature hand, with picked words in Syne Bold,

Two of those three follow from each other. Dropping the card is what
takes the caption off a ground somebody chose and puts it on forty
photographs nobody chose the contrast of, which is why `shadow`
comes back below and why `uppercase` and the highlight are worth
reading as decisions about legibility rather than about style.
The third is the face, and it is what the other two are in service
of. A signature hand is a person's handwriting: a card under it
would turn a signature into a label, which is the one thing a
signature must not read as.

_comment_face: Brittany Signature, a joined signature hand and the only cut of
it there is - the whole of what that means for the family name
and for what happens when the file is missing is written out in
content/faces/brittany-signature.json rather than repeated here.
It is the lightest face under this heading by some distance, and
on Hall of Femme that would be the argument FOR a card: a
200-weight hairline over an unknown photograph disappears. The
answer here is not a card but a halo - see `shadow` below, which
is the same problem solved the way a caption on the picture has
to solve it.
_comment_uppercase: Off, and this pack is the second under the Snapchat heading where
it is - Killer Bites is the other, and its note is worth reading
beside this one because the reasons are different.
The preset's argument for capitals is that at 40px with twenty
characters to a line a caption is three short beats rather than a
paragraph, and beats are what capitals are for. That argument is
about grotesques. This face is a signature hand, and a signature
hand has no capitals in the sense the preset means: its letters
are drawn to JOIN, and the joins live in the lower case. Set in
capitals it comes apart into twenty unconnected swash initials -
not a louder version of the same hand but a different and much
harder-to-read object, and the one thing that made it worth
choosing is gone.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so turning
it off changes only what the canvas does: the text box held the
user's own casing all along, and the highlight buttons already
offered the words as the canvas would set them (see the `cased`
note in js/text.js and editor.renderWordButtons).
It reaches the picked words too - `uppercase` is the block's and
there is one of it - so Syne Bold is set in lower case as well.
That is the right answer for the same reason at one remove: what
separates a picked word here is that it is suddenly a typeface
instead of a hand, and it does not need a second difference
stacked on top of it.
_comment_color: The show's purple, and it is what every frame is set in for good
rather than what one opens on: this channel offers no palette
(see `_comment_colors` below), so there is no swatch that could
change it.
It is also the colour of a picked word - see `highlight` - which
makes it the colour of the whole caption. That is the deliberate
half of what makes this show read as handwriting: a signature is
written in one ink, and a caption in two colours would be a
graphic rather than something somebody wrote.
_comment_colors: Absent, deliberately, and worth the note because the pack this
one was cut from is the pack that INTRODUCED the feature, and the
next person to copy this folder will wonder where it went.
Hall of Femme offers four colours for the letters and four for
the card, and the point there is the pairing: what that show is
set in is which of sixteen combinations the user picked, so the
choice is genuinely part of the look. This show has one colour
and no card. `colors.panel` could not be offered even if somebody
wanted it - a palette for a slab needs a slab (see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js) - and `colors.text` with a single
entry in it would be a row containing one button that repaints
the caption the colour it already is.
So the purple is stated as the channel's own answer above and
nothing is handed over. If the show ever gains a second colour
this is two lines and the row appears with it; a palette is for a
channel where the choice is part of the look, and not a way for a
pack to avoid deciding.
_comment_shadow: Back, and this is the one place this pack contradicts a sentence
the preset writes. Every channel under this heading that keeps
its card sets `shadow` to null, on the argument that a drop
shadow is what keeps type legible over a photograph nobody chose
the contrast of and there is no photograph under those letters -
there is a solid card doing the job completely.
The argument is right, and it is exactly why dropping the card
means picking the shadow back up. There IS a photograph under
these letters, on all forty stills, and this is the thinnest face
on the heading set in a dark colour: #431C64 on a night scene, on
dark hair, on a shadow in the corner of a room is a caption
nobody can read at all.
The numbers are NOT the skeleton's, and that is the whole of what
is different here. Every other channel in this app shadows LIGHT
type, so it throws black down and to the right and the dark rim
is what the letters are found against. Black behind dark purple
adds dark to dark: on the frames where the caption is in trouble
it would be invisible in a slightly larger way. What separates
dark ink from a dark picture is light, so the shadow is white.
Centred rather than offset, which is the other consequence of
the colour being inverted. An offset shadow reads as a shadow -
a direction, a light source, something the letters are casting -
and white light falling three pixels down and to the right reads
as a printing misregistration instead. With no offset it is a
halo: the letters lifted off the picture on every side equally,
which is what they need when the picture could be anything.
0.9 and blur 12 rather than something softer and wider. This is a
hairline hand - the strokes are a pixel or two across at the
thinnest, and a faint wide glow behind a stroke that thin is a
smudge the stroke disappears into. It has to be nearly solid and
tight to the letterform to read as an edge rather than as fog.

colour is stated and it is the block's, so the recolour draws
what its neighbours are drawn in and the FACE is the whole of the
difference - with the one change that the two faces here are not
two cuts of a family but two different kinds of writing.

far as anyone scrolling is concerned. Nothing here is slightly
different: a bold grotesque in the middle of a signature hand is
the loudest change two words can make without changing colour,
and it makes it at a glance on a phone.
Colour mode and word scope are the preset's, and the argument for
picking out words rather than lines lives there: a caption's line
breaks are wherever the sentence ran out of width, so picking a

_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, and the fourth cut to Hall
of Femme's design. The heading names the network these frames are cut
FOR and the channel is the show they are cut from, so another show
cutting for the same network is one more folder under it rather than
a heading of its own.
Like every channel under this heading it is a frame fetcher rather
than a thumbnail maker: a video goes in and a numbered grid of
vertical stills comes out, each captioned with what was being said
over it.
Hall of Femme is the pack to read first. The frame fetch, the
vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite, the card at the foot
of the frame and every number in that card are that pack's design,
reached here through the same two presets it reaches them through.
The prose below points at it wherever the reasoning is the same, and
states its own only where this pack actually decides something -
which is the face the words are set in, the face a picked word
changes to, and the four colours they are set in.

the slider's range, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription,
and the rewrite that turns the transcript from speech into reported
information before anything is set.
Stated as a reference and not as numbers, because this channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not - and a
pack that restates a shared answer is a pack that can be missing a
piece of it. That is not hypothetical: channels arrived under this
heading captioning their frames with the transcript as spoken,
because the folder they were copied from predated `rewrite`.
_comment_framing: How the frames are chosen and cropped, from
content/presets/snapchat-framing.json: the picture is the product, so
it is fitted to the canvas centred and left alone, and no frame is
rejected for failing to leave a column beside the subject that this
channel never sets anything in.
_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs beside it, and it is one
sentence long: it is set in Neue Montreal Bold, with picked words in
Anton, on a violet card, in colours the user picks per frame.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
shape of the card, where it stands on the frame, what a picked word
does - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once, in
content/presets/snapchat-caption.json. This pack states only what
makes it this show.
The pairing of faces is what needs arguing, because it is not the
move its siblings make. Hall of Femme and Fitness Story both
highlight by WEIGHT - the two ends of one family's axis, 200 against
800 and 250 against 800, the same letterforms under a different
light. Fight Source and Determined do the same thing across a smaller
gap. Neue Montreal has a Bold in this app and nothing else, so that
route is closed here, and what replaces it suits this show better
anyway: Anton is not a heavier Neue Montreal, it is a condensed
display face, and what changes at a picked word is WIDTH.
Measured rather than asserted, at the 40px the preset sets every
caption at: across a caption's worth of strings Anton runs 26% to 31%
narrower than Neue Montreal Bold. A full line reading THE VERDICT
CAME DOWN is 508px in the block's face and 371px in the highlight's,
and a single word like STARS is 132px against 91px. That is four to
five times the gap Fitness Story's two cuts have, and it is the point
rather than a cost to be minimised: a change nobody can miss at a
glance on a phone is what a highlight is for, and it is one signal
rather than two - the colour does not move (see `highlight` below).
Three consequences follow, and all three are worth knowing before
changing either face.
The first is free, and it is the direction that costs nothing. A
picked word can only make its line SHORTER, never longer, so it can
never push a line past the width and force the caption to rewrap
around the word being emphasised. The box behind that line is cut to
its own line's width (see `panel.scope` in the preset), so it steps in
by roughly what the word gave back - visibly here, where on the
sibling packs it is a few pixels. A background that steps in and out
with the sentence is what this design already is; this makes it do so
more.
The second is a real difference between two frames of the same run,
and it is accepted rather than unnoticed. Anton's capitals are taller
than Neue Montreal's at the same size - a cap height of 0.859 em
against 0.715, so 34px against 29px at 40px type. Every box in a block
takes one shared vertical band, and that band is the union of what
every row needs measured in the face each run is actually drawn in
(see computeLayout in js/text.js), so nothing is clipped and the boxes
stay one height as they must. What it means is that a caption with a
picked word in it wears a band about six pixels taller than the same
caption without one. The block stands on the bottom margin and grows
upward, so the card's foot does not move and its head does. That is a
difference a viewer scrolling a grid will not see and somebody
comparing two stills side by side will, which is the right way round.
The third is the one to argue with. Anton has no lower case anybody
would call the face - it is a display capital, drawn to be set large -
and it is usable at caption size here only because the preset sets the
whole block in capitals. A pack under this heading that ever turned
`uppercase` off, as Killer Bites does, could not keep this highlight.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the four in `colors` below, so
the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame - the swatch is found by matching this value rather than by
being listed first.
White letters on the violet card is the pairing this show opens
on, and it is the strongest of the sixteen: white on #5B21B6 is a
contrast ratio of about 9 to 1, the widest gap in this palette
that is not black on white. The violet is the brand, so it is the
CARD - the shape that is a fifth of the frame and reads before
anything on it - and the type is what has to stay legible against
it.
Pure white rather than an off-white, for fitness-story's reason:
there is nothing here for a true white to be too harsh against,
because the card is a flat shape somebody chose and not a
photograph seen through it, and an off-white that reads as white
on a monitor is a grey caption on a phone.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason
hall-of-femme states at length: the point is the PAIRING. Sixteen
combinations of a deep violet, a light violet, a white and a
black, and the ones worth having are the ones that read.
This palette is two violets rather than a violet and its opposite,
which is what makes it this show and also what has to be said
plainly. #5B21B6 and #A855F7 are one hue at two brightnesses, so
the pairings that carry are the ones with the white or the black
in them: white on the deep violet is about 9 to 1, black on the
light violet about 5 to 1, white on the light violet about 4 to 1,
and black on the deep violet about 2.3 to 1 - legible at 40px
capitals on a solid card, and not much more than that. The two
violets against EACH OTHER are about 2.3 to 1 either way round,
and that is the one pairing here to treat as an effect rather than
as a caption: it reads as a tone-on-tone card at a glance and the
words arrive second.
It is offered all the same, and the packs beside it are the
precedent. Nothing stops the user setting white on white or black
on black on those either. The two lists are independent because
the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the combinations
somebody should think twice about would cost the panel more
explaining than a quiet caption costs the user, who can see it is
quiet and presses another swatch.
Absolute black and absolute white rather than a soft near-black
and an off-white, and they are the two values here that have to be
exact: the violets are the brand and are ink or card either way
round, and the black and the white are what both of them are
loudest against.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type
is has one answer and not two, and a user who picks black gets a
black caption with black picked words in Anton rather than one
word left behind in white.

_comment_shadow: No drop shadow on the type. The slab under it is opaque and the
glow under that is what lifts the whole thing off the photo, so a
shadow would only be a smudge inside an object that already has an
edge of its own.
_comment_layout: The one channel that is NOT justified. Every other channel fits
each line to the full width at its own size, so the block comes out
with two straight edges; here the whole block is set at one size
and a short line is allowed to be short, centred over the lines
around it.
The slab is what makes the difference. Justified, it is a plain
rectangle and the type inside it has to be resized line by line to
keep it one; unjustified, the slab takes the shape of the words —
stepping in and out around a short line — and that silhouette is
the thing this channel is recognisable by. It also means the type
keeps one size, so nothing is enlarged for the sake of the edge.
_comment_outline: The keyline between the white letters and the slab. Thin on
purpose — it is there to stop the two reading as one another,
not to be seen as an outline.
_comment_sticker: The second, much wider outline, drawn under the letters and under
their keyline. At 25px it runs into itself between neighbouring
letters and between the lines, so the strokes stop being outlines
and become one solid block with the type cut into it.
The gradient is mapped across that whole block, corner to corner:
bottom-left to top-right, in three bands rather than one even
fade. Red is the block's own colour and holds flat across the
middle 30%; the corners take 35% each, one coming up out of the
pale pink and one dropping into the deep red. Keeping a flat band
in the middle at all is the point — a wash between the same three
colours over the whole run would leave no field of red anywhere,
only a different colour in every letter.
_comment_glow: Built the way the Karens halo is — the shape drawn again underneath
and blurred, stacked three times so the falloff stays soft while
the core gains body — but written out here rather than taken from
the `karen-glow` preset.
It started as that preset with overrides, and the overrides ate it:
different colour, different opacity, different radius, with only
the layer count left in common. A preset is for one design two
channels share, and this is no longer that design — sharing it
would only mean each channel's halo could be changed by an edit
aimed at the other one. Karens keeps the preset untouched.
The radius is 15 against Karens' 55, and the gap is not as wide as
it looks: this halo is thrown by the SLAB and not by the letters
(what the renderer does wherever a sticker exists, since the slab
is the shape on screen and so the shape the light comes off), so it
starts from a shape 25px larger in every direction. It is meant to
read as light coming off the block, not as weather around it — the
block already has an edge of its own, and all this has to do is put
it in front of the photo rather than printed on it.
The number that was actually chosen is the REACH: 19px of visible
light past the slab, which 15 happens to produce. Radius is not a
good handle on this halo, because `layers` stacks three passes at
full opacity and each one re-darkens the faint outer edge of the
one below into visibility — so the light carries about a quarter
further than the radius alone suggests, and halving the radius does
not halve what anyone sees. Anything that changes `layers` or
`opacity` changes the reach too, and the reach is the thing this
channel was tuned by.
_comment_highlight: This channel has no highlight feature. Every line gets the same
treatment — white on the one slab — and there is nothing a
highlighted line could be that would not just look like a mistake
in the block. `null` says so outright, and the Highlight Line
buttons go dead for it rather than doing nothing visible.

_comment_branding: Title left, subject right — what the automatic framing already
produces, so neither flip is needed.
No dark gradient behind the title, which is the one place this channel
departs from the default. The gradient exists to hold white type off a
bright photo; here the type is on an opaque slab that does that job
completely, so all a gradient would add is a dark smear across the
photo beside it. Per frame it is still a button away.

_comment_layout: Every line spans the same width, the font size compensating for
how many characters it has — the block reads as one justified slab
with both edges flush, which is this channel's look.

_comment_face: New Order Medium. A wide geometric with a circular O and a W a

It costs the line what it gains in the letterform, and the number
is worth knowing before the preset's maxChars is ever touched: its
capitals average 0.620em, so twenty of them at the preset's 40px
are 496px against the 486px the block is given. A twenty-character
line of solid capitals would therefore be the one width this face
cannot hold - it does not happen because real lines carry spaces,
which are narrower than the average capital and pull a full line
back to around 450px, but the margin is thin enough that raising
maxChars here would break lines the width has to break again.

that possible - the same argument Hall of Femme makes for being

show opened on absolute white, as the brand stated it, and the
numbers against the card it opens on are unusual enough to be
worth keeping written down: #FFFFFF on #F9F268 is a contrast ratio
of 1.17:1, and at that ratio the letters are not faint, they are

note below), so that opening pairing was two of them, and the

_comment_colors: The five colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - five buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). The same five in both lists,
deliberately, and for Hall of Femme's reason: what the show is set
in is the PAIRING, so what is offered is twenty-five combinations
rather than five cards.
The five are not five equals, though, and this is the one thing to
know before reading the row as a palette. One of them is absolute
black and the other four are light - a white, a butter yellow at
0.85 luminance, a lilac at 0.55 and a mint at 0.74. Contrast runs
across that line and nowhere else. Black against the four lights is
21.00, 17.93, 12.04 and 15.89 to one; every pairing of two lights is
between 1.13 and 1.74, which is a caption nobody can read at arm's
length or at any other length.
So eight of the twenty-five combinations are captions and the rest
are a card with something on it. That is stated rather than designed
around: the two lists stay independent, as they are on every pack
under this heading, because the pairing is the feature and a rule
barring the seventeen would cost the panel more explaining than an
unreadable caption costs the user, who can see it is unreadable and
presses another swatch. Hall of Femme makes the same argument about
the four ways of setting a colour on itself; here it simply covers
more of the grid.

happens to open each row on that row's default - white first for the
letters - except the card's, whose #F9F268 is third; the two rows
are written identically and the chosen swatch is found by matching,
so neither position means anything (see `panel` below).
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on

FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type is has one

_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Mongoose Bold, in the same colour as the
rest of the block. The highlight here is WIDTH: an ultra condensed
bold inside a wide geometric medium, which on one line is as loud as
a box would be and leaves the card one clean shape instead of a
shape with a second shape inside it.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - and moved to black with it, since a highlight
that changed colour as well as face would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives. What is this
channel's own is how FAR apart the two faces are, and it has three
consequences the pack should own rather than discover:
A picked word is about 48% of the width the same word would be in
the block's face - 0.300em of capital against 0.620em. That is the
effect, and it is also why the card moves: the panel is drawn one
box per line, cut to each line's own measured width (see
`panel.scope` in the preset), so picking two words out of a line
visibly pulls that line's box in. On a joined panel the shape steps
further in and out with the sentence than it does on any sibling.
A picked word is also slightly SHORTER. Mongoose's capitals stand at
0.680em against New Order's 0.733, so at the one stated size of 40px
the picked run is around 7% lower than the capitals either side of
it, sitting on the same baseline. Between two faces this unlike,
that reads as the second voice it is meant to be rather than as a
size that slipped - and it is not adjustable in any case: a block
takes one size, and the renderer has no per-highlight size to give
(see `highlight.face` in content/README.md).
And two picked words in a row are set tight. Neighbouring picked
words are ONE run with the space between them inside it (see
treatmentRuns in js/text.js), so that space is Mongoose's own
0.080em - 3.2px at 40px, against the 10px the block's face sets. It
is the condensed face's own spacing and it is right for the
condensed face; it simply means a picked phrase reads as one word
more than a picked word does. The space on either side of a run
belongs to the unpicked side and is the block's, so a single picked
word keeps its ordinary word spaces.

_comment_face: Proxima Nova Bold. Which cut that is, why the full name rather
than 'Proxima Nova' is declared, and what the machine may already
know it by are written out in
content/faces/proxima-nova-bold.json rather than repeated here;
what capitals at the preset's 40px cost this face, which is
nothing, is written out in beauty-hacks.
The Bold and not the Black, so that a picked word has the heavier
cut to climb into - the argument, and what this pack did before
it, are in beauty-hacks with the measurements.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is the first of the four in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - though nothing requires that, and the swatch is
found by matching this value rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the red card is the pairing this show opens on,
and it is the soundest pairing in the palette as well as the brand
one: white on #C50000 is 6.2 to 1, which is past the threshold for
type of any size and not merely for type this big. Black on the
same card is 3.4 to 1 - still sound for a 700-weight grotesque at
40px, which is the case the 3:1 large-text threshold exists to
describe, but the thinner of the two neutrals here, and that is
the other way round from the magenta-carded packs under this
heading, where it is the white that is the thin one.
_comment_colors: The four colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - four buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same four in both lists, which is what every pack under this
heading that offers a palette does and for their reason: the point
is the PAIRING. Sixteen combinations of a white, a black, a deep
red and a magenta, and the ones worth having are the ones that
read. A palette that could only ever be used one way round would
be a palette of four cards, and this show's look is the pairing
rather than any one of them.
Written in the order the show states its colours in - the two
neutrals, then the two brand colours - and the two defaults are
picked out of it by value rather than by position: the type opens
on the first entry and the card on the third. That is the freedom
Hall of Femme's note describes, used here to keep both rows in one
order.
#FF00F0 is the fourth entry and it is beauty-hacks' card colour,
which is worth knowing rather than a coincidence: the shows are
neighbours cut to one design, and the palettes overlapping is what
makes them a family instead of four unrelated brands.
The one pairing worth knowing about before somebody reports it is
that magenta on the red card: #FF00F0 on #C50000 is 1.9 to 1 - the
red is a dark magenta and the magenta is a bright one, close
enough in hue that only the value separates them, and at that
distance a caption in one on a card of the other is a caption
nobody can read. It is left available all the same, for the reason
the packs either side give about white on white - the two lists
are independent because the pairing is the feature, and a rule
barring the combinations that fail would cost the panel more
explaining than an invisible caption costs a user who can see it
is invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Proxima Nova Black, in the same colour as
the rest of the block: the highlight is WEIGHT, which is Hall of
Femme's highlight and beauty-hacks' both. That the step climbs -
700 to 900, the way Hall of Femme climbs 200 to 800 - and that a
step this short makes a quiet highlight are measured out in
beauty-hacks, which is where that argument belongs and is not
repeated. This pack ran it the other way round until the seven
shows cut to that design were turned together.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as
weight would be two highlights.
No shadow stated, so the preset's null stands: these letters are
on a solid card in a colour the user picked, and the card casts
the one shadow there is.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
_comment_panel: Deep red, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the
first, which is the same freedom `color` uses at the other end of
the row - the swatch that shows as chosen is found by matching
this value and not by being listed first, so both rows can be
written in the order the show states its colours in while the
channel still opens on white type and a red card.
#C50000 is a true red, which is the far side of the wheel from
the pinks and magentas the packs it was cut from are carded in,
and that is the whole of what makes this show itself at a glance.
The card is the shape that is a fifth of the frame and reads
before anything on it, so it is what carries the colour, and the
type is what has to stay legible against it - which at 6.2 to 1
for the white it opens on it comfortably is, and that is the one
thing this card asks less of its type than the magenta and pink
ones next door do.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
